The day in „am 23. Oktober 1940“; the dot after the numeral makes it an ordinal, read „am dreiundzwanzigsten Oktober“.
Der Fußballer: a man who plays football; a profession stands without an article: „Sein Vater war Fußballer“.
Der Fußball: the game (and its ball); as a game it takes no article: „Fußball spielen“, „jemandem Fußball beibringen“ = to teach somebody football.
Zeitung (newspaper) + s + Papier: the paper of old newspapers as a material, here used to fill the sock.
The Brazilian football club that Pelé joined at fifteen: „zum Verein Santos“, „bei Santos“.
A country in the north of Europe; most country names are neuter and take no article: „in Schweden“, „gegen Schweden“.
A score is written with a colon in German and read „fünf zu zwei“: „Brasilien hat 5:2 gewonnen“ = Brazil won 5–2.
The name of Pelé's father, a footballer, who taught his son the game.
Fußball + spielen written as one noun: a verb used as a noun is neuter and takes a capital letter, „das Fußballspielen“.
Präteritum of üben (to practise), a regular verb: übt, übte, hat geübt; „übte mit einer Socke“ = practised with a sock.
Partizip II of ausstopfen (to stuff, to fill tightly); ge- stands between particle and stem: „mit Zeitungspapier ausgestopft“ = stuffed with newspaper.
Präteritum of unterschreiben (to sign); here unter- does not separate: „unterschrieb bei Santos“ = signed for Santos.
The day in „am 29. Juni 1958“ and „am 29. Dezember 2022“; the dot after the numeral makes it an ordinal, read „am neunundzwanzigsten“.
Der Juni; months are masculine: „am 29. Juni“ = on 29 June.
Welt (world) + Meisterschaft (championship): die Weltmeisterschaft, often shortened to die WM.
Der Spieler, from spielen (to play); the plural has the same form: die Spieler.
Präteritum of stopfen (to stuff). Separable: … aus = ausstopfen, to stuff, to fill out; „stopfte sie mit Zeitungspapier aus“ = stuffed it with newspaper.
Gives the reason for the sentence before it and never stands first: „Einen echten Ball konnte sich seine Familie nämlich nicht leisten“ = for his family could not afford a real ball.
Der Vertrag; „jemanden unter Vertrag nehmen“ = to sign somebody, literally to take him under contract.
Präteritum of berufen (to call up, to appoint): a national team „beruft“ its players; „Brasilien berief ihn“ = Brazil picked him.
Erzielen (to achieve, to score), the formal word of sports reports: „ein Tor erzielen“ = to score a goal; erzielte is the Präteritum, erzielt the Partizip II.
Siebzehn + Jahr + -ig, used as a noun: „als Siebzehnjähriger“ = as a seventeen-year-old, at seventeen.
Das Turnier: a competition of many games with one winner; the stress falls on the second syllable.
A year (neunzehnhundertzweiundsechzig); a year stands without a preposition: „auch 1962 und 1970“ = in 1962 and 1970 as well.
Un- + erreicht (reached): what nobody else has reached; „unerreicht geblieben“ = has remained unmatched.
Zwei + und + achtzig = 82, the units before the tens; „mit zweiundachtzig Jahren“ = at the age of eighty-two.
Leder (leather) + Ball: a compound takes the gender of its last word, so der Lederball.
Partizip II of formen (to shape, to form): „Nicht der Ball hat ihn geformt“ = it was not the ball that shaped him.
A year (neunzehnhundertvierundsiebzig); a year stands without a preposition: „Es ist 1974“, „Aber 1974 haben Väter …“.
Das Gesetz, plural die Gesetze: a rule made by the state; „ein neues Gesetz“ = a new law.
Plural of der Vater: an umlaut and no ending, die Väter; the dative plural adds -n: „den Vätern“ = to the fathers.
A year (neunzehnhundertfünfundneunzig); it can open the sentence, and the verb follows at once: „1995 ist ein Monat …“, „Ab 1995“ = from 1995.
Papa (daddy) + Monat: the everyday name for the month of parental leave that is reserved for the father; a compound takes the gender of its last word, so der Papamonat.
Ehe (marriage) + Mann: the man a woman is married to; „ein Ehemann oder Partner“ = a husband or partner.
Rauchen (to smoke), er/sie/es form; nicht comes after the verb: „Er raucht nicht“ = he does not smoke.
Null Komma fünf: German writes decimals with a comma, not a point; „0,5 Prozent“ = 0.5 per cent.
Partizip II of reservieren (to reserve); verbs in -ieren take no ge-: „hat … reserviert“ = has reserved, „wurde … reserviert“ = was reserved.
Plural of der Termin (appointment); the dative plural adds -n: „zu den Terminen mitgehen“ = to go along to the appointments.
Mit + gehen, a separable verb, written as one word in the infinitive: „Er kann zu den Terminen mitgehen“; in the present it splits: er geht … mit.
german.translation: to go along, to go with someone

german.note: An infinitive used as a noun is neuter and takes a capital: das Rauchen = smoking; „mit dem Rauchen aufhören“ = to stop smoking. With a small letter, rauchen is the verb.
Eltern (parents) + Zeit (time): time off work for a mother or a father after a birth; „Elternzeit nehmen“ = to take parental leave.
Hundertachtzig: „180 bezahlte Tage“ = 180 paid days.
Plural of die Mutter: only the umlaut marks it, there is no ending: die Mütter.
Neunundneunzig Komma fünf: German writes decimals with a comma, not a point; „99,5 Prozent“ = 99.5 per cent.
Der Rauch: what rises from a fire or a cigarette; it stands without an article when smoke in general is meant: „weil Rauch … schädlich sein kann“.
From der Schaden (harm) + -lich; it takes für: „für das Baby schädlich sein“ = to be harmful for the baby.
Plural of die Mahlzeit (meal); each time a baby is fed is a Mahlzeit: „einen Teil der Mahlzeiten übernehmen“ = to do some of the feeds.
Traurig (sad) + -keit makes a feminine noun: die Traurigkeit; „die Traurigkeit der ersten Tage“ = the sadness of the first days.
Präteritum of ersetzen (to replace); the new thing follows durch + accusative: „ersetzte den Mutterschaftsurlaub durch eine Elternzeit“.
Mutterschaft (motherhood) + -s- + Urlaub (leave): leave for the mother only; the compound is masculine like der Urlaub.
Plural of der Elternteil (one parent); „jeder der beiden Elternteile“ = either of the two parents, with the genitive plural after jeder.
Präteritum of verfallen (verfällt, verfiel, ist verfallen): a right that is not used in time is lost; „ein Monat, den der Vater nicht nutzte, verfiel“ = a month the father did not use was lost.
Die Reform: a planned change to a law or a system, with the stress on the second syllable; „vor der Reform“ = before the reform.
Ordinal of fünf; „jeder fünfte“ = every fifth one, that is one in five: „weniger als jeder fünfte“ = fewer than one in five.
Präteritum plural of the strong verb schaffen (schuf, geschaffen), to create: „Raum schaffen“ = to make room. The weak verb schaffen (schaffte) means to manage.
Passiv + Rauch: the smoke that other people breathe in when someone smokes near them; der Passivrauch.
Gedrückt, the Partizip II of drücken (to press), used for feelings: „eine gedrückte Stimmung“ = a low mood, as if something were pressing on it.
Anhalten (to last), er/sie/es form with umlaut, written as one word at the end of a relative clause: „die länger als zwei Wochen anhält“; in a main clause it splits: sie hält … an.
First name of Virginia Woolf (1882–1941), the English writer who gave the Cambridge talks that became Ein Zimmer für sich allein.
Surname of Virginia Woolf, English novelist and essayist; a name, so it takes no article: „Virginia Woolf ist Schriftstellerin“.
Der Abschluss is what you finish a course of study with; „einen Abschluss bekommen“ = to get a degree.
Read neunzehnhundertneunundzwanzig; a year stands alone without „im“: „1929 macht sie … ein Buch“.
Read neunzehnhundertachtundvierzig; „erst 1948“ = not until 1948.
Plural of der Vortrag (a talk given to an audience), with umlaut; -n in the dative plural: „aus ihren Vorträgen“. „Einen Vortrag halten“ = to give a talk.
Die Tür + das Schloss (lock): a compound takes the gender of its last part, so das Türschloss. Das Schloss also means castle.
Newnham College, founded in 1871, one of the two colleges for women at Cambridge in 1928.
Girton College, founded in 1869, the other college for women at Cambridge where Woolf spoke in October 1928.
Der Preis is both a price and a prize; „einen Preis nennen“ = to name a price.
Numbers below a million are written as one word: fünf + hundert = fünfhundert.
Das Pfund is the British pound and an old weight; after a number it stays singular: „fünfhundert Pfund“.
Stören (to disturb) + -ung makes a feminine noun; „ohne Störung“ = without anyone interrupting.
Plural of die Vorlesung, a university lecture; „Vorlesungen besuchen“ = to attend lectures.
Ablegen means to put down or take off, and with Prüfung to take an exam; it is separable: „sie legt die Prüfung ab“.
Die Universität, often shortened to die Uni; nouns in -tät are always feminine.
Der Kern (core) + die Idee: the idea at the heart of something; feminine like die Idee.
Plural of die Erzählung (from erzählen, to tell): a piece of narrative prose, usually shorter than a novel.
The verb nachdenken (to think something over) used as a noun: das Nachdenken; „Zeit zum Nachdenken“ = time to think.
Frei + -heit makes a feminine noun; „die Freiheit, selbst zu denken“ = the freedom to think for yourself.
Plural of der Romanautor (Roman + Autor), someone who writes novels; the masculine plural covers men and women.
Plural of die Zuhörerin, from zuhören (to listen): the women in the audience.
Frauen + Colleges in one compound: das Frauencollege, plural with -s; in 1928 Cambridge had two, Newnham and Girton.
Partizip II of überarbeiten (to revise), an inseparable verb, so no ge-; at the start of the sentence it stands for a whole clause.
Partizip II of erweitern (to expand, make wider), with no ge- because of the prefix er-.
Partizip II of verdichten (to condense); „ist … verdichtet“ is a state passive: it has been compressed and stays so.
Verschaffen, er/sie/es form: to get something for someone, usually something you need; „verschafft Zeit“ = buys time.
Das Privileg, a right that only some people have; „ein Privileg der Reichen“ = a privilege of the rich, with the genitive.
The year the sanatorium opened, said „neunzehnhundertvier“; German gives a year on its own, never „in 1904“.
First name of Maximilian Bircher-Benner (1867–1939), the Zurich doctor who served the first muesli.
Surname of the Swiss doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner; a name, so it takes no article: „Bircher-Benner ist Arzt“.
The largest city in Switzerland; city names take no article: „in Zürich“.
Adjectives made from city names end in -er and never change: „der Zürcher Arzt“ = the Zurich doctor.
Die Haferflocke is almost always used in the plural: „ein Löffel Haferflocken“ = a spoon of oats, with no „von“ after the measure.
Die Speise is a slightly formal word for a dish; you know it from „die Speisekarte“ (the menu).
Swiss German for „die Speise“: „d'“ is the shortened article „die“; Bircher-Benner's own name for his apple dish.
Das Schweizerdeutsch, the German dialects spoken in Switzerland; languages are neuter and need no article after „für“.
Der Zitronensaft = die Zitrone + der Saft; a compound takes the gender of its last part.

Du-imperative of raspeln (to grate), the usual word for grating fruit and vegetables. Separable: … hinein = hineinraspeln, to grate into; „Raspel einen großen Apfel hinein“ = grate a big apple into it.
Forms of roh (uncooked): „aus rohem Apfel“ (dative after aus), „roher Apfel“ and „rohe Nahrung“ without an article.
Die Schale is the skin of a fruit; „mit Schale“ = with the skin on. It can also mean a shallow bowl, which is why the recipe says „Schüssel“.
Das Sanatorium, a clinic where patients stay for rest and diet; plural die Sanatorien.
Takes the genitive: „oberhalb der Stadt“ = above the town, higher up the hill.
Partizip II of raspeln used as an adjective, with the masculine ending -er and no article: „geraspelter roher Apfel“.
Marks a story people tell without vouching for it: „Die Idee stammt angeblich …“ = the idea is said to come …
Die Wanderung, a long walk in the countryside or the mountains; the verb is wandern.
Die Alpen is plural only and always takes the article: „in den Alpen“ (dative), „aus den Alpen“.
Das Müsli, from Swiss German „Müesli“, a small mash; the dish Bircher-Benner served became its model.
Continent names are neuter and take no article: „in ganz Europa“ = all over Europe.
Das Obst is a collective word with no plural: „etwas Obst“ = a little fruit; one piece is „eine Frucht“.
Partizip II of einweichen (to soak) used as an adjective; ge- stands between the particle ein and the stem: ein-ge-weicht.
Der Esslöffel, the spoon you eat soup with; the plural is the same: „drei Esslöffel Wasser“.
Der Joghurt (also das Joghurt in Austria and Switzerland).
A formal preposition with the dative: „samt Schale“ = skin and all.
Partizip II of zuckern (to sugar) used as an adjective: „gezuckerte Kondensmilch“ = sweetened condensed milk.
Die Kondensmilch, milk thickened by cooking, sold in tins; it keeps without a fridge.
Die Tuberkulose, a lung disease that could then pass to people through raw milk.
Bestehen aus + dative = to consist of: „besteht meist aus Haferflocken“ = is mostly oats.
Das Original, the first version of something, as opposed to a copy.
Read achtzehnhundertvier; the year Haiti became independent, given on its own or after a date: „am ersten Januar 1804“.
The country on the western part of the island of Hispaniola, independent since 1804; country names take no article, and the genitive adds -s: „die Unabhängigkeit Haitis“.
Der Haitianer, plural die Haitianer (same form): a person from Haiti; like many nouns in -er, the plural adds nothing.
Haitianisch with the -en ending in the dative plural: „in haitianischen Familien“ = in Haitian families; adjectives of nationality are written in lower case.
The first half of the Haitian name soup joumou, kept as it is, like a proper name; in German it is die Suppe.
Joumou is the Haitian Creole word for the pumpkin; soup joumou is the pumpkin soup Haitians eat on the first of January.
Der Kürbis, so a pumpkin is „er“: „püriere ihn, bis er glatt ist“; after a measure no „of“ is needed: „ein Kilo Kürbis“.
Der Kürbis + die Suppe: a compound takes the gender of its last part, so die Kürbissuppe.
Plural of die Kartoffel; feminine nouns in -el add only -n in the plural.
Plural of die Nudel; German uses the plural for pasta in general: „etwas Nudeln“ = a little pasta.
Die Limette (lime) + der Saft: a compound takes the gender of its last part, so der Limettensaft.
UNESCO + die Liste, joined with a hyphen because the first part is an abbreviation; feminine like die Liste.

Partizip II of versklaven (to enslave), used as an adjective; German says „versklavte Menschen“ (enslaved people) to name what was done to them, and „versklavt worden waren“ is the past perfect passive.
Der Besitzer, plural die Besitzer (same form), from besitzen (to own); „für die französischen Besitzer“ = for the French owners.
Die Plantage + der Besitzer: the compound is masculine like its last part, and the plural has the same form as the singular.
Partizip II of verbieten (to forbid) used as an adjective; „etwas ist verboten“ = something is not allowed.
Das Erbe is what is handed down, an inheritance or heritage; the genitive is des Erbes, and der Erbe (masculine) is the heir.
First name of Jean-Jacques Dessalines (1758–1806), the leader who proclaimed Haiti's independence; the hyphenated name is one word.
Surname of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who declared Haiti independent in Gonaïves on 1 January 1804; a name, so it takes no article.
A town on the west coast of Haiti where independence was declared; town names take no article: „in der Stadt Gonaïves“.
Unabhängig (independent) + -keit makes a feminine noun; „die Unabhängigkeit von Frankreich“ = independence from France.
Die Revolution, like all nouns in -tion feminine and stressed on the last syllable.
Der Liter in the dative plural after in: „in anderthalb Litern Wasser“ = in one and a half litres of water.
Das Rind (cattle) + das Fleisch (meat): German names meat by the animal, as in Schweinefleisch (pork).
Partizip II of the separable verb anführen (to lead), so ge- goes between an and führt; „angeführt von“ = led by.
Partizip II of the separable verb anerkennen (to recognise officially): an + erkannt, with no extra ge- because of the prefix er-; „wurde … anerkannt“ is the passive.
Read fünfhunderttausend; German groups thousands with a full stop where English uses a comma.
Read fünfhundertachtzehntausenddreihundertzweiundsiebzig; the full stop separates the thousands, so 518.372 is more than half a million, not a decimal.
Read hundertvierzigtausend; German writes the thousands point where English writes a comma.
Read achtzehnhundertachtundneunzig; a year alone needs no „im Jahr“: „1898 gibt es …“.
Written „91.“ it is an ordinal: „zum 91. Mal“ is read „zum einundneunzigsten Mal“ = for the 91st time.
„Vom 13. bis 18. Oktober“ is read „vom dreizehnten bis achtzehnten Oktober“: the full stop makes the day an ordinal.
„Am 15. Juni“ is read „am fünfzehnten Juni“; the full stop after the number marks the ordinal.
The French capital; the adjective is „Pariser“ (der Pariser Autosalon).
Words from city names end in -er: as an adjective it never changes (der Pariser Autosalon); as a noun, "die Pariser" are the people of Paris or, in sport, the Paris team.
german.translation: Parisian, of Paris; die Pariser = the Parisians, the Paris team

german.note: The town with the royal palace south-west of Paris, the goal of the 1898 test drive.
French for gate; „Porte de Versailles“ is the exhibition grounds in the south-west of Paris, kept in French in German.
The French word for „of“, here only as part of the name Porte de Versailles.
Der Tuileriengarten, the park beside the Louvre in central Paris; „des Tuileriengartens“ is the genitive.
Auto (car) + Messe (trade fair): die Automesse; compound nouns take the gender of the last part.
Die Messe is a big exhibition where makers show new products; the same word also means a church mass.
Der Autosalon is the usual name of the big car shows in Paris and Geneva.
Der Salon, short here for der Autosalon; the word comes from French.
Auto + Hersteller: der Autohersteller, plural die Autohersteller (no ending added).
Der Hersteller, from herstellen (to make); singular and plural look the same.
Das Elektroauto, plural die Elektroautos; Elektro- in front of a noun means electric.
Plural of das Elektrotaxi; nouns ending in a vowel like Taxi or Auto take -s in the plural.
Elektro- + Version: die Elektroversion, the battery-powered form of an older model.
Der Besucher, plural die Besucher; from besuchen, to visit.
Der Veranstalter, plural unchanged; from veranstalten, to organise an event.
Plural of die Masse; „die Massen anziehen“ = to draw the crowds.
Das Publikum is singular in German even when it means many people: „das Publikum drängte sich“.
Plural of das Modell, a particular type of car from a maker.
Plural of das Fahrzeug (fahren + Zeug): the formal word for anything that drives.
Der Bauer is a weak noun: every form except the nominative singular ends in -n, so „für Bauern“, „zwei Bauern“.
Der Acker is a field for crops; „über einen gepflügten Acker“ takes the accusative because it shows movement across.
Die Terrasse; „auf der Terrasse“ (dative) says where something is.
Der Sommer; „in jenem Sommer“ = that summer, in a story about the past.
Stadt + Verkehr: „für den Stadtverkehr“ = for driving in town.
Plural of die Stadtstraße; compounds take the gender of the last noun, die Straße.
After „sein“ the adjective has no ending: „Die Autos sind elektrisch“; before a noun it declines: elektrische Autos.
Comparative of günstig (inexpensive, good value) with the plural ending -e: „kleine, günstigere Elektroautos“.
Comparative of erschwinglich (affordable), from erschwingen, to manage to pay for; a more formal word than günstiger.
Participle of pflügen (to plough) used as an adjective, with the ending of „einen gepflügten Acker“ (accusative).
Partizip II of ausstellen (to exhibit): „ausgestellt werden“ = to be exhibited; the ge- sits between aus- and -stellt.
„Etwas wieder aufleben lassen“ = to bring something back to life; auf + leben, here an infinitive after „ließen“.
german.translation: to revive, come back to life

german.note: A formal verb for carrying people or goods: „um zwei Bauern … zu befördern“ = in order to carry two farmers.
Partizip II of veranstalten (to organise an event); „wurde … veranstaltet“ is the Präteritum passive = was held.
The day in „der 17. Oktober“; the dot after the numeral makes it an ordinal, read „der siebzehnte Oktober“.
„Bis zur Minute 77“ = until the 77th minute; with the number after Minute, the press reads it as a plain number: siebenundsiebzig.
A score is written with a colon in German and read with zu: „6:1“ = sechs zu eins; „Bayern gewinnt 6:1“ needs no preposition.
Read „drei zu null“; „zur Pause stand es 3:0“ = it was 3–0 at half-time.
Read „drei zu zwei“; „mit 3:2“ = by 3–2, a one-goal win.
Read „eins zu null“; „nach einem 1:0“ = after a 1–0 win, the score standing for the whole game.
Read „drei zu eins“; „3:1 gewinnen“ = to win 3–1.
Read „null zu eins“; said from the trailing team's side, „0:1 im Rückstand“ = 1–0 down.
A hyphen joins the score to the noun: „Arsenal, 1:0-Sieger bei Nottingham Forest“ = Arsenal, 1–0 winners at Nottingham Forest.
The first name of Luis Díaz, the Bayern München forward.
Luis Díaz, the Colombian forward who scored three goals for Bayern München against RB Leipzig on 17 October 2026.
The first name of Aleksandar Pavlović, the Bayern München midfielder.
Aleksandar Pavlović, the Bayern München midfielder who scored against RB Leipzig on 17 October 2026.
The first name of Michael Olise, the Bayern München winger.
Michael Olise, the Bayern München winger who scored against RB Leipzig on 17 October 2026.
The first name of Harry Kane, the Bayern München striker.
Harry Kane, the English striker of Bayern München who scored against RB Leipzig on 17 October 2026.
Short for the club FC Bayern München, which takes a singular verb: „Bayern gewinnt“; as a region, Bayern is the state of Bavaria.
The capital of Bavaria and home of FC Bayern; „Bayern München“ is the club's name in the press.
A noun from München with -er; the press calls Bayern's players „die Münchner“ = the Munich team.
german.translation: the Munich side, people from Munich

german.note: The letters in the club name RB Leipzig, from „RasenBallsport“ (lawn ball sport).
A city in eastern Germany; RB Leipzig is its Bundesliga club, beaten 6:1 in Munich on 17 October 2026.
Part of the name of the Allianz Arena, FC Bayern's stadium in Munich.
Die Arena; „in der Allianz Arena“ = in Bayern's stadium in Munich.
Part of the club name Borussia Dortmund, an old Latin name for Prussia; the press often says just „Dortmund“.
A city in western Germany; here short for its club Borussia Dortmund, level with Bayern on 14 points.
Die Bundesliga: Bund (federation) + Liga (league), the first division of German football.
A city in north-west England; Manchester City is one of its two big clubs.
English for Stadt; part of the club name Manchester City.
A town in eastern England; its club Ipswich Town lost 3:2 at Manchester City on 17 October 2026.
English for Stadt or Kleinstadt; part of the club name Ipswich Town.
The London club Arsenal, „der FC Arsenal“ in German, second in the Premier League after a 1:0 at Nottingham Forest.
A city in the English Midlands; Nottingham Forest is its club.
English for Wald; part of the club name Nottingham Forest.
The club FC Barcelona; the genitive adds -s with no apostrophe: „Barcelonas Saisonstart“ = Barcelona's start to the season.
Spanish for „royal“ (königlich); part of the club name Real Betis.
Real Betis, the club from Seville that lost 5:2 to Barcelona on 17 October 2026.
The Milan club Internazionale, called „Inter“ or „Inter Mailand“ in the German press.
Part of the club name Paris Saint-Germain, after a district west of Paris; one hyphenated word.
The German name of Strasbourg, the French city on the Rhine; city names take no article: „in Straßburg“.
Das Land Spanien; country names like this take no article: „in Spanien“.
Das Land Italien; country names like this take no article: „in Italien“.
Präteritum of besiegen (to defeat), from der Sieg; be- is not separable: „besiegte RB Leipzig 6:1“.
Präteritum of bezwingen (to overcome, beat), a strong verb of written reports: bezwingt, bezwang, hat bezwungen.
Der Dreierpack: three goals by one player in one game; Hattrick, in the strict sense, means three in a row.
german.translation: three goals by one player, hat-trick

german.note: A written synonym of bevor that sends the verb to the end: „ehe die Pariser dreimal trafen“; not to be confused with die Ehe (marriage).
Gleich (same) + auf: two teams with the same number of points are „gleichauf“.
Knapp means tight or narrow; „sich knapp durchsetzen“ = to win narrowly, by one goal.
From kommen (to come); „am kommenden Wochenende“ = next weekend, a little more formal than „nächstes Wochenende“.
Das Ligaspiel, plural die Ligaspiele: Liga (league) + Spiel (game), a game that counts for the table.
Die Pause is any break; in football it is half-time: „zur Pause“ = at half-time, the same as „zur Halbzeit“.
Punkt (point) + gleich (same): „punktgleich mit Borussia Dortmund“ = with the same number of points as Dortmund.
Der Saisonstart: Saison (season) + Start; the last noun gives the gender.
Das Spiel, plural die Spiele: „sieben Spiele, sieben Siege“ = seven games, seven wins.
Die Tordifferenz: goals scored minus goals let in; with equal points, the better Tordifferenz puts a team higher in the table.
Präteritum of treffen (to hit, meet); in football „treffen“ means to score: „traf dreimal“ = scored three times.
Der Treffer, from treffen: a goal in the press; the plural has the same form: „die übrigen Treffer“.
The day in „der 6. Januar“ and „am 6. Januar 1907“; the full stop makes it an ordinal, read „am sechsten Januar“.
The year the first Casa dei Bambini opened in Rome, read neunzehnhundertsieben; a year stands alone, without „im“.
The year Maria Montessori finished her medical studies, read achtzehnhundertsechsundneunzig; „1896 hat sie …“ needs no preposition.
The year Maria Montessori died, read neunzehnhundertzweiundfünfzig: „bis zu ihrem Tod 1952“ = until her death in 1952.
The first name of Maria Montessori (1870–1952), the Italian doctor in this story; A1 to B1 call her by it alone, B2 by her family name.
The family name of Maria Montessori, the doctor whose way of teaching small children is still used in schools around the world.
Das Rom of the story, the Italian capital; city names take no article: „in Rom“, and the genitive is „Roms“.
First word of „San Lorenzo“, Italian for Saint Lawrence: the name of a poor district of Rome.
Second word of „San Lorenzo“, the district of Rome where the first room for children opened in 1907.
Der Stuhl, plural die Stühle: the umlaut ü marks the plural, as in „kleine, leichte Stühle“.
Die Kanne: a jug with a spout for pouring, as in „eine kleine Kanne“ for water.
Der Besen, plural also die Besen: what you sweep the floor with; „einen kleinen Besen“ is the accusative.
Die Möbel is plural in German where English uses one uncountable word: „die schweren Möbel“ = the heavy furniture.
Fegen is regular: „sie fegen“ (present), „sie fegten“ (Präteritum), „haben gefegt“ (Perfekt).
Drei + Jahr + -ig, an adjective with the neuter ending after „ein“: „ein dreijähriges Kind“ = a three-year-old child.
Partizip II of abschließen: „ein Studium abschließen“ = to complete a degree; in the participle, -ge- sits between the particle and the verb.
Das Medizinstudium = die Medizin + das Studium; a compound takes the gender of its last part.
„Ihre Art zu unterrichten“ = her way of teaching: after „Art“ (way, manner) German uses zu + infinitive.
Hoch + heben, a separable verb; after a modal it stays one word at the end: „konnte einen Stuhl hochheben“.
german.translation: to lift up, to pick up

german.note: Sich verbreiten is reflexive: „ihre Methode hat sich weltweit verbreitet“ (Perfekt, as people say it) = her method spread around the world.
Das Mietshaus = die Miete (rent) + das Haus: a building with flats for rent, with the linking -s-.
Fang is the du imperative, without the umlaut of „du fängst“: „Fang mit einer Kanne an“ = start with a jug. Separable: … an = anfangen, to start.
Partizip II of aufmachen, the everyday word for opening a shop or a place: „sie hat einen Raum aufgemacht“; -ge- sits between auf- and -macht.
Partizip II of aussuchen, the spoken word for choosing: „ihre Arbeit selbst ausgesucht“ = chose their work themselves.
Eingießen = to pour a drink into a glass or cup; irregular like gießen: eingießen – goss ein – eingegossen.
Zu-infinitive of sich einmischen: „ohne sich einzumischen“ = without stepping in; in a separable verb „zu“ sits between the particle and the verb.
Sich hinsetzen is reflexive and separable; after a modal it stays one word at the end: „konnte sich hinsetzen, wo es wollte“.
Plural of die Kinderhand (Kind + Hand); „Besen, die in Kinderhände passen“ = brooms that fit a child's hands.
Spoken short form of „kommt es“; „Und jetzt kommt's“ = and here's the thing, a way to announce a surprise.
Partizip II of mitschreiben, to write down what happens while it happens: „sie hat mitgeschrieben“ = she took notes.
Nagelneu (literally nail-new) is the everyday word for brand-new; dative ending after „in einem“: „in einem nagelneuen Mietshaus“.
Der Neubau = neu + der Bau: a building that has just been put up; „in einem Neubau“ (dative).
Spoken short form of herausbringen/hinausbringen; with „lassen“ it means having it done: „hat die Möbel rausbringen lassen“ = had the furniture taken out.
Partizip II of rausräumen (raus = heraus, out + räumen, to clear): „die Möbel rausgeräumt“ = cleared the furniture out.
Partizip II of reinstellen (rein = herein, in + stellen, to put): the spoken pair of rausräumen, out with the old, in with the new.
An adjective used as a noun: der/die Sechsjährige, plural die Sechsjährigen; „die Drei- bis Sechsjährigen“ = the three- to six-year-olds, the hyphen saving one „-jährigen“.
Der Tod; „bis zu ihrem Tod“ = until her death, a common way to say until she died.
Partizip II of weitermachen (weiter + machen): „sie hat weitergemacht“ = she kept at it.
Partizip II of zuschauen (to watch), the everyday twin of zusehen; -ge- sits between zu- and -schaut: „Maria hat nur zugeschaut“.
A year: „neunzehnhunderteinundsiebzig“.
A year from 2000 on is said „zweitausendvierzehn“; a bare year needs no „im“: „bis 2014“ = by 2014.
„Achtzig“; „um mehr als 80 Prozent“ = by more than 80 percent, with „um“ for the size of a change.
Partizip II of abschauen, colloquial for copying what someone else does; with „sich“: „sich die Idee abgeschaut“ = picked up the idea from them.
„Den Anstoß geben“ = to give the push that starts something.
Plural of die Beere (berry); Finland is known for its wild berries.
Das Fett, the fat in food; „fettarm“ = low-fat.
Fett (fat) + arm (poor in): „fettarme Milch“ = low-fat milk.
The country in northern Europe; „im Osten Finnlands“ = in the east of Finland, with the genitive -s.
Partizip II of schmieren, the everyday word for spreading butter: „sich Butter aufs Brot schmieren“.
Partizip II of streichen (to spread, also to paint), an irregular verb: streichen – strich – gestrichen.
Masculine form of herrlich after „ein“: „ein herrlicher Ort“ = a lovely place.
Plural of die Herzkrankheit (Herz = heart + Krankheit = illness); „an Herzkrankheiten sterben“ = to die of heart disease.
Die Hilfe; „um Hilfe bitten“ = to ask for help.
Infinitive after the modal „konnte“, at the end of the clause: „Magermilch kaufen konnte“.
The comparative of „gern“: „lieber Margarine nehmen“ = to prefer margarine, to take margarine instead.
Mager (lean) + Milch: milk with almost all the fat taken out.
Die Margarine: a spread made from plant oils, used on bread instead of butter.
Das Medikament, a medicine you take; the everyday word in German.
Partizip II of the separable verb mitbringen, with -ge- after mit-: „hat … mitgebracht“.
„In den mittleren Jahren“ = in middle age, the years between young and old.
Die Molkerei, where milk is made into butter, cheese and other products; plural Molkereien.
„Nirgendwo … so viele … wie hier“ = nowhere as many as here, i.e. more here than anywhere else.
A region in eastern Finland, on the border with Russia.
The health project started in 1972 in North Karelia, Finland; a hyphen joins a name to a noun.
First name of Pekka Puska, the young Finnish doctor who led the North Karelia Project from 1972.
Surname of Pekka Puska, the Finnish doctor who led the North Karelia Project.
Die Petition, a written request that many people sign.
Der Politiker; the plural has the same form: „die Politiker der Region“.
Die Regierung, the people who run a country; plural Regierungen.
Der Rekord, the highest (or here the worst) number anyone has reached.
„Keine Rolle spielen“ = to play no part, not to matter.
Schrecklich with the ending -en after „einen“: „einen schrecklichen Rekord“.
„In den Sechzigerjahren“ = in the 1960s; dative plural of die Sechzigerjahre.
Du imperative of sprechen: the e turns to i as in „du sprichst“, and -st falls away.
Partizip II of umsteigen (to change trains; here: to switch to), with -ge- after um- and the helper sein: „sind auf Margarine umgestiegen“.
Partizip II of unterschreiben, an inseparable verb, so no ge-: „haben … unterschrieben“.
From verteilen: to hand out, or to spread over a space (über die Stadt verteilt).
Du form of wollen: „Du willst was ändern?“ = want to change something?
Partizip II of the separable verb zusammenarbeiten, with -ge- after zusammen-; „mit … zusammenarbeiten“ = to work with.
A year, read „neunzehnhundertdreiundneunzig“.
„Um 300 vor Christus“ = around 300 BC, when the Guodian slips were written.
„Kapitel 64“ = chapter 64 of the Laozi, where the line about the thousand li is.
„Rund 800“ = about 800, the number of bamboo strips in the tomb.
Die Abschrift: a copy written out by hand; „die älteste Abschrift“ = the oldest copy.
Plural of der Archäologe, a weak noun: every form except the nominative singular ends in -n.
Der Autor: the person who wrote a book; a woman is die Autorin.
Der Bambus: the tall grass with hollow stems; in old China people wrote on thin strips of it.
Compound of Bambus + Streifen (strip); the plural looks like the singular: ein Bambusstreifen, 800 Bambusstreifen.
Superlative of bekannt (known) with a case ending: „seinen bekanntesten Satz“ = its best-known line; „einer der bekanntesten Sätze“ = one of the best-known lines.
The country in East Asia; usually without an article: „in China“.
Another name for the Laozi, the old Chinese book of the Way (Dao); also spelled Tao Te King in German.
„Auf Deutsch“ = in German; the language is written with a capital: das Deutsch.
Spoken short form of „darin“ or „drinnen“: „Drin waren rund 800 Streifen“ = there were about 800 strips in there.
Partizip II of the separable verb einbrechen (to break in), with -ge- after ein- and the Perfekt with sein: „Räuber waren eingebrochen“ = robbers had broken in.
Partizip II of klettern (to climb); movement from one place to another takes sein: „sind in ein Grab geklettert“.
Das Grab, plural die Gräber: a place where someone is buried.
A talk particle that says „that's just how it is“: „Große Dinge bestehen halt aus kleinen“ = big things are just made of small ones; it is not the verb halten.
First name of James Legge, the Scottish scholar who put the Laozi into English in 1891.
A city in Hubei province in central China; the Guodian tomb is near it.
Das Kapitel, plural die Kapitel; „in Kapitel 64“ = in chapter 64, with no article before the number.
Der Kilometer, plural die Kilometer: „ein halber Kilometer“ = half a kilometre.
An old Chinese book of short wise sayings, also called the Daodejing; nobody knows for sure who wrote it.
Surname of James Legge, the Scottish scholar whose English Laozi came out in 1891.
Das Li: an old Chinese measure of distance, about half a kilometre; „tausend Li“ = a thousand li, a very long way.
Die Maßeinheit, compound of Maß (measure) + Einheit (unit): „eine alte Maßeinheit“ = an old unit of measure.
Der Räuber, plural die Räuber (the same form): someone who steals; „Grabräuber“ = tomb robbers.
Die Schrift: written signs on a surface, or a writing system; „mit alter Schrift“ = with old writing.
Die Sprache, plural die Sprachen: „eine Sprache lernen“ = to learn a language.
Der Spross: the first little stem a plant pushes out of the ground.
Inseparable (um- is unstressed): „du umarmst“, „hat umarmt“; „zu dick zum Umarmen“ = too big to hug, with the infinitive as a noun.
The opposite of wichtig (important), with the prefix un-: „das Ziel ist unwichtig“ = the goal doesn't matter.
Compound of zentral + China, the middle part of the country (Hubei, where Jingmen is).
Das Ziel, plural die Ziele: where you want to arrive, in a journey or in life.
Stands alone without a noun (unlike the preposition „vor“): „Räuber waren schon vorher da“ = robbers had been there before (them).
Spoken: „Bei Regen fährt sowieso keiner Rad“ = nobody cycles in the rain anyway.
Partizip II of nachzählen (to count up, to check by counting): nach-ge-zählt.
Spoken: „ewig brauchen“ = to take ages.
Partizip II of wagen: „etwas Neues gewagt“ = tried something bold.
In speech also an intensifier: „sich furchtbar aufregen“ = to get terribly worked up.
Partizip II of sich aufregen (to get worked up): „haben sich aufgeregt“.
Partizip II of schimpfen (to grumble, to scold).
Partizip II of feststecken (to be stuck): fest-ge-steckt; „im Stau festgesteckt“ = stuck in traffic.
Contraction of für + das: „nur fürs Rad“ = only for bikes.
Comparative of schlimm (bad): „nur noch schlimmer“ = only worse.
Partizip II of protestieren; -ieren verbs take no ge-.
Partizip II of vorkommen, with sein: „jemandem sicher vorkommen“ = to seem safe to someone.
Partizip II of sich wohlfühlen (to feel comfortable, at home).
In speech mostly „strange“: „das klingt komisch“ = that sounds odd; it can also mean funny.
Gießen, du/er/sie/es form: „du gießt sie jeden Tag“ = you water them every day.
Partizip II of säen (to sow): „habe Blumen gesät“.
Partizip II of aushalten (to bear): „hat es nicht mehr ausgehalten“ = couldn't take it any more.
Partizip II of blühen: „haben Blumen geblüht“.
Infinitive: „ohne es zu merken“ = without noticing.
Der Gefallen: „jemandem einen Gefallen tun“ = to do someone a favour (the verb gefallen means to please).
Die Ferne: „in die Ferne schauen“ = to look into the distance.
Partizip II of brennen: „seine Augen haben gebrannt“ = his eyes stung.
Partizip II of ausprobieren (to try out); -ieren verbs take no ge-: aus-probiert.
Partizip II of starren: „auf Bildschirme gestarrt“ = stared at screens.
Zu-infinitive of durchziehen (spoken: to see something through, to stick with it): durch-zu-ziehen.
Takes no ending: „eine lila Zwiebel“.
Bunt = colourful, many-coloured: „buntes Gemüse“; as a noun, „alles Bunte“ = anything colourful.
Spoken short form of „darüber“: „Dann kommen Olivenöl und Salz drüber“ = then oil and salt go on top.
Spoken short form of herausholen: „wenn Sie das Blech rausholen“ = when you take the tray out.
Spoken short form of herausziehen (to pull out).
Spoken: „ordentlich Olivenöl“ = a good glug of olive oil; as an adjective it means tidy, proper.
Glänzen, er/sie/es form: „bis jedes Stück schön glänzt“.
Die Neunziger (short for die Neunzigerjahre), plural like Leute: „Anfang der Neunziger“ = in the early nineties.
Rutschen, er/sie/es and man form: „in den Tiefschlaf rutschen“ = to slip into deep sleep.
Partizip II of sich durchkämpfen (to fight your way through): durch-ge-kämpft.
Der Nachtschlaf: Nacht (night) + Schlaf (sleep).
From passen (to fit): „im passenden Alter“ = of the right age.
From dazugehören (to belong, to be part of it); joined at the end of an „obwohl“ clause.
Das Ärmchen, diminutive of der Arm; nouns in -chen are always neuter.
Partizip II of hoffen: „als die Optimisten gehofft hatten“.
Partizip II of einführen (to introduce): ein-ge-führt.
Spoken short form of irgendetwas.
Partizip II of ruhen: „Die Doktorarbeit hat geruht“ = the doctorate was put on hold.
Declined form of normal: „langsame, normale Arbeit“.
Partizip II of bekämpfen (to fight, to combat); be- verbs take no ge-.
A year (zweitausendelf); German says „2011“ or „im Jahr 2011“, never „in 2011“.
Partizip II of vergrößern (to make bigger), from groß; ver- verbs take no ge-.
„Es geht bergauf“ = things are looking up, getting better.
A soft „but“ in speech; it stands inside the clause: „Der Bericht warnt allerdings …“.
From angehen (to tackle a problem); joined here because it ends a „solange“ clause: „solange man die Ursachen nicht angeht“.
Klappen, er/sie/es form; spoken for „to work“: „Das klappt“ = that works.
Das Plastik: the material; „viel Plastik“ = a lot of plastic.
„Die Flüsse spülen Müll ins Meer“ = the rivers wash rubbish into the sea.
Solar + Strom (electricity): power from the sun.
Partizip II of landen, with sein: „ist im Meer gelandet“ = ended up in the sea.
„Das Spannende“ = the exciting thing, the interesting part: an adjective used as a noun.
Spoken short form of „über das“: „übers Wasser gleiten“ = glide over the water; „etwas übers Stillen lernen“ = learn something about breastfeeding.
Lenken, er/sie/es form: „lenkt Flaschen in einen Korb“ = guides bottles into a basket.
„Das Clevere“ = the clever thing about it: an adjective used as a noun.
Zu-infinitive of ausbeißen: „sich an etwas die Zähne ausbeißen“ = to struggle in vain with something too hard.
Partizip II of freigeben: „hat die Pläne für alle freigegeben“ = made the plans available to everyone.
Infinitive of sich herausstellen: „sich als … herausstellen“ = to turn out to be …
Partizip II of vorbeikommen, with sein: vorbei-ge-kommen.
Partizip II of abwägen (words) and abwiegen (flour): „hat ihre Worte abgewogen“ = weighed her words.
Partizip II of zeichnen (to draw): „hat gezeichnet“ = drew.
Partizip II of auffressen: fressen is how animals eat; „hätte die Nachmittage aufgefressen“ = would have swallowed up the afternoons.
Infinitive of aufmachen, everyday for öffnen or eröffnen: „einen zweiten Laden aufmachen“ = open a second shop.
Everyday word for „ganz“ or „vollständig“: „komplett aufgefressen“.
Partizip II of kapieren, a casual word for verstehen: „hat es kapiert“ = finally got it.
From vergrößern (to make bigger).
Lachen, er/sie/es form: „Er sieht sie essen und lacht.“
„Ich bin satt“ = I'm full; „voll“ would sound like drunk or crowded.
Partizip II of hinlegen: hin-ge-legt; „den Löffel hingelegt“ = put the spoon down.
Spoken: „es andersherum probieren“ = try it the other way round.
Partizip II of ausbleiben, with sein: „der Hunger ist ausgeblieben“ = the hunger never came.
Zu-infinitive of hochschauen: „ohne hochzuschauen“ = without looking up.
Ticken: „dein Gehirn tickt langsamer“ = your brain runs at a slower pace (casual).
„zufrieden mit“ + dative = pleased with.
„Das Dumme ist, dass …“ = the annoying thing is that …: an adjective used as a noun.
Partizip II of ablegen (to put down): ab-ge-legt.
Partizip II of melden; „sich melden“ = to get in touch, here: to make itself felt.
Says that something seems clear from what happened.
Tief (deep) + rot (red).
Spoken short form of darauf: „Der Deckel kommt drauf“ = the lid goes on.
Gleich (same) + Zeit (time).
From glänzen (to shine); neuter form: „ein glänzendes Rot“.
Konjunktiv II of kommen: „kein Mensch käme auf die Idee“ = nobody would dream of it.
Du imperative of laufen: „Lauf schneller!“ = run faster.
Partizip II of weglegen: weg-ge-legt.
Partizip II of anrufen: an-ge-rufen; „hat ihren Vater angerufen“.
Der Anruf, from anrufen: „ein Anruf beim Vater“ = a call to her father.
A spoken word for complaining a lot: „Alle jammern, wie kurz das Leben ist.“
„unendlich viel“ = an endless amount.
Gelassen: calm and unbothered; here declined: „seine gelassene Antwort“.
Voll (full) + packen (to pack): „jede Stunde vollpacken“ = cram every hour full.
Anfangen with the particle joined, because it stands at the end of a „bevor“ clause: „bevor dein Leben anfängt“.
„für etwas zuständig sein“ = to be in charge of something.
Possessive of Colette, without an apostrophe: „Colettes Enkel“.
„ein Fenster einschlagen“ = to smash a window.
Mix eggs and liquid quickly with a fork or whisk.
Kalb (calf) + Fleisch (meat).
Der Speck: cured pork belly; Italian pancetta is a kind of Speck.
From die Schrift (writing): „ein schriftliches Rezept“ = a written recipe.
Participle of aufschreiben used as an adjective: „die ersten aufgeschriebenen Rezepte“.
Plural of der Platz; in a race „Plätze verlieren“ = to lose places.
Neun + mal, like zweimal, dreimal.
Partizip II of ausgehen, with sein: „leer ausgehen“ = to come away empty-handed.
Stresses that it was this time of all times: „ausgerechnet bei seinem 250. Grand Prix“.
Partizip II of klappen, spoken for „to work“: „Es hat geklappt“ = it worked.
Infinitive of losfahren, joined at the end of the clause after „musste“.
german.translation: to set off, to drive off

german.note: Partizip II of kämpfen: „hat sich nach vorn gekämpft“ = fought his way forward.
Partizip II of zurückfallen, with sein: „ist auf Rang sechs zurückgefallen“.
Welt (world) + Meister (champion); for a woman Weltmeisterin.
Partizip II of sich ausdenken (to think up): „sich eine Methode ausgedacht“ = came up with a method.
Partizip II of wegbleiben (to stay away), with sein: „die Vögel sind weggeblieben“.
Spoken: „Normalerweise pflanzt man …“ = normally you plant …
Reichen, er/sie/es form: „Ein Stück Erde reicht“ = a patch of ground is enough; „Es reicht, wenn …“ = it's enough if …
Points back to a cause: „Sie wachsen dadurch schneller“ = that's what makes them grow faster.
„Barfuß im Gras“ = barefoot in the grass; it never changes its ending.
Partizip II of auffallen, with sein; the person who notices is in the dative: „Es ist ihr aufgefallen“ = it struck her.
„Mit etwas mithalten können“ = to be able to keep up, to measure up.
Zuschreiben, er/sie/es and man form, joined at the end of a clause: „den man Mark Twain zuschreibt“ = that people put down to Mark Twain.
Only in the idiom „etwas auf Vordermann bringen“ = to get something into shape, to sort it out.
Zu-infinitive of sich aufraffen (to pull yourself together and start), with zu between particle and stem.
Comparative of machbar (doable): „viel machbarer“ = far more manageable.
Before an adjective or adverb it means „surprisingly“: „erstaunlich wenig“ = surprisingly little.
Infinitive of erwähnen: „Kein Geschichtsbuch wird ihn erwähnen“.
„Berufe ohne Zukunft“ = jobs with no future.
Partizip II of mitnehmen (to take along): „hat sie zu Oma mitgenommen“.
Declined form of leise used before a noun: „ein leiser Erfolg“ = a quiet success.
As a noun: „Das Seltsame an so einem Erfolg“ = the strange thing about a success like this.
A numeral + -er makes a decade: „die 1970er Jahre“ = the 1970s (read: neunzehnhundertsiebziger).
„Die meisten Länder jagen keine Wale mehr“ = most countries don't hunt whales any more.
Das Verbot, from verbieten (to forbid): „ein internationales Verbot“ = an international ban.
Comparative of still: „immer stiller“ = quieter and quieter.
Plural of der Walbestand (Wal + Bestand): how many whales there are.
Der Stil; „im großen Stil“ = on a large scale.
Partizip II of zusammenbrechen (to collapse), with sein; ge- sits between particle and stem: zusammen-ge-brochen.
Die Atempause (Atem + Pause): a short rest to catch your breath.
From beeindrucken (to impress): „es ist beeindruckend“ = it's impressive.
Die Größe, from groß: „die Größe dieser Rückkehr“ = the size of this comeback.
Danken, er/sie/es form; the person thanked is dative: „dann dankt dir dein Körper“ = then your body thanks you.
Partizip II of aufbleiben (to stay up), with sein: „sie ist lange aufgeblieben“ = she stayed up late.
Partizip II of achten: „hat darauf geachtet, dass …“ = made sure that …
Die Schlafregel (Schlaf + Regel): the compound takes the gender of its last part, die Regel.
Die Marotte: a harmless little habit people find a bit odd.
Das Amerika, used without an article: „eine Dichterin aus Amerika“.
Superlative of schlimm (bad): „im schlimmsten Sturm“ = in the worst storm.
Infinitive after „kann“: „etwas, das man fast anfassen kann“ = something you can almost touch.
Das Theater; „kein Theater machen“ = not to make a fuss, not to show off.
„Am wenigsten“ = (the) least, superlative of wenig: „wenn man sie am wenigsten spürt“.
Feiern, er/sie/es form: „Niemand feiert“ = nobody celebrates.
Kleben: „er klebt Etiketten auf Gläser“ = he sticks labels on jars; „musste … kleben“ = had to stick.
Widersprechen, er/sie/es form; wider- is not separable: „John widerspricht“ = John disagrees.
Declined participle of vollenden used as an adjective: „seinem letzten vollendeten Roman“ = his last finished novel.
Partizip II of einsperren (to lock up); ge- sits between particle and stem: ein-ge-sperrt.
Das Lob, from loben (to praise): „mit Lob rechnen“ = to expect praise.
Partizip II of hinhalten (to hold out to someone): „hat ihm den Spiegel hingehalten“.
From üben (to practise): „eine geübte Hand“ = a skilled hand.
Erwischen, everyday German for to catch: „er hat ihn erwischt“ = he caught him (also the Partizip II).
Spoken short form of daran; „jetzt ist Singapur dran“ = now it's Singapore's turn.
Partizip II of wegkommen, with sein: „schlecht weggekommen“ = made a bad start, got away slowly.
Partizip II of verfallen, with sein: „der Monat ist verfallen“ = the month was lost (it expired).
Partizip II of schaffen in the sense to create: „Platz geschaffen“ = made room. (Schaffen = to manage takes „geschafft“.)
The verb füttern (to feed) used as a noun, das Füttern: „beim Füttern helfen“ = to help with feeding.
Merken, er/sie/es form and Partizip II; spoken for „to notice“: „wenn etwas nicht stimmt, merkt sie es“.
Zurückhalten, er/sie/es form, joined at the end of a „wann“ clause: „wann sie sich besser zurückhält“ = when she had better hold back.
„Auf etwas aufpassen“ = to look after something, to take care of it; separable: „sie passt auf“.
The verb verdauen (to digest) used as a noun, das Verdauen: „hilft beim Verdauen“ = helps digestion.
Partizip II of sich einreden (to talk yourself into believing): „sich eingeredet, dass …“ = kept telling himself that …
Partizip II of vorschlagen (to suggest); ge- stands between the particle and the stem: vor-ge-schlagen.
Zu-infinitive of fertigwerden: „mit etwas fertigwerden“ = to deal with something, to cope with it.
„Klein und persönlich“ = small and personal; after „ist“ the adjective takes no ending.
Zu-infinitive of ausprobieren, with zu between particle and stem: „um das selbst auszuprobieren“ = to try it for yourself.
Partizip II of mitprägen (to help shape, mit- = along with others): „haben moderne Regierungen mitgeprägt“.
Zumuten, er/sie/es form, joined at the end of a relative clause: „was das Leben einem zumutet“ = what life throws at you.
Anspruchsvoll (demanding, challenging) with the ending -es after „kein“ + neuter noun: „kein anspruchsvolles Buch“.
Partizip II of herauskommen, with sein: „dabei ist die kleinste Zahl herausgekommen“ = the result was the smallest number.
Der Vortag (vor + Tag): „mit dem vom Vortag“ = with the one from the day before.
Der Kreuzkümmel, the spice; „Kreuzkümmelsamen“ are its seeds.
Zu-infinitive of aushalten: „nicht mehr auszuhalten sein“ = to be impossible to resist, to be too much to bear.
Du-imperative of stehlen, with the vowel change e → ie: „Stiehl nicht“ = do not steal.
Infinitive of lügen (to lie, to say what is not true); the noun is die Lüge.
Spoken for being unfaithful: fremd (strange, other) + gehen; separable: „er geht fremd“.
Partizip II of stoßen, with sein in „auf etwas stoßen“ = to come across something: „ist auf ein Buch gestoßen“.
Der Sündenkatalog (Sünden + Katalog): a list of sins, said a little ironically.
Die Hauptidee (Haupt- = main + Idee); a compound takes the gender of its last part.
Der Luxus, no plural in this sense: „ein Luxus für Reiche“ = a luxury for the rich.
At the end of a clause, „hinaus“ is usually the detached half of a separable verb: „läuft auf … hinaus“ (hinauslaufen auf, to come down to).
The number 18 (acht + zehn): „minus achtzehn Grad“ = minus eighteen degrees.
Said before a temperature below zero: „minus achtzehn Grad“.
Der Grad; after a number it stays singular: „achtzehn Grad“ = eighteen degrees.
Plural of die Kopie (copy); here the spare seeds kept in the vault.
Ausfallen, said of power or a machine: „wenn der Strom ausfällt“ = if the power goes off; joined here because „sollte“ sends the infinitive to the end.
Everywhere around something: „der gefrorene Boden ringsum“ = the frozen ground all around.
Partizip II of einschlafen (to fall asleep), with „ge“ between particle and stem; Perfekt with „sein“: „er ist eingeschlafen“.
Die Lampe: any light you switch on indoors.
Partizip II of aufgehen (to rise, of the sun); „ihm ist ein Licht aufgegangen“ = it finally dawned on him.
Streichen: to spread (butter, avocado) on bread; „Streichen Sie …“ is the polite imperative, „es lässt sich streichen“ = it can be spread.
„Lust haben“ = to feel like (doing) something: „Wenn Sie Lust haben“ = if you feel like it.
Löffeln (from der Löffel, spoon): to move or eat with a spoon; „Löffeln Sie …“ is the polite imperative.
Spoken word for „danach“: „hinterher gibt es fast nichts abzuwaschen“ = afterwards there's almost nothing to wash up.
Abwaschen (to do the dishes) as a „zu“-infinitive, with „zu“ inside the separable verb: ab-zu-waschen; „nichts abzuwaschen“ = nothing to wash up.
From sättigen (to fill you up): food that keeps you full: „ein sättigendes Frühstück“.
Partizip II of zumachen, the everyday word for schließen, with „ge“ in the middle: zu-ge-macht; „das Café hat zugemacht“ = the café closed.
Partizip II of vertrauen (to trust), with no „ge“ after the prefix ver-; it takes the dative: „sie hat keiner Waage vertraut“.
Auslaufen: a liquid running out of something; joined here after „kann“: „der Honig kann nicht auslaufen“.
Das Salzwasser (Salz + Wasser): in a recipe, the salted water for cooking pasta.
Durchscheinen (to shine through), joined at the end of a „dass“ clause: „so dünn, dass das Licht durchscheint“.
Spoken: „Riesen-“ (giant) makes a noun bigger: „einen Riesenhunger haben“ = to be starving.
Planen, er/sie/es form: „weil sie niemand plant“ = because nobody plans it.
Partizip II of (sich) ansehen, to take a look at, with „ge“ in the middle: an-ge-sehen; „sie hat sich ihr Essen angesehen“.
Raten (to advise), er/sie/es form with a → ä: „heute rät man …“ = today the advice is …
Partizip II of zusehen (to watch), with „ge“ in the middle: zu-ge-sehen; „zugesehen, wie …“ = watched as …
Not enough or of poor quality: „ihr Essen war zu dürftig“ = their food was too meagre.
Plural of der Franzose, a Frenchman: „für die Franzosen“ = for the French.
Schütten, er/sie/es form. Separable: … hinein = hineinschütten, to pour in; „schüttet kleine Steine hinein“ = pours small stones in.
Partizip II of hineinschütten (to pour in): the -ge- sits between hinein- and -schüttet: „hat kleine Steine hineingeschüttet“.
Partizip II of durchziehen; in everyday speech „etwas durchziehen“ = to see something through to the end: „Sie hat das Abend für Abend durchgezogen“.
german.translation: kept it up, saw it through

german.note: Partizip II of abhören: what a doctor does with a stethoscope; „Die Ärztin hat ihr Herz abgehört“.
Umgehen mit (to deal with, to cope with): infinitive and du form, joined at the end of a clause: „wie du damit umgehst“; in a main clause it splits: „er geht damit um“.
Partizip II of kippen (to tip over), with „sein“: „der Tag ist ins Schlechte gekippt“ = the day tipped into a bad one.
Das Poster, plural Poster; -n is the dative plural after „auf“: „auf Postern“ = on posters.
Partizip II of sich zuwenden (to turn to), with the dative: „hat sich der Lehre des Buddha zugewandt“.
Schattig (shady, giving shade), dative plural ending -en: „von schattigen Bäumen“.
Partizip II of sich drängen (to push, to crowd): „die Autos, um die sich die Leute gedrängt haben“ = the cars people crowded around.
The everyday word for thanks; „vielen Dank“ is a little warmer.
Partizip II of spenden (to donate), with haben: „Sie hat Blut gespendet“ = she gave blood.
Partizip II of hineinlegen (to put in): hinein-ge-legt; „hat einen Stein hineingelegt“ = put a stone in.
Partizip II of daraufstellen (to put on top of it): darauf-ge-stellt.
Partizip II of sitzen: „hat um den Topf gesessen“ = sat around the pot (in the south also „ist gesessen“).
Mostly in „sich nicht beirren lassen“ = not to let yourself be put off.
Partizip II of auftauchen (to turn up), with sein: „ist aufgetaucht“.
Partizip II of mitbekommen, the same as the infinitive: „hat das mitbekommen“ = caught what was said; everyday word for noticing.
Partizip II of mitessen (to eat with the others): mit-ge-gessen; „das ganze Dorf hat mitgegessen“ = the whole village joined in the meal.
From das Misstrauen (mistrust); describes someone who does not quite trust you.
Borrowed from French; in speech it means right away, without being asked twice.
Der Kapitän commands a ship; „ein alter Kapitän“ = an old (sea) captain.
Present tense, plural: „ihre Hände zittern“ = her hands are shaking.
„Wie verrückt“ = like mad: „das Herz hat wie verrückt geklopft“ = her heart was pounding.
Partizip II of klopfen: „an die Tür geklopft“ = knocked on the door; of a heart, pounded.
Partizip II of rasen: „das Herz hat gerast“ = the heart was racing (for a car speeding along: „ist gerast“).
Treten, er/sie/es form: „auf die Bremse treten“ = to step on the brake.
Wecken, er/sie/es form: to wake someone or something up.
Bremsen, er/sie/es form: „bremst das Herz“ = slows the heart down; from die Bremse (brake).
Softens an image in speech: „tritt sozusagen auf die Bremse“ = steps on the brake, so to speak.
Borrowed from French; with „nicht“ it means simply refused to: „wollten sich partout nicht beruhigen“.
Partizip II of einbauen used as an adjective: „die eingebaute Bremse“ = the built-in brake.
Das Militär; „beim Militär“ = in the army, in military training.
Der Klassiker: a book (or film, dish …) everyone knows and keeps coming back to.
Das Gedächtnis; „im Gedächtnis bleiben“ = to stick in the memory.
Der Dickkopf, literally 'thick head'; „einen Dickkopf haben“ = to be stubborn, said with some affection.
From that moment on; in speech more common than „seither“.
Das Unwetter: a storm with heavy rain, hail or thunder.
Stürmen, impersonal: „es stürmt“ = there is a storm; „wenn es im Leben stürmt“ = when life gets stormy.
Schmecken, er/sie/es form: „sie schmeckt wie eine warme Umarmung“ = it tastes like a warm hug.
Dünsten, er/sie/es form: to cook gently in a little fat until soft.
Die Zehe, plural die Zehen; „zwei Zehen Knoblauch“ = two cloves of garlic.
Partizip II of schneiden (to cut): „hat eine Zwiebel geschnitten“.
Partizip II of köcheln (to simmer): „hat zwanzig Minuten geköchelt“.
Partizip II of einrühren (to stir in): ein-ge-rührt; the particle comes before ge-.
Partizip II of abschmecken (to taste and season): ab-ge-schmeckt.
Partizip II of andünsten: an-ge-dünstet; „an-“ means just a little, until it starts to soften.
Comparative of kühl (cool): „die Abende sind kühler geworden“ = the evenings got cooler.
„Etwas gern tun“ = to like doing something: „hat er gern gesagt“ = he liked to say.
Suchen, er/sie/es form: „sucht jeden Beweis selbst“ = looks for every proof himself.
Partizip II of entstehen, with sein: „sind neue Ideen entstanden“ = new ideas came about.
Partizip II of zusammennehmen: „seinen Mut zusammennehmen“ = to pluck up one's courage.
Fünfzehn + -jährig, with adjective endings: „der fünfzehnjährige Ramanujan“.
Partizip II of ausleihen: „sich ein Buch ausleihen“ = to borrow a book.
Die Mathe: the everyday short form of die Mathematik.
Partizip II of sich vornehmen: „hat sich vorgenommen, … zu beweisen“ = set out to prove …
Partizip II of beilegen (to enclose with a letter): bei-ge-legt.
„Sich etwas ausdenken“ = to make something up; it splits in a main clause: „er denkt sich … aus“.
Partizip II of kaputtmachen (to break, to ruin), the everyday word: „hat seine Gesundheit kaputtgemacht“.
Partizip II of zurückliegen: zurück-ge-legen; „hat 0:1 zurückgelegen“ = was 1–0 down.
Partizip II of schnüren (to lace up); „einen Dreierpack schnüren“ is football talk for scoring three goals.
Partizip II of beisteuern (to contribute): bei-ge-steuert; „Tore beisteuern“ = to add goals.
Partizip II of sich durchsetzen: durch-ge-setzt; „hat sich knapp durchgesetzt“ = won narrowly.
Partizip II of drehen; „einen Rückstand drehen“ = to turn a deficit into a win.
Partizip II of liegen: „hat 0:1 hinten gelegen“ = was 1–0 down (in the south also „ist … gelegen“).
Amy March, the youngest of the four sisters; „Amys“ is possessive, without an apostrophe.
The year the second part of Little Women came out.
„Keine Ahnung haben“ = to have no idea; in talk often just „keine Ahnung!“.
„Anfangs“ means the same as „am Anfang“: at the beginning, at first.
Separable verb (aus + bleiben); here joined because it stands at the end of a „dass“ clause: „dass die Stürme ausbleiben“.
german.translation: to not come, to stay away

german.note: Too proud of yourself or your looks.
„Erwachsen werden“ = to grow up; the noun is „der/die Erwachsene“.
Before a participle „frisch“ means only just: „frisch verheiratet“ = newly married.
Present of reden for er/sie/es: „sie redet mit ihrer Mutter“ = she talks with her mother.
„Verheiratet sein“ = to be married; it describes a state, so it works in the present.
From verwöhnen (to spoil, pamper): „ein verwöhntes Kind“ = a spoiled child.
Du-imperative of decken. Separable: … ab = abdecken, to cover; „Deck die Schüssel ab“ = cover the bowl.
„Streich“ is the du-imperative, „streichst“ the du form of streichen: to spread (butter, avocado) on bread.
Du form of rausholen, the spoken short form of herausholen: „wenn du das Blech rausholst“ = when you take the tray out.
Du form of rausziehen, the spoken short form of herausziehen (to pull out).
Du-imperative of versprechen, with the vowel change e → i: „versprich dir selbst nur das allererste“ = promise yourself only the very first one.
A year: „aus dem Jahr 1923“ = from the year 1923 (read: neunzehnhundertdreiundzwanzig).
Die Werbung: an ad, or advertising in general; „eine Werbung von einer Bank“ = an advertisement for a bank.
Die Bank, plural Banken: the bank for money. (A bench is also „die Bank“, plural Bänke.)
Der Haken is a hook; „der Haken an der Sache“ = the catch.
As an adverb: surely, I bet: „Irgendwo hat bestimmt gerade jemand … gesucht“ = somewhere someone was surely looking right now.
„0,179 Sekunden“ = 0.179 seconds, read null Komma eins sieben neun; German writes a decimal comma.
„13,078 Sekunden“ = 13.078 seconds, read dreizehn Komma null sieben acht; German writes a decimal comma.
„123 Punkte Vorsprung“ = a 123-point lead; read (ein)hundertdreiundzwanzig.
A year, read neunzehnhundertdreiundfünfzig; „seit Alberto Ascari 1953“ needs no „im“ before the year.
Ordinal of acht used as a noun for a place in a race, with a capital letter and no article: „ist Achter“ = is eighth.
The first name of Alberto Ascari, the Italian driver who won the Formula 1 title in 1952 and 1953.
Alberto Ascari, Italy's last Formula 1 world champion so far, in 1953.
First word of „Circuit of the Americas“, the race track in Austin, Texas; the name stays in English: „auf dem Circuit of the Americas“.
Last word of „Circuit of the Americas“, the English name of the race track in Austin, Texas.
The US state where Austin lies; „in Austin, Texas“, as in English.
Mexiko-Stadt, the capital of Mexico, where the next Formula 1 race is on 1 November 2026; one word with a hyphen: „in Mexiko-Stadt“.
Der November; months are masculine: „am 1. November“ = on 1 November.
Die Führung, from führen (to lead): „die Führung verlieren“ = to lose the lead.
Der Boxenstopp, plural Boxenstopps: Box (the pits) + Stopp; „bei den Boxenstopps“ = during the pit stops.
Der Stopp: in Formula 1 a pit stop for new tyres; „ein Stopp“ = one stop.
Short for die Pole-Position, first place on the starting grid; „auf die Pole stellen“ = to put the car on pole.
Die Pole-Position: first place on the starting grid, earned in qualifying; „von der Pole-Position starten“ = to start from pole.
In Formula 1 the middle tyre compound, said in English: „von Medium auf Hart“ = from the medium to the hard tyres.
Der Italiener, a man from Italy; for a woman die Italienerin: „der erste Italiener seit 1953“.
Partizip II of abgeben (to give up, hand over), with haben: „die Führung kurz abgegeben“ = briefly gave up the lead.
Partizip II of kontern (to counter, hit straight back), with haben; sports talk: „hat direkt gekontert“ = struck straight back.
Partizip II of vorbeifahren (to drive past), with sein: „Leclerc ist vorbeigefahren“ = Leclerc got past.
Partizip II of vorbeiziehen (to pull past, overtake), with sein; the ist is shared in „Verstappen ist schlecht weggekommen und Leclerc vorbeigezogen“.
Partizip II of vorbeischlüpfen (to slip past), with sein: „ist vorbeigeschlüpft“ = slipped through and past.
Partizip II of zurückschlagen (to strike back), with haben: „hat sofort zurückgeschlagen“ = hit straight back.
Spoken short form of „geht es“: „Am 1. November geht's nach Mexiko-Stadt“ = on 1 November it's off to Mexico City.
Spoken short form of „war es“; „das war's“ = that was it, that's all.
Said „sechshundert“: „600 g Hähnchen“ = 600 grams of chicken, with no „of“ in German.
The English word, kept in dish names: „Chicken Tikka Masala“, „Butter Chicken“; for the meat itself German says „Hähnchen“.
Short for das Gramm, written after a number with a space: „600 g“, said „sechshundert Gramm“.
Dative plural of das Gewürz (spice), with -n after „mit“ or „aus“: „mit Joghurt, Sahne und Gewürzen“.
Du imperative of grillen (to grill): „grill das Fleisch!“ = grill the meat!
Das Hähnchen, the everyday word for chicken as food; the plural is the same: die Hähnchen.
Compound of Hähnchen + Oberschenkel (thigh); „600 g Hähnchenoberschenkel“ = 600 g of chicken thighs.
Der Ingwer, the hot root used fresh or ground in Indian cooking.
Mahal = palace (Urdu, Hindi): „das Shish Mahal“ (palace of glass) in Glasgow, „das Moti Mahal“ (pearl palace) in Delhi; neuter, like „das Restaurant“.
Short for der Milliliter, written after a number: „100 ml Sahne“, said „hundert Milliliter“.
From Kohle (coal): „bis sie leicht verkohlen“ = until they char a little at the edges.
A year, read „neunzehnhundertsiebenundvierzig“; it goes straight to the front with no „in“, and the verb follows: „1947 gehen zwei Köche …“.
A year, read „zweitausendvierundzwanzig“; with a month: „im Januar 2024“ = in January 2024.
Said „fünfzig“: „50 g Butter“ = 50 grams of butter, with no „of“ in German.
Partizip II of austrocknen (to dry out), with „sein“: „ist ausgetrocknet“; the -ge- sits between „aus“ and „trocknet“.
Part of „der Delhi High Court“, the high court of Delhi; German keeps the English name, where its own word would be „das Gericht“.
Der Cousin, said the French way („ku-SÄNG“); a female cousin is die Cousine, and the old-fashioned word is der Vetter.
India's capital, used without an article: „nach Delhi“ = to Delhi, „in Delhi“ = in Delhi.
Partizip II of grillen, with „haben“: „sie haben Hähnchen gegrillt“ = they grilled chicken.
Partizip II of teilen; „als Indien geteilt wurde“ = when India was divided, the passive (werden + Partizip II).
Partizip II of ziehen; with „sein“ it means moving house or country: „sind nach Delhi gezogen“ = moved to Delhi.
Kundan Lal Gujral, one of the two cooks from Peshawar who opened Moti Mahal in Delhi in 1947; a family name + -s means the whole family: „die Gujrals“.
german.translation: Gujral; die Gujrals = the Gujral family

german.note: Part of the English name „Delhi High Court“, which German keeps as it is: „beim Delhi High Court verklagt“ = sued at the Delhi High Court.
Der Hochofen, from hoch (high) + Ofen (oven), the furnace that melts iron; „heiß wie ein Hochofen“ = as hot as a furnace.
Kundan Lal Jaggi, Kundan Lal Gujral's cousin and the other cook from Peshawar at Moti Mahal; „die Jaggis“ = the Jaggi family.
german.translation: Jaggi; die Jaggis = the Jaggi family

german.note: First part of „Kundan Lal“, the first name both cooks had: Kundan Lal Gujral and his cousin Kundan Lal Jaggi.
Second part of the shared first name „Kundan Lal“; Gujral and Jaggi are the family names.
Der Lehmofen, from Lehm (clay) + Ofen (oven); a tandoor is a Lehmofen.
Part of „Moti Mahal“ (pearl palace), the restaurant the two Kundan Lals opened in Delhi in 1947; like most restaurant names it is neuter: „das Moti Mahal“.
Der Perlenpalast, from Perle (pearl) + Palast (palace): what the name „Moti Mahal“ means.
A city in north-west British India, in Pakistan since 1947; used without an article: „von Peshawar nach Delhi“.
„Schwarz werden“ = to go black; after „werden“ or „sein“ the adjective takes no ending.
Der Tandoor, the very hot clay oven of Indian and Pakistani cooking; „im Tandoor“ = in the tandoor.
From the tandoor; German keeps the name and never adds an ending: „das Tandoori Chicken“.
Die Teilung, from teilen (to divide); German calls the 1947 Partition of British India into India and Pakistan „die Teilung Indiens“: „bei der Teilung Indiens“ = at Partition.
Partizip II of verklagen (to sue, to take to court), with no ge- because ver- never splits off: „haben … verklagt“.
Accusative of der Vorname, with -n: „denselben Vornamen“ = the same first name; the family name is der Nachname.
Du imperative of zerlassen, the kitchen word for melting butter or fat: „Zerlass 50 g Butter“ = melt 50 g of butter.
Das Zuhause, the place where you live and belong: „ihr Zuhause verloren“ = lost their home; written apart, „zu Hause“ = at home.
Partizip II of zurücklassen (to leave behind), with -ge- between „zurück“ and „lassen“: „haben alles zurückgelassen“.
The German name for Beijing, the capital of China, home of Shiqian Ding's team; „in Peking“ = in Beijing.
Genitive of das Atom (the tiny building block of everything): „das Herz eines Atoms“ = the heart of an atom.
german.translation: of an atom, of the atom

german.note: Der Laser, said as in English „lay-zer“; „Stimmt der Laser nicht?“ = is the laser wrong?
Scheinen, er/sie/es form, here in its first meaning, to shine (like the sun): „Ein Laser scheint darauf“ = a laser shines on it; it can also mean to seem.
Sich freuen (to be glad) is reflexive: „Das Team freut sich“ = the team is happy; Perfekt „hat sich gefreut“.
Read „zweitausenddrei“; a year stands alone in German, with no „in“: „die Idee ist von 2003“.
Das GPS, said „ge-pe-ess“: the satellite system that tells your phone or car where it is; „beim GPS helfen“ = to help with GPS.
In a date German writes the number with a full stop: „am 7. Oktober“, said „am siebten Oktober“.
First name of Thorsten Schumm, the physicist who leads the nuclear clock team at TU Wien, the technical university of Vienna.
Thorsten Schumm, Austrian physicist at TU Wien; with a name, the genitive is just -s and goes before the noun: „Schumms Team“ = Schumm's team.
First name of Shiqian Ding, the physicist who leads the nuclear clock team at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
Shiqian Ding, Chinese physicist at Tsinghua University in Beijing; name + -s = whose: „Shiqian Dings Team“ = Shiqian Ding's team.
Die Kernuhr, from der Kern (the nucleus of an atom) + die Uhr; plural die Kernuhren. It has nothing to do with nuclear power.
Present participle of schwingen (to swing) used as an adjective, with -es for a neuter noun after „ein“: „ein schwingendes Pendel“.
Das Pendel, the weight that swings to and fro in an old clock.
Die Atomuhr, plural die Atomuhren: a clock that counts the jumps of electrons, the most exact clocks before nuclear ones.
Plural of der Sprung (jump), with an umlaut: „Sprünge von Elektronen“ = electron jumps.
Plural of das Elektron, the tiny particles that move around the nucleus of an atom.
Der Atomkern = das Atom + der Kern, the tiny heart of an atom; in a compound the last word gives the gender.
Die Zeitschrift, a magazine or a scientific journal: „in der Zeitschrift Nature“ = in the journal Nature.
The English name of a famous science journal, kept in German: „in der Zeitschrift Nature“; feminine like die Zeitschrift.
Present participle of funktionieren (to work) used as an adjective: „eine funktionierende Kernuhr“ = a nuclear clock that works.
Das Ticken, the verb ticken used as a noun (capital T): „das Ticken der Elektronen“ = the ticks of the electrons.
Das Thorium-229, said „Thorium zweihundertneunundzwanzig“: the kind of thorium whose nucleus a laser can nudge, the heart of the new clocks.
Der Kristall, a clear solid whose atoms sit in neat rows; „in einem Kristall“ = in a crystal (dative).
Das Laserlicht = der Laser + das Licht; the last part of a compound gives the gender.
Verrutschen (to slip out of place), er/sie/es form: „wenn der Laser verrutscht“ = if the laser slips; ver- is not separable.
Die Abweichung, from abweichen (to deviate): how far off a value is; „eine Sekunde Abweichung“ = a second off.
Read „dreißig“: „in 30 Millionen Jahren“ = in 30 million years (dative plural Jahren after in).
Der Physiker, same form in the plural: „zwei Physiker“ = two physicists; a woman is eine Physikerin.
Partizip II of präsentieren (to present, to show); verbs in -ieren take no ge-: „haben … präsentiert“.
Read „zehntausend“: German groups thousands with a dot, not a comma: „über 10.000 Mal kleiner“ = over 10,000 times smaller.
Das Calciumfluorid (also spelled Kalziumfluorid), the clear crystal that holds the thorium; „aus Calciumfluorid“ = made of calcium fluoride.
Driften, er/sie/es form. Separable: … weg = wegdriften, to drift away; „Driftet der Laser weg, …“ = if the laser drifts off, …
First name of Ekkehard Peik, German physicist in Braunschweig, who wrote down the idea of a nuclear clock in 2003.
Ekkehard Peik, German physicist who proposed the thorium nuclear clock with Christian Tamm in 2003.
First name of Christian Tamm, the German physicist who proposed the nuclear clock with Ekkehard Peik in 2003.
Christian Tamm, German physicist, co-author of the 2003 nuclear clock idea with Ekkehard Peik.
Vorgeben, separable (vor + geben): „den Takt vorgeben“ = to set the beat, to call the tune; here the clocks would keep time for GPS.
A year, read „neunzehnhundertsechsundsechzig“: the first issue came out in March 1966.
Das (frühere) Westdeutschland, the Federal Republic before 1990; „in Westdeutschland“ needs no article.
Die Stiftung, an organisation set up with money for a lasting purpose; „die Stiftung Warentest“ is the one in Berlin that tests products.
Der Warentest = Waren (goods) + Test; part of the name „Stiftung Warentest“, the foundation for testing goods.
Plural of die Nähmaschine: nähen (to sew) + Maschine.
Der Mixer, a kitchen machine that mixes or blends; the plural is the same: „die Mixer“.
Neben (next to) + einander (each other): „nebeneinander testen“ = to test side by side.
german.translation: side by side, next to each other

german.note: Read „hunderttausend“: German groups thousands with a dot, not a comma.
Spoken word for kostenlos: „gratis an Zeitungen geben“ = to give to newspapers for free.
Read „fünfhundert“: „500 Gramm“ = 500 grams.
Read „zwei“: „2 Euro“ = two euros.
Der Euro; after a number it stays singular: „2 Euro“, „4 Euro pro Kilo“.
German writes a decimal comma: „3,50“ is read „drei fünfzig“ (three fifty), short for 3,50 Euro.
Die Überraschung, from überraschen (to surprise); on its own, „Überraschung!“ = surprise!
Das EU-Recht, the law all EU countries share: EU + Recht (law); „das EU-Recht sagt“ = EU law says.
Partizip II of herausbringen (separable: heraus + bringen, ge- in the middle): „eine Zeitschrift herausbringen“ = to bring out a magazine.
Das Heft is one issue of a magazine (also an exercise book); plural die Hefte.
Plural of der Abonnent, someone who pays to get every issue (das Abo).
A year, read „neunzehnhundertachtundsechzig“.
The capital of Germany.
Der Käufer, from kaufen (to buy); the plural is the same: „für Käufer“ = for shoppers.
Read „zweihundertzehntausend“: German groups thousands with a dot.
Partizip II of weitergeben (separable: weiter + geben, ge- in the middle): to pass something on to others.
Der Grundpreis, the price per kilo or litre shown in small print under the price, so you can compare packs of different sizes.
Partizip II of rauskommen, spoken for herauskommen; it takes sein: „ist rausgekommen“ = came out.
A year, read „neunzehnhundertvierundsechzig“: when the foundation was set up.
Partizip II of gründen; „gegründet hatte“ is the Plusquamperfekt: had set up.
From die Wissenschaft (science); German uses the same form as an adverb: „wissenschaftlich vergleichen“.
Partizip II of nebeneinanderstellen (separable: nebeneinander + stellen): to put next to each other.
Das Handtuch; „das Handtuch werfen“ = to throw in the towel, to give up.
Infinitive; „statt das Handtuch zu werfen“ = rather than throw in the towel.
Das Regalschild = Regal (shelf) + Schild (sign): the small label on the shelf with the price.
Der Tester, a person who tests things; the plural is the same: „die Tester“.
Das Regal, plural die Regale: „für ganze Regale“ = for whole shelves.
Plural of das Produkt, a thing made to be sold: „eine Stiftung, die Produkte testet“.
A year, read „zweitausendfünf“; a bare year needs no „im Jahr“: „Wir sind 2005 in Neapel“.
Read „zweihundertachtzig“: „280 Väter“ = 280 fathers.
German writes a decimal comma where English has a point; read „vier Komma fünf“.
Part of the name Alfredo Pisacane, the children's doctor in Naples whose father study came out in 2005.
Part of the name Alfredo Pisacane, the children's doctor in Naples whose father study came out in 2005.
Der Kinderarzt = Kinder (children) + Arzt (doctor); a woman is „die Kinderärztin“.
Der Babykurs = Baby + Kurs: a class for parents about caring for a baby.
Der Stillkurs, from stillen (to breastfeed) + Kurs; „zum Stillkurs gehen“ = to go to a breastfeeding class.
Plural of das Stillproblem: German glues stillen (to breastfeed) and Problem into one noun.
Die Stillzeit, the weeks and months a mother breastfeeds; the gender comes from the last part, die Zeit.
Stillen = to breastfeed (not the adjective still, quiet): „während sie stillt“ (present), „haben voll gestillt“ (Perfekt); „voll stillen“ = to give only breast milk.
Die Muttermilch = Mutter (mother) + Milch: „nur Muttermilch geben“ = to give only breast milk.
Häufig (frequent, common) as an adjective: „häufige Stillprobleme“ = common problems; „am häufigsten“ = most often, the commonest.
Die Uniklinik, the everyday short form of Universitätsklinik.
Die Unterstützung, the noun of unterstützen (to support); -ung nouns are always feminine.
Das Baden, the verb baden (to bath) used as a noun, so it takes a capital: „übernimm Baden und Windeln“.
Plural of die Windel; „Windeln übernehmen“ = to take on the nappy changing.
Das Selbstvertrauen = selbst (self) + Vertrauen (trust).
„Sagt euch gegenseitig“ = tell each other; gegenseitig makes it clear that euch means each other, not yourselves.
Er/sie/es form of wehtun (to hurt), written as one word when the parts stand together: „wenn das Stillen wehtut“ = if breastfeeding hurts. In a main clause it splits: „es tut weh“.
Read siebzehnhundertneunundfünfzig; „im Februar 1759“ = in February 1759.
