Jugo de lima = lime juice; jugo is the word across Latin America and is understood in Spain, where zumo is also common.
Present of rodar, ellos form; the o becomes ue when stressed: rodar → ruedan.
Ustedes command of poner, the same form as the subjunctive: pongan primero las piedras = put the stones in first, and hasta que se pongan negros = until they turn black (ponerse + colour).
A single grain of sand, rice or salt: ni un grano más = not one grain more.
Gerund of rodar; bajar rodando = to roll down.
Future of ver, ustedes/ellos form: y verán = and you'll see.
One word with an article, el porqué is a noun = the reason; por qué (two words) asks why.
Gerund of fijarse (en) with se attached: fijarse en algo = to notice something.
Gerund of guardar: los estaba guardando = she was saving them.
Present of preferir, él/ella/uno form; the e becomes ie when stressed.
Infinitive; un día que uno prefiere olvidar = a day you'd rather forget.
Proponerse (to set out to do) + lo; sin proponérselo = without meaning to.
Gerund of juntar; ir juntando = to gather little by little.
Subjunctive of sentir, tú form: la taza que más sientas tuya = the cup that feels most like yours.
Perder + la; sin perderla de vista = without taking your eyes off it.
Tú command of tomarse: tómate tu tiempo = take your time.
Present of recetar, ellos form: what a doctor writes on a receta (prescription).
Infinitive; con cara de no entender nada = looking completely puzzled.
Plural of probabilidad; tener más probabilidades de = to be more likely to.
Nouns ending in -dad are feminine: la felicidad.
Imperfect subjunctive of ocurrir, used after antes de que in a past story.
Subjunctive of ir: no promete que vaya a hacer… = it doesn't promise that it will make…
Pretérito indefinido of lavar, ellos form: se lavaron la cara = they washed their faces.
Plural of rostro, a slightly warmer word than cara for a person's face.
Same form for masculine and feminine; hacerlo oficial = to make it official.
Gerund of oscurecer; se va oscureciendo = it keeps getting darker.
Plural cicatrices: z becomes c before e.
Pretérito indefinido of deportar, ellos form: to force people to leave their land.
Plural of tropa; sus tropas = his soldiers.
Plural of conquista; renunciar a las conquistas = to give up conquering.
Infinitive; cuidar la salud = to look after health.
Respeto entre las religiones = respect between religions.
Present of alimentar; with se, si se alimenta de odio = if it feeds on hatred.
Pretérito indefinido of cruzar, ellos form; cruzar las puertas = to come through the doors.
Pretérito indefinido of desempolvar (polvo = dust): to bring something old back into use.
Remontarse a = to date back to: se remonta a 1898.
Nouns ending in -ción are feminine: una condición.
Enterarse = to find out, to hear about something: nadie se iba a enterar = nobody was going to find out.
Quitarse algo de la cabeza = to get something out of your head; the se can go before poder: no se podía quitar.
Gerund of vaciar (to empty): estaría vaciando el bolso = was probably emptying the bag.
La cantidad justa = just the right amount; justa agrees with cantidad.
Juntar = to put together: junta gotas de sangre = he puts drops of blood together.
Leche agria = sour milk, milk that has gone off.
Ciento veinticinco: how many years old the blood group letters are in 2026 (1901 + 125).
Una apuesta desesperada = a desperate gamble; desesperada agrees with apuesta.
OMS = Organización Mundial de la Salud, the World Health Organization; said la OMS.
Pretérito indefinido of rendirse (e→i): no se rindió = she did not give up.
Diminutive of pueblo; -ecito makes a place sound small and homely.
Educado means well-mannered, not "educated": un no muy educado = a very polite no.
From confianza (trust) with the prefix des-, which turns a word into its opposite.
Acabar + adjective = to end up (acabó reunido); acabarse = to come to an end; acabar con = to ruin (acabó con su salud).
spanish.translation: to end, to be over; ended up

spanish.note: Faltan diez minutos = there are ten minutes to go; the verb agrees with the time that is left. Faltaban is the imperfect.
spanish.translation: to be left, to be missing

spanish.note: Present of latir, used for the heart: el corazón late = the heart beats.
Present of temblar (e→ie): le tiemblan las manos = her hands are shaking.
Soltar el aire = to breathe out. Suelta is the tú imperative (o→ue); soltarlo = to let it out, lo attached to the infinitive.
spanish.translation: to let go, to let out

spanish.note: Present of servir (e→i): servir para algo = to be good for something; sirve en cualquier sitio = it works anywhere.
Se acordó de = she remembered; acordarse (o→ue) is reflexive and takes de.
Infinitive used like a noun: respirar lento = breathing slowly.
Tú imperative of relajarse with te attached; the accent keeps the stress on -lá-.
Any machine or piece of equipment: no necesita ningún aparato = you need no equipment.
El puente (de mando) is where the captain steers a ship.
No es una impresión = it is not just a feeling.
Se puede medir = it can be measured; medir changes e→i in some forms (mide).
From entrenar, to train: el entrenamiento militar = military training.
Present of publicar, used here to tell a past event as if it were happening now.
Present of repetir (e→i): la gente repite la frase = people say the line again and again.
Plural of peor; with an article it means worst: sus peores momentos = her worst moments.
A sailor's word: the storm amaina when the wind drops.
spanish.translation: to die down (of wind or a storm)

spanish.note: Capear (un temporal) is a sailing word for getting through a storm; las = the storms, attached to the infinitive.
Encajar un golpe, una decepción = to take it and keep going.
spanish.translation: to take, to cope with (a blow)

spanish.note: Feminine plural of feo; las cosas se ponen feas = things turn nasty.
Present of triturar: to blend or purée in a blender.
Pretérito indefinido of servir (e→i): la sirvió = he served it.
Sencilla + -ísima: the ending -ísimo/-ísima means "very" and is very common in speech.
Diminutive of despacio; the -ito ending makes it gentler and warmer.
Imperfect of sofreír: to fry lightly in a little oil, the first step of many Spanish sauces.
Nosotros present of leer: todavía leemos sus cuadernos = we still read his notebooks.
Pretérito indefinido of perder: perdió la beca = he lost his scholarship.
Imperfect of traer (to bring); for a book, traer means to contain: el libro no traía = the book did not have it.
Gerund of ganar: iba ganando 3-0 = they were winning 3-0.
Empatado con = level on points with; from empatar, to draw.
Turno de = someone's turn: turno de la Fórmula 1 = it is Formula 1's turn.
Amy March, the youngest of the four sisters in Little Women.
The year the second part of Little Women came out.
From madurar (to ripen, to mature); said of a person it means to grow up: madura mucho, acaba madurando.
Feminine of casado; estar casada = to be married, recién casada = newly married.
Present of charlar: to chat, to talk in a relaxed way.
No va a durar = it isn't going to last; cuánto va a durar = how long it will last.
Works like gustar: a la gente le encantan sus palabras = people love her words (the words delight people).
Feminine of mimado: a child who gets too much attention and everything she wants.
Feminine of vanidoso: too proud of yourself or your looks.
Present subjunctive of venir: lo que venga = whatever comes, something not known yet.
The year of the oldest known version of the line: an unsigned bank advertisement.
Gerund of acabar; acabar con algo = to wipe something out: estaba acabando con las ballenas = it was wiping out the whales.
Un anuncio de un banco = a bank advertisement.
Atribuir una frase a alguien = to credit a line to someone.
Infinitive; cuesta creer = it's hard to believe.
Gerund of darse with se attached; darse cuenta = to realise: acabó dándose cuenta = he ended up realising.
Preguntar + le: puede preguntarle a la matrona = she can ask the midwife. The le doubles the person, as people say it.
Infinitive of salvar: salvar algo enorme = to save something huge.
Sentirse un vago = to feel like a lazybones; as an adjective vago also means lazy.
Preposition, no accent: hacia el mar = toward the sea. Don't confuse with hacía (was doing), from hacer.
Veinti- + cinco: 21 to 29 are written as one word.
Read "cero coma ciento setenta y nueve": Spanish writes the decimal with a comma; "0,179 segundos por delante" = 0.179 seconds ahead.
Read "trece coma cero setenta y ocho": Spanish writes the decimal with a comma; "a 13,078 segundos" = 13.078 seconds behind.
Read "ciento veintitrés": 100 becomes "ciento" before another number; "123 puntos de ventaja" = a 123-point lead.
Read "mil novecientos cincuenta y tres": the year of Alberto Ascari's second world title.
Alberto Ascari, the Italian driver who was Formula 1 world champion in 1952 and 1953.
Alberto Ascari, Formula 1 world champion in 1952 and 1953 and the last Italian champion so far.
"El Circuito de las Américas" is the race track in Austin, Texas, where the United States Grand Prix is held.
A state in the south of the United States; Austin is its capital. Spanish writes it with x and says it with a j sound: "Téjas".
"Ciudad de México" = Mexico City, where the next race is on 1 November 2026; Spanish writes México with x but says it with a j sound.
Months are written without a capital letter in Spanish: "el 1 de noviembre" (read "el uno de noviembre").
Nationality adjectives take no capital letter in Spanish: "es italiano"; the feminine is italiana.
Ordinal of ocho: séptimo, octavo, noveno = seventh, eighth, ninth; as a place in a race it stands without an article: "Russell es octavo".
From English "box"; in Formula 1 "entrar en boxes" = to come into the pits, "las paradas en boxes" = the pit stops.
"Recuperó la posición" = he got his place back; nouns in -ción are feminine and the plural drops the accent: posiciones.
Kundan Lal was the first name of both cooks, Kundan Lal Gujral and his cousin Kundan Lal Jaggi, who opened Moti Mahal in Delhi.
The second half of Kundan Lal, the name the two cooks shared; Gujral and Jaggi are their family names.
spanish.translation: Lal (in the first name Kundan Lal)

spanish.note: Family name of Kundan Lal Gujral, one of the founders of Moti Mahal; los Gujral = the Gujral family, with the surname left in the singular.
Family name of Kundan Lal Jaggi, Gujral's cousin and partner at Moti Mahal; los Jaggi = the Jaggi family.
A city in the north-west of today's Pakistan, part of British India until 1947; Spanish keeps the name as it is.
India's capital region; Spanish keeps the English spelling, and the h is silent: DEL-i.
Part of the restaurant name Moti Mahal, "pearl palace" in Hindi and Urdu (moti = pearl); Spanish says el Moti Mahal, masculine like el restaurante.
Mahal = palace in Urdu and Hindi: el Shish Mahal (Glasgow), el Moti Mahal (Delhi); masculine, like el restaurante.
A deep clay oven from South Asia, heated with charcoal or wood until it is very hot; Spanish keeps the word: un tandoor.
Says that food was cooked in a tandoor; it never changes its form and goes after the noun: el pollo tandoori.
An English word kept in the name butter chicken; in Spanish the dish is masculine, el butter chicken, and many menus also call it pollo a la mantequilla.
spanish.translation: butter (English, part of the dish's name)

spanish.note: An English word kept in the names chicken tikka, chicken tikka masala and butter chicken; in Spanish the dish is masculine, like el pollo: el chicken tikka.
spanish.translation: chicken (English, part of the dish's name)

spanish.note: The everyday word for chicken as food and as a bird; muslos de pollo = chicken thighs.
Plural of muslo; muslos de pollo (chicken thighs) stay juicier than breast when grilled.
The spice or the fresh root; the j is said like a throaty h: jen-HEE-bre.
Plural of especia (spice); do not mix it up with especie, which means species or kind.
Partición means a division into parts; with a capital, la Partición is the split of British India into India and Pakistan in August 1947.
A palace; el Palacio de las Perlas (the Pearl Palace) is what the name Moti Mahal means.
Plural of perla (pearl); in everyday speech de perlas also means "perfectly": me viene de perlas = it suits me perfectly.
Acabar en los tribunales = to end up in court; el Tribunal Superior de Delhi is the Delhi High Court.
Una nuez is a walnut, and una nuez de mantequilla is a walnut-sized knob of butter; the plural is nueces (z becomes c before e).
Negro agrees with its noun: un poco negro (el pollo), negros (los bordes); ponerse negro = to turn black.
Participle of chamuscar used as an adjective, masculine plural to agree with los muslos: hasta que queden un poco chamuscados = until they are a little charred.
Imperfect of secarse (to dry out), for what kept happening: se secaban = they kept drying out; secar without se means to dry something.
Imperfect of resecarse, a stronger secarse: re- adds "right through", so se resecaban = they kept drying out completely.
Imperfect of asar (to roast or grill over strong heat), for what they did every day; pollo asado = roast chicken.
Tú imperative of hacer (haz) with lo (it) attached; haz has one syllable, so hazlo needs no written accent: hazlo a la parrilla = grill it.
Tú imperative of freír (to fry), with the stem e → í: fríe una cebolla = fry an onion; with lo attached it becomes fríelo.
Tú imperative of triturar (to blend, to purée) with lo attached; the written accent keeps the stress on -tú-.
Tú imperative of rematar (to finish off) with lo attached; the written accent keeps the stress on -má-.
Said twice, chup chup is the Spain kitchen word for a pot bubbling gently: déjalo haciendo chup chup = let it simmer.
spanish.translation: blub (the sound of a gentle simmer)

spanish.note: The symbol for gramos; read 600 g as "seiscientos gramos", and it never takes a plural s or a full stop.
The symbol for mililitros; read 100 ml as "cien mililitros".
Read "seiscientos"; 600 g de pollo = six hundred grams of chicken.
Read "cincuenta"; 50 g de mantequilla = fifty grams of butter.
Read "mil novecientos cuarenta y siete"; the year of the Partition of India, when the two cooks left Peshawar for Delhi.
Read "dos mil veinticuatro"; the year the two families went to court in Delhi over butter chicken.
Ir with se attached: irse de un sitio = to leave a place; after tener que the pronoun joins the infinitive, so tuvieron que irse = they had to leave.
Dejar with lo (it) attached to the infinitive; in a recipe, hasta dejarlo + adjective says how it should end up: hasta dejarlo un poco negro = until it's a bit black.
spanish.translation: to leave it, to get it (+ adjective)

spanish.note: The Spanish name for Beijing, the capital of China, home of Shiqian Ding's team; «en Pekín» = in Beijing.
El átomo, the tiny building block of everything; «el corazón del átomo» = the heart of the atom (de + el = del).
El láser, with a written accent; «luz láser» = laser light, where láser stays the same like an adjective.
Iluminar (to light up): ilumina is the present, iluminaba the imperfect for the background: «un láser lo iluminaba» = a laser was shining on it.
From equivocarse (to be wrong, to make a mistake), always with se: «¿el láser se equivoca?» = is the laser wrong?; equivocaba is the imperfect.
Corregir (to correct): the e becomes i in corrige; corregía is the imperfect, for each time it happened.
Exacto (feminine exacta): «muy exacto» = very exact; in speech «¡exacto!» alone also means exactly, right.
Read «dos mil tres»: «la idea es de 2003» = the idea is from 2003.
El GPS, said letter by letter «ge-pe-ese»: the satellite system that tells your phone or car where it is.
Read «siete»; dates use the plain number: «el 7 de octubre» = on 7 October.
First name of Thorsten Schumm, the physicist who leads the nuclear clock team at TU Wien, the technical university of Vienna.
Thorsten Schumm, Austrian physicist at TU Wien, whose team ran a nuclear clock on its own in 2026.
First name of Shiqian Ding, the physicist who leads the nuclear clock team at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
Shiqian Ding, Chinese physicist at Tsinghua University in Beijing; in Chinese the family name, Ding, comes first.
From el núcleo of an atom; «un reloj nuclear» = a clock that listens to the nucleus, nothing to do with nuclear power.
El vaivén, from va y viene (goes and comes): «el vaivén de un péndulo» = the back-and-forth swing of a pendulum.
El péndulo, the weight that swings to and fro in an old clock.
From el átomo; «un reloj atómico» counts the jumps of electrons, the most exact clocks before nuclear ones.
Plural of el salto, from saltar (to jump): «saltos de electrones» = electron jumps.
Plural of el electrón (the accent goes in the plural): the tiny particles that move around the nucleus.
El núcleo, the centre of an atom, its tiny heart; also the core of anything.
La revista, a magazine or a scientific journal: «en la revista Nature» = in the journal Nature.
The English name of a famous science journal, kept as it is: «la revista Nature».
Separado (separate, apart); «por separado» = separately, each on its own.
El tictac, the sound of a clock written as one word: «el tictac de los electrones» = the ticks of the electrons.
El torio is thorium; torio-229 (read «torio doscientos veintinueve») is the kind whose nucleus a laser can nudge, the heart of the new clocks.
Absorber, él/ella form: «el torio absorbe luz láser» = the thorium takes in laser light.
From desviarse (to drift off course), with se and an accent on the í: «si el láser se desvía» = if the laser slips.
Read «treinta»: «30 millones de años» = 30 million years, with de after millones.
Plural of el físico (physicist); la física is both a woman physicist and physics.
Pretérito of presentar, ellos form: «dos equipos presentaron…» = two teams presented…
Marcar la hora = to show or keep the time, what any clock does: «relojes que marcan la hora sin ayuda».
Marcar + le (to it), joined: «marcarle la hora al GPS» = to keep time for GPS; Spanish repeats the object with le.
Read «diez mil»: Spanish marks thousands with a dot or a space, not a comma: «10.000 veces» = 10,000 times.
El fluoruro; «fluoruro de calcio» = calcium fluoride, the clear crystal that holds the thorium.
El calcio, the same mineral as in milk and bones: «un cristal de fluoruro de calcio».
First name of Ekkehard Peik, German physicist in Braunschweig, who wrote down the idea of a nuclear clock in 2003.
Ekkehard Peik, German physicist who proposed the thorium nuclear clock with Christian Tamm in 2003.
First name of Christian Tamm, the German physicist who proposed the nuclear clock with Ekkehard Peik in 2003.
Christian Tamm, German physicist, co-author of the 2003 nuclear clock idea with Ekkehard Peik.
Plural of la punta (tip, end); «en dos puntas del mundo» = at two ends of the world, far apart.
A year, read «mil novecientos sesenta y seis»: the first issue came out in March 1966.
«Alemania Occidental» = West Germany, the country from 1949 to 1990.
German for foundation; Spanish keeps the German name: «la Stiftung Warentest», a foundation in Berlin that tests products.
German Waren (goods) + Test: the second half of the name «Stiftung Warentest», which Spanish does not translate.
Infinitive; «una máquina de coser» = a sewing machine: de + infinitive says what a machine is for.
Plural of la batidora, the kitchen machine that beats or blends food.
Read «cien mil»: Spanish groups thousands with a dot, not a comma.
El precio; «el precio por kilo» = the price per kilo, the small number that lets you compare.
Plural of el euro: «2 euros», «4 euros el kilo» = 4 euros a kilo.
Spanish writes a decimal comma: «3,50» is read «tres cincuenta» (three fifty), short for 3,50 euros.
Feminine of europeo; «la ley europea» = EU law, the rules all EU countries share.
Pretérito of lanzar (to throw, to launch): «lanzó una revista» = it started a magazine.
Plural of el suscriptor, someone who pays to get every issue of a magazine.
A year, read «mil novecientos sesenta y ocho».
La fundación, an organisation set up with money for a lasting purpose, here to test products.
Plural of el comprador, a person who buys things.
Read «doscientos diez mil»: Spanish groups thousands with a dot.
Obligar, él/ella form: «obligar a alguien a + infinitive» = to make someone do something, by law.
A year, read «mil novecientos sesenta y cuatro»: when the foundation was set up.
Científica + -mente: in a careful, scientific way.
Plural of el producto, a thing made to be sold.
El comienzo; «un comienzo prometedor» = a promising start.
La toalla; «tirar la toalla» = to throw in the towel, to give up.
La estantería, the shelves in a shop; «estanterías enteras» = whole shelves.
The year Pisacane's study of fathers in Naples came out: «en octubre de 2005».
Said doscientos ochenta: «los 280 papás» = all 280 fathers.
Said noventa y uno: «el 91 por ciento» = 91 percent, with el before the figure.
Spanish writes a decimal comma and says cuatro coma cinco.
Part of the name Alfredo Pisacane, the children's doctor in Naples whose father study came out in 2005.
Part of the name Alfredo Pisacane, the children's doctor in Naples whose father study came out in 2005.
Plural of papá, the everyday word for dad; unlike padres, it never means parents.
El pediatra / la pediatra: the same form for a man or a woman.
El apoyo; «el mismo apoyo» = the same support.
Plural of frecuente: «los problemas frecuentes» = the problems that often come up.
Plural of el baño; here the baby's baths, not bathrooms.
La sesión, the plural loses the accent: sesiones.
Afrontar + los attached to the infinitive: «cómo afrontarlos» = how to deal with them.
spanish.translation: to face them, to handle them

spanish.note: From toparse con, to run into: «se habían topado con dificultades» = they had run into difficulties.
«Ninguno de los dos» = neither of the two, with a singular verb and no extra no.
«Ninguno de los dos es adivino» = neither of you can read minds.
Voltaire (1694–1778), the French writer of Candide, who lived at Ferney from 1759.
Voltaire's short book of 1759 and its hero; the French name is kept for both here (older Spanish editions call him Cándido).
A village in France near Geneva, where Voltaire bought a house in 1759; a place name, so no article.
Today's name of Ferney, official since 1878 in honour of Voltaire; one hyphenated word.
French title kept as it is in Spanish: Madame Denis = Mrs Denis.
Madame Denis, Voltaire's niece, in whose name the house at Ferney was bought.
Read "mil setecientos cincuenta y nueve"; en febrero de 1759 = in February 1759.
Read "mil ochocientos setenta y ocho"; en 1878 = in 1878.
Months are written with a small letter in Spanish: en febrero de 1759.
Note the preposition: vivir en una granja = to live on a farm.
Una casa señorial is a lord's country house, the right word for a French château; castillo would be a fortress.
Someone who lives off the land; un viejo campesino = an old farmer.
Alejar algo = to keep something away: el trabajo aleja el aburrimiento = work keeps boredom away.
From aburrirse, to get bored; el aburrimiento = boredom.
A bad habit or moral fault; in everyday speech also a habit you can't stop, like a game.
From pantano (swamp); it agrees with its noun: un pueblo pantanoso, tierras pantanosas.
Plural of pantano; sanear los pantanos = to clean up (drain) the swamps.
Imperfect subjunctive of querer, required after como si: como si quisiera decir = as if it meant.
Diminutive of trozo; el trocito que tienes delante = the little patch in front of you.
From empedrar, to pave with stones; calles empedradas = paved streets.
Feminine of sobrino (nephew): su sobrina = his niece.
The main character of a story; the feminine is heroína.
Plural of the noun el mal (evil); tres grandes males = three great evils.
Reflexive encerrar: encerrarse = to lock yourself in, to shut out the world.
Imperative of ocuparse de with the pronoun attached and an accent added: ocúpate de = look after.
spanish.translation: look after, take care of (tú imperative)

spanish.note: Pretérito of predicar; predicar con el ejemplo = to practise what you preach, to lead by example.
Pretérito of sanear, to make healthy: saneó los pantanos = he drained the swamps.

grammar.body: "There's" (there is) says that something exists or is in a place. Use it with a singular or uncountable noun: there's a city, there's less traffic.
grammar.example: After one year, there's less traffic, and the air is cleaner.
grammar.title: There's for one thing that exists

grammar.body: "So" joins a reason and its result: the lanes feel safe, and because of that, children use them.
grammar.example: The lanes feel safe, so even children use them.
grammar.title: So for a result

paragraphs: So there's a city, and every street is full of cars. Walking isn't safe. Then the city tries something new: bike lanes.
A lot of drivers are angry. "This means more traffic!" they say.
But then more and more people ride to work and school. The lanes feel safe, so even children use them.
After one year, there's less traffic, and the air is cleaner. Giving space to people doesn't empty a city. It can fill it with life.

grammar.body: "Be going to" + verb predicts something you can see coming: this is going to make traffic worse. In speech it is more common than "will" for this.
grammar.example: "This is going to make traffic worse," they said.
grammar.title: Going to for a prediction

grammar.body: "Start" can be followed by the -ing form to say a new habit began: people started riding = they began to ride, and kept doing it.
grammar.example: More and more people started riding to work and to school.
grammar.title: Started + -ing for the beginning of a habit

paragraphs: For years, cars filled every street in the city, and walking felt dangerous. So the city tried something new: wide, safe lanes just for bikes.
A lot of drivers were angry. "This is going to make traffic worse," they said. "And nobody rides a bike in the rain."
But then something surprising happened. More and more people started riding to work and to school. The lanes felt safe, so even kids and older people used them.
After a year, car traffic was actually down, and the air was cleaner. The shops on the bike streets had more customers, too.
Turns out, giving space back to people doesn't empty a city. It fills it with life.

grammar.body: A short question at the end (are they?, isn't it?) turns a statement into a request for agreement. After a negative like "nobody", the tag is positive.
grammar.example: "And nobody's going to cycle in the rain, are they?"
grammar.title: A question tag to invite agreement

grammar.body: "So" + adjective + "that" says how strong something was and what followed from it: so safe that even kids used them.
grammar.example: The lanes felt so safe that even kids and older people began using them.
grammar.title: So … that for a result

grammar.body: "It turns out (that)" introduces something you found out, often a surprise. In casual speech people drop "it": "Turns out…".
grammar.example: It turns out that giving space back to people doesn't empty a city.
grammar.title: It turns out that

paragraphs: For years, cars filled every street in the city. Buses crawled along, and just crossing the road felt dangerous. So the city tried something new: wide, safe lanes just for bikes.
Plenty of drivers were furious. "It's only going to make traffic worse," they complained. "And nobody's going to cycle in the rain, are they?"
Then something surprising happened. More and more people started cycling to work, to school and to the shops. The lanes felt so safe that even kids and older people began using them.
After a year, car traffic had gone down, the air was noticeably cleaner, and shops along the bike routes were getting more customers.
Other cities are watching closely now. It turns out that giving space back to people doesn't empty a city. If anything, it fills the streets with life.

grammar.body: "Had taken over" looks back from the moment of the story to what was already true before it: the cars had been there for years when the city acted.
grammar.example: For years, cars had taken over every street in the city.
grammar.title: Past perfect for an earlier state

grammar.body: "What happened next" works as one noun, the thing that happened; the verb "caught" then belongs to the whole clause.
grammar.example: What happened next caught almost everyone off guard.
grammar.title: A what-clause as the subject

grammar.body: With many phrasal verbs the object can sit between the verb and the particle: hollow a city out. With a pronoun it must: hollow it out, not hollow out it.
grammar.example: Giving space back to people doesn't hollow a city out.
grammar.title: Phrasal verbs with a separable object

paragraphs: For years, cars had taken over every street in the city. Buses crept along in permanent traffic jams, and people on foot didn't feel safe crossing the road. So the city tried something nobody expected: wide, protected lanes just for bikes.
Plenty of drivers were outraged. "This is only going to make traffic worse," they said, and anyway, who in their right mind would cycle in the rain?
What happened next caught almost everyone off guard. More and more people started getting around by bike, because the lanes felt so safe that even kids and elderly neighbors were happy to use them.
A year later, car traffic had really dropped, the air was clearly cleaner, and shops along the bike routes were seeing more customers.
Other cities are watching closely, because the drivers turned out to be wrong. Giving space back to people doesn't hollow a city out. If anything, it breathes new life into it.

stories.summary: One city gives space back to bikes and people on foot, and the traffic actually gets better, not worse.
stories.title: A City Learns to Share Its Streets

grammar.body: The present simple says what is generally true or what happens again and again: rivers carry, robots float.
grammar.example: Rivers carry a lot of plastic to the sea.
grammar.title: Present simple for facts and habits

grammar.body: "Why clean…?" is a short spoken question with no subject: it means "why should anyone clean…?".
grammar.example: Why clean the whole ocean?
grammar.title: Why + base verb for a question

paragraphs: Rivers carry a lot of plastic to the sea. Out there, it's hard to catch. So engineers catch it early, in the rivers.
Their small solar robots float like boats. A barrier pushes bottles and bags into a basket.
In one month, they catch thousands of kilograms!
Why clean the whole ocean? Most plastic comes from a few rivers. The plans are free, so other cities can build them too. A small robot in a river is good news.

grammar.body: Many common verbs are irregular in the past simple: build → built, go → went, catch → caught.
grammar.example: In one month, they caught thousands of kilograms of plastic.
grammar.title: Past simple: built, went, caught

grammar.body: The past negative uses didn't and the base verb, not the past form: didn't try, not didn't tried.
grammar.example: They didn't try to clean the whole ocean.
grammar.title: Didn't + base verb for the negative

grammar.body: "Might be" says something is possible without being sure; it is softer than "is".
grammar.example: A small robot in a river might be some of the best news this year.
grammar.title: Might for a careful guess

paragraphs: Every year, rivers carry millions of tons of plastic into the sea. Out at sea, it's almost impossible to collect. So engineers decided to catch it in the rivers.
They built small solar-powered robots that float like little boats. A barrier guides bottles and bags into a basket, and the fish are fine.
The first ones went into a busy river near a big city. In one month, they caught thousands of kilograms of plastic.
They didn't try to clean the whole ocean. They picked the few rivers that carry most of the plastic.
The plans are free, so other cities can build their own. A small robot in a river might be some of the best news this year.

grammar.body: "Would have ended up" talks about a past that did not happen: without the robots, the waste would have reached the sea.
grammar.example: In one month, they caught thousands of kilograms of waste that would otherwise have ended up in the sea.
grammar.title: Would have + past participle

grammar.body: After "instead of" English uses the -ing form: instead of cleaning, not instead of clean.
grammar.example: It's the idea: instead of cleaning a whole ocean, focus on the few rivers that carry most of the plastic.
grammar.title: Instead of + -ing

grammar.body: In speech, "though" can come in the middle or at the end of a sentence to mean "however".
grammar.example: What's clever, though, isn't the technology.
grammar.title: Though at the end of a phrase

paragraphs: Every year, millions of tons of plastic flow down rivers into the ocean, where it's almost impossible to collect. So engineers decided to stop it earlier, in the rivers.
They built solar-powered machines that float like little boats. Each one has a barrier that steers bottles and bags into a basket without harming the fish.
They tested the first ones in a busy river near a big city. In one month, they caught thousands of kilograms of waste that would otherwise have ended up in the sea.
What's clever, though, isn't the technology. It's the idea: instead of cleaning a whole ocean, focus on the few rivers that carry most of the plastic.
The engineers now share their designs for free. A small robot, floating in a river, might be some of the most hopeful news this year.

grammar.body: In everyday speech "get" often replaces "be" in the passive, especially for things that just happen: plastic gets carried down rivers.
grammar.example: Every year, millions of tons of plastic get carried down rivers and out to sea, where it's practically impossible to get back.
grammar.title: Get + past participle: the spoken passive

grammar.body: Spoken English prefers phrasal verbs: come up with (invent), try out (test), step in (intervene), take on (attempt).
grammar.example: They tried the prototypes out on a busy river near a major city.
grammar.title: Phrasal verbs instead of Latin words

grammar.body: "May well" says something is quite likely, more confident than "may" alone.
grammar.example: A modest robot drifting quietly along a river may well turn out to be some of this year's most hopeful news.
grammar.title: May well for a likely outcome

paragraphs: Every year, millions of tons of plastic get carried down rivers and out to sea, where it's practically impossible to get back. So a team of engineers stepped in earlier, at the source: the rivers.

They came up with small solar-powered machines that drift along like quiet little boats. Each one uses a floating barrier to funnel bottles, bags and wrappers into a basket, without harming the wildlife.
They tried the prototypes out on a busy river near a major city. Within a month, they'd caught thousands of kilograms of waste that would otherwise have drifted out to sea.
The clever bit, though, is the thinking. Rather than taking on the near-impossible job of cleaning an entire ocean, the team goes after the few rivers that carry most of the plastic.
The designs are now free for anyone. A modest robot drifting quietly along a river may well turn out to be some of this year's most hopeful news.

stories.summary: Small floating robots catch plastic in the rivers, before it ever gets to the sea.
stories.title: The Ocean Clean-Up Robots

grammar.body: "There's" (there is) says that something exists somewhere. In speech, people almost always say "there's", not "there is".
grammar.example: Between a parking lot and a busy road, there's a little forest.
grammar.title: There is for something in a place

grammar.body: Short adjectives add -er to compare: fast → faster. "Much" makes the difference bigger: much faster than.
grammar.example: They grow much faster than in a normal forest.
grammar.title: Comparatives with much … than

grammar.body: The base verb with no subject tells someone what to do: plant lots of trees.
grammar.example: Plant lots of different trees, close together.
grammar.title: The imperative for an instruction

paragraphs: Between a parking lot and a busy road, there's a little forest. It's only as big as a tennis court.
The neighbors plant it in one weekend. The method comes from a Japanese scientist, Akira Miyawaki.
The idea is simple. Plant lots of different trees, close together. They grow much faster than in a normal forest.
Soon the street is cooler, and the birds come back. Nature doesn't need a big wild place. Just a small piece of ground.

grammar.body: "Planted" and "used" are in the past simple: the weekend is over. Regular verbs add -ed.
grammar.example: The neighbors planted it in just one weekend.
grammar.title: Past simple for a finished event

grammar.body: "Have planted" (have + past participle) talks about what has happened up to now, without saying when.
grammar.example: Cities from the Netherlands to India have planted pocket forests too.
grammar.title: Present perfect for results up to now

grammar.body: In everyday English, "get" + adjective means "become": it gets thick, it gets cold, I'm getting tired.
grammar.example: In a few years, a patch like this gets thick and green.
grammar.title: Get + adjective for a change

paragraphs: Between a parking lot and a busy road, there's a new forest. And it's only the size of a tennis court.
The neighbors planted it in just one weekend. They used a method from a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki.
His idea was simple: plant lots of different native trees, close together. That way, the young forest grows several times faster than a normal plantation.
In a few years, a patch like this gets thick and green. It cools the street, and the birds come back.
Cities from the Netherlands to India have planted pocket forests too. So you don't need a wilderness to bring nature home. You just need a patch of ground and a good method.

grammar.body: "Has been growing" describes something that started in the past and is still happening now.
grammar.example: Between a parking lot and a busy road, something unusual has been growing: a forest no bigger than a tennis court.
grammar.title: Present perfect continuous for something still going on

grammar.body: "Come up with" means to think of an idea or a plan. It is far more common in speech than "invent" or "devise".
grammar.example: They followed a method that a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, came up with decades ago.
grammar.title: Phrasal verb: come up with

grammar.body: "Enough" comes after the adjective: thick enough, warm enough. Then "to" + verb says what it makes possible.
grammar.example: In just a few years it's thick enough to cool the street.
grammar.title: Enough after an adjective

paragraphs: Between a parking lot and a busy road, something unusual has been growing: a forest no bigger than a tennis court.
The neighbors planted it themselves in a single weekend. They followed a method that a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, came up with decades ago.

Normally you'd plant a few kinds of trees far apart. Miyawaki did the opposite: lots of different native trees, packed close together. The plot is tiny, but the forest actually grows several times faster than a normal plantation.
In just a few years it's thick enough to cool the street. And the birds that had stayed away start coming back.
Since then, cities in the Netherlands, India and France have planted their own. Turns out you don't need a wilderness to bring nature home, just a small patch of ground and the right idea.

grammar.body: "Squeezed in between…" opens the sentence with a past participle that describes the subject, the forest, before we even meet it.
grammar.example: Squeezed in between a parking lot and a busy road, in a pretty ordinary neighborhood, something unusual has taken root: a forest no bigger than a tennis court.
grammar.title: Participle clause at the start of a sentence

grammar.body: "You'd think" (you would think) sets up what most people expect, and "but" turns it around. It is a very common spoken way to introduce a surprise.
grammar.example: You'd think that would slow them down, but it actually makes them grow several times faster.
grammar.title: You'd think … but

grammar.body: "Birds that had long given up" goes further back in time: the birds left long before the forest was there.
grammar.example: Within a few years, the tangle of saplings is a real little forest, cooling the pavement and bringing back birds that had long given up on the area.
grammar.title: Past perfect: had given up

paragraphs: Squeezed in between a parking lot and a busy road, in a pretty ordinary neighborhood, something unusual has taken root: a forest no bigger than a tennis court.
The neighbors planted it themselves over a single weekend, using a method worked out decades ago by the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki.

Where a normal plantation puts a handful of species far apart, his method crams dozens of native trees in tight, so they compete for light. You'd think that would slow them down, but it actually makes them grow several times faster.
Within a few years, the tangle of saplings is a real little forest, cooling the pavement and bringing back birds that had long given up on the area.

Cities across the Netherlands, India and France have picked up the idea. And they all prove the same thing: you don't need a wilderness, just a patch of ground and a method that lets trees do what they do best.

stories.summary: It's only the size of a tennis court, but this little forest is bringing birds and cool shade back to a city street.
stories.title: The Pocket Forest

grammar.body: Speakers often tell a past story in the present to make it feel close: "So it's the 1970s" = it was the 1970s.
grammar.example: So it's the 1970s, and the ocean is getting quiet.
grammar.title: Present tense to tell a story

grammar.body: "Is the sea going to be silent?" asks about what will happen next. Questions put "is" before the subject.
grammar.example: Is the sea going to be silent forever?
grammar.title: Be going to + verb for the future

paragraphs: So it's the 1970s, and the ocean is getting quiet. Hunters kill too many whales. In some places, only five in a hundred are still alive.
Scientists are worried. Is the sea going to be silent forever?
Then it's 1986, and most countries stop hunting whales. Year after year, the whales come back.
Today humpback whales sing again. In some seas, it's the first song in a hundred years! So when people really decide to fix something big, they can.

grammar.body: "Was going quiet" and "were disappearing" show something happening over a long time in the past, not a single moment.
grammar.example: Fifty years ago, the ocean was slowly going quiet.
grammar.title: Past continuous for a slow change

grammar.body: After "agree", English uses to + the base verb: agreed to stop, agreed to help.
grammar.example: Then, in 1986, most countries agreed to stop hunting whales for money.
grammar.title: Agree to + verb

grammar.body: "For good" is an everyday way to say forever, for all time.
grammar.example: Scientists thought the seas could soon go silent for good.
grammar.title: For good = forever

paragraphs: Fifty years ago, the ocean was slowly going quiet. Whales were disappearing, and fast.
Hunters killed far too many. In some places, only about five in a hundred were left. Scientists thought the seas could soon go silent for good.
Then, in 1986, most countries agreed to stop hunting whales for money. That gave the whales a chance to come back.
It took a long time, decades actually. But today humpback whales sing again, even in waters that were quiet for a hundred years.
So the whales are one of nature's great comeback stories. When people really decide to fix something huge, sometimes they actually do.

grammar.body: "So many that" links an amount to its result: there were so many killed that only a few were left.
grammar.example: Hunters had killed so many that in some places only about five in a hundred were left.
grammar.title: So many … that for a result

grammar.body: "Nobody had heard it for a century" looks back from a past point over a long stretch of time before it.
grammar.example: And their song is back too, even in waters where nobody had heard it for a century.
grammar.title: Past perfect with nobody … for

grammar.body: "Put a stop to something" means make it end, usually by a decision.
grammar.example: Then, in 1986, an international ban put a stop to most commercial whaling, and the whales finally had room to recover.
grammar.title: Put a stop to

paragraphs: Fifty years ago, the ocean was falling silent, because whales were disappearing so fast.
Hunters had killed so many that in some places only about five in a hundred were left. Scientists were afraid the seas would soon go quiet for good.
Then, in 1986, an international ban put a stop to most commercial whaling, and the whales finally had room to recover.

The recovery took decades, but it's been amazing. Some humpback populations are almost back to their numbers from before whaling. And their song is back too, even in waters where nobody had heard it for a century.
That's why the whales have become one of nature's clearest success stories. When people really decide to fix something enormous, sometimes they actually do.

grammar.body: "Had been killed" puts the focus on the whales, not the hunters, and places the killing before the moment the story describes.
grammar.example: In some regions so many whales had been killed that barely five in a hundred were left.
grammar.title: Past perfect passive

grammar.body: "What makes it … is" puts the important part at the end of the sentence, where the listener's attention is.
grammar.example: What makes it one of conservation's clearest success stories isn't just the size of the comeback.
grammar.title: A wh-clause as the subject

grammar.body: "Nothing short of remarkable" means completely remarkable; it adds strong emphasis to the adjective that follows.
grammar.example: It's taken decades, but the comeback has been nothing short of remarkable.
grammar.title: Idiom: nothing short of

paragraphs: Fifty years ago the ocean was going quiet, because whales were being hunted on an industrial scale.
In some regions so many whales had been killed that barely five in a hundred were left. Scientists worried, and with good reason, that the seas might soon go silent for good.
Then, in 1986, an international ban put a stop to most commercial whaling. It was controversial back then, but it finally gave the whales the breathing room they needed to start recovering.

It's taken decades, but the comeback has been nothing short of remarkable. Several humpback populations are close to their pre-whaling numbers. And their song, which nearly disappeared, is back again in waters where nobody had heard it in a century.

What makes it one of conservation's clearest success stories isn't just the size of the comeback. It's what it proves: when people really commit to fixing even the most enormous damage, sometimes they actually pull it off.

stories.summary: Fifty years ago the ocean was going quiet, and now humpback whales are singing again in waters where nobody had heard them for a hundred years.
stories.title: The Whales That Sing Again

grammar.body: "Who" asks about a person. Here it is the subject, so the word order stays the same as in a normal sentence: who holds it.
grammar.example: Who holds it first?
grammar.title: Who in a question

grammar.body: "When to help" and "when to wait" are short ways to say the right moment for doing something.
grammar.example: She knows when to help and when to wait.
grammar.title: When + to + verb

paragraphs: So a baby is born. Who holds it first? It's often not a doctor. It's a midwife.
Before the birth, the midwife visits the mother. She checks the baby and answers questions. The mother feels less afraid.
On the night of the birth, she stays calm. She knows when to help and when to wait. Later, she helps with feeding.
In December 2023, the United Nations calls midwifery a world treasure. But families know that already.

grammar.body: "A doctor's" and "a midwife's" mean a doctor's hands, a midwife's hands: the noun is not repeated because it is clear.
grammar.example: They're a midwife's.
grammar.title: A possessive without the noun

grammar.body: "She keeps coming" means she continues to come, again and again.
grammar.example: In the weeks after, she keeps coming.
grammar.title: Keep + verb-ing

paragraphs: The first hands that hold most of the world's babies aren't a doctor's or a parent's. They're a midwife's. It's a job older than anyone can remember.
Long before the birth, the midwife comes to visit. She checks the baby, answers questions and calms the mother's fears.
On the night of the birth, she's often the calmest person in the room. She knows when to help and when to just wait.
In the weeks after, she keeps coming. She helps with feeding, and she's often the first to see a problem.
In December 2023, the United Nations put midwifery on its list of human treasures. It's like an old song or an old craft. Millions of families already knew why.

grammar.body: "Years of experience have taught her": have + past participle shows that the learning happened over time and still helps her now.
grammar.example: Years of experience have taught her when to step in and when to wait.
grammar.title: Present perfect for experience

grammar.body: "Had known that all along" means the families knew it long before 2023; the past perfect looks back from that moment.
grammar.example: Millions of families had known that all along.
grammar.title: Past perfect with all along

grammar.body: "Does" stands for the whole verb (notices a problem), so it is not repeated.
grammar.example: In the weeks after, she helps with feeding and often notices a problem before anyone else does.
grammar.title: Before anyone else does

paragraphs: The first hands to hold most of the world's babies aren't a doctor's or a parent's, but a midwife's. It's a job so old that nobody can say when it began.
Long before the birth, she starts visiting the mother. She checks the baby, answers questions, and calms the fears that feel too big to say out loud.
On the night of the birth, she's often the calmest person in the room. Years of experience have taught her when to step in and when to wait.
And her visits don't stop there. In the weeks after, she helps with feeding and often notices a problem before anyone else does.
In December 2023, UNESCO put midwifery on its list of human treasures. It's knowledge worth protecting, like an old song or a craft. Millions of families had known that all along.

grammar.body: "Don't belong to a doctor or a parent, but to a midwife" corrects with but and repeats the preposition: not to X, but to Y.
grammar.example: The first hands to hold most of the world's newborn babies don't belong to a doctor or a parent, but to a midwife.
grammar.title: Belong to … but to

grammar.body: "Keeping an eye on…, calming…" are -ing clauses that say what she does on those visits without a new sentence.
grammar.example: Long before the birth, she starts visiting the mother regularly, keeping an eye on the baby and calming the fears that are hard to put into words.
grammar.title: Participle clauses for what she does

grammar.body: "Let the mother's body do its work": after let + object the verb has no to.
grammar.example: Years of experience have taught her when to step in and when to step back and let the mother's body do its unhurried work.
grammar.title: Let + object + bare verb

paragraphs: The first hands to hold most of the world's newborn babies don't belong to a doctor or a parent, but to a midwife. It's a job so old that nobody can say when it began.
Long before the birth, she starts visiting the mother regularly, keeping an eye on the baby and calming the fears that are hard to put into words.
On the night itself, she's often the calmest person in the room. Years of experience have taught her when to step in and when to step back and let the mother's body do its unhurried work.
And it doesn't end with the birth. In the weeks that follow, she helps with feeding and often notices that something's wrong before anyone else would.

In December 2023, UNESCO added midwifery to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage, knowledge worth looking after just like an old song or a craft. Millions of families had known that for generations.

stories.summary: The first hands to hold most of the world's babies belong to a midwife, and in December 2023 UNESCO called what she knows a treasure.
stories.title: First Hands

grammar.body: "There's" (there is) says that something exists somewhere. It comes first, and the thing comes after it.
grammar.example: There's an island near the North Pole.
grammar.title: There's for something in a place

grammar.body: In a spoken story, "so" at the start of a sentence shows a result: this happens, so people do that.
grammar.example: So people open the vault and grow new plants from the copies.
grammar.title: So for what happens next

paragraphs: There's an island near the North Pole. On it, a gray door goes into a mountain.
Behind it, long cold halls are full of seed packets. The seeds come from almost every country. More than a million packets!
Then a war puts one country's seeds in danger. So people open the vault and grow new plants from the copies.
And it works. The vault is a spare copy of the world's food. It waits, safe, for whoever needs it someday.

grammar.body: Many common verbs have their own past form: put → put, take → took, grow → grew. Regular verbs add -ed: opened, worked.
grammar.example: So workers opened the vault, took out the copies and grew the plants again.
grammar.title: Past simple: put, took, grew

grammar.body: "Just as planned" means exactly the way it was planned. "As" + a past participle is a short way to say it: as expected, as promised.
grammar.example: And it worked, just as planned.
grammar.title: As planned: as + past participle

paragraphs: There's a frozen island halfway between Norway and the North Pole. On it, a plain gray door goes into a mountain.
Behind that door, long cold halls run into the rock. Small packets of seeds sleep there at minus eighteen degrees.
The seeds come from almost every country: rice from Asia, wheat from Africa, beans from South America. There are more than a million packets.
Then a war put one country's seeds at risk. So workers opened the vault, took out the copies and grew the plants again.
And it worked, just as planned. The vault is a spare copy of the world's food. It waits in the mountain for whoever needs it, someday, somewhere.

grammar.body: "Where" adds information about a place you have just named: the halls, where the packets sleep.
grammar.example: Behind it, though, long cold halls run into the rock, where small packets of seeds sleep in the dark at minus eighteen degrees.
grammar.title: Where in a relative clause for a place

grammar.body: "Turns out" (short for "it turns out") introduces something people found out, often a small surprise.
grammar.example: Turns out the vault isn't just an odd idea.
grammar.title: Turns out: spoken English for a discovery

grammar.body: "It was meant to" means it was planned or built to do that; the verb after "to" is left out because it is clear: meant to work.
grammar.example: It worked exactly the way it was meant to.
grammar.title: Was meant to: what was planned

paragraphs: On a frozen island halfway between Norway and the North Pole, a gray door goes straight into a mountain. Honestly, it doesn't look like much.
Behind it, though, long cold halls run into the rock, where small packets of seeds sleep in the dark at minus eighteen degrees.
The seeds come from almost every country: rice from Asia, wheat from Africa, beans from South America. That's over a million packets, each one a spare copy of a crop somewhere.
Then a war put one country's own seed bank in danger. So workers opened the vault and grew the plants again from its copies.
It worked exactly the way it was meant to. Turns out the vault isn't just an odd idea. It's a spare copy of the world's food, waiting in the mountain for whoever needs it, someday, somewhere.

grammar.body: "If the power ever fails" talks about something that could really happen; English uses the present after "if", not "will".
grammar.example: Machines keep them at minus eighteen degrees, and if the power ever fails, the frozen ground around them keeps them cold.
grammar.title: If + present for a real possibility

grammar.body: "Turns out to be" says what something really is, once you know more: it looked like a curiosity, but it is a safety net.
grammar.example: The vault turns out to be a real safety net for the world's food, quietly waiting inside a mountain for whoever, someday, somewhere, might need it.
grammar.title: Turn out to be: a discovery

grammar.body: "Had hoped" puts the hoping before the working: the designers hoped first, years earlier, and then it worked.
grammar.example: It worked exactly as its designers had hoped.
grammar.title: Past perfect: had hoped

paragraphs: On a frozen island halfway between Norway and the North Pole, a gray door is set into a mountainside, and nothing about it tells you what's behind it.

Inside, long tunnels run into the rock, where more than a million packets of seeds lie asleep. Machines keep them at minus eighteen degrees, and if the power ever fails, the frozen ground around them keeps them cold.
They come from almost every country: rice from Asia, wheat from Africa, beans from South America. Each packet is basically a backup of a crop that's growing, and maybe under threat, somewhere.
When a war put one country's seed bank in danger, workers took the matching copies out of the vault and grew those crops again.
It worked exactly as its designers had hoped. The vault turns out to be a real safety net for the world's food, quietly waiting inside a mountain for whoever, someday, somewhere, might need it.

stories.summary: Deep inside a frozen mountain, the world keeps a spare copy of its food.
stories.title: The Vault in the Mountain

grammar.body: "Put them in first": the base verb with no subject gives an instruction or advice.
grammar.example: Put them in first.
grammar.title: The imperative to tell someone what to do

grammar.body: With the verb be, a question puts is or are before the subject: it is full → is it full?
grammar.example: "Is it full?" she asks.
grammar.title: Questions with be

paragraphs: One day, a teacher brings a big jar to class. She has stones and sand too.
First, she puts in the big stones. "Is it full?" she asks. "Yes!" say the students.
Then she adds small stones. "Full now?" Nobody is sure. Then she pours in the sand. Now the jar is really full.
"This jar is your life," she says. "The big stones are your family, your health, your goals. Put them in first. Everything else finds its place."

grammar.body: Regular verbs add -ed (poured, rolled); common verbs are irregular: come → came, bring → brought, get → got.
grammar.example: She also brought stones and a bag of sand.
grammar.title: Past simple: regular and irregular

grammar.body: "If the sand goes in first, there's no room": if + present, then present, for something that is always true.
grammar.example: If the sand goes in first, there's no room for them.
grammar.title: If + present for a general truth

paragraphs: One day, a teacher came to class with a big empty jar. She also brought stones and a bag of sand.
First, she put the big stones in. "Is it full?" she asked. "Yes!" said the students.
Then she poured in small stones, and they rolled into the gaps. "Is it full now?" This time nobody was sure.
Last came the sand. It got into every little space, and now the jar was really full.

"This jar is your life," she said. "The big stones are what really matters: your family, your health, your goals. If the sand goes in first, there's no room for them. Put the big stones in first, and everything else finds its place."

grammar.body: After a time word like next, English sometimes puts the verb first: next came the smaller stones.
grammar.example: Next came the smaller stones, which rolled into the gaps.
grammar.title: Next came …: verb before subject

grammar.body: "Only then was the jar full": after only then, the verb comes before the subject, which stresses the moment.
grammar.example: It trickled into every last gap, and now the jar was really full.
grammar.title: Only then + inverted verb

grammar.body: "If you fill your life with sand first, there won't be any room": a real possibility and its result.
grammar.example: If you fill your life with sand first, there won't be any room left for them.
grammar.title: First conditional: if + present, will

paragraphs: One day, a teacher walked into class with an empty jar, some big stones, some smaller ones and a bag of sand.
First, she put the big stones in until the jar looked full. "Is it full?" she asked. "Yes!" the students said, sure of themselves.
Next came the smaller stones, which rolled into the gaps. "Is it full now?" she asked, and this time nobody was so sure.
Finally, she poured in the sand. It trickled into every last gap, and now the jar was really full.

"This jar is your life," she said. "The big stones are what matters most: your family, your health, your goals. If you fill your life with sand first, there won't be any room left for them. But put the big stones in first, and everything else still finds a way to fit."

grammar.body: "Fill your days with small stuff, and there won't be room" means if you fill them, there won't be room: a spoken way to say a condition.
grammar.example: Fill your days with small stuff first, the way sand fills every gap, and there won't be room for what counts.
grammar.title: Imperative + and for a condition

grammar.body: "She started with the large stones, packing them in": the -ing clause adds what she was doing at the same time.
grammar.example: She started with the large stones, packing them in until the jar looked full to the top.
grammar.title: -ing clause for a second action

grammar.body: An idiom: things fall into place when they settle in the right order without much effort.
grammar.example: But put the big stones in first, and somehow everything else still falls into place.
grammar.title: Fall into place

paragraphs: One day, a teacher came into class with a big empty jar, a handful of large stones, some smaller pebbles and a bag of fine sand.
She started with the large stones, packing them in until the jar looked full to the top. "Is it full?" she asked. "Yes!" the students said, without a moment's doubt.
Then she poured in the pebbles, which rattled down into the gaps between the big stones. "Is it full now?" she asked, and this time the room went quiet.
Finally came the sand, trickling into every last crack until the jar really was full.

"This jar is your life," she said. "The big stones are what matters most: your family, your health, your dreams. Fill your days with small stuff first, the way sand fills every gap, and there won't be room for what counts. But put the big stones in first, and somehow everything else still falls into place."

stories.summary: A teacher fills a jar with big stones, small stones and sand, and then asks what it means.
stories.title: The Jar of Stones

grammar.body: "There's" is the short, spoken form of "there is": it says that something exists in a place. With "no", it says it doesn't.
grammar.example: But there's no name.
grammar.title: There is / there's + noun

grammar.body: People often tell a story in the present to make it feel close: he sees, he gives, she writes.
grammar.example: So he gives it to a train worker.
grammar.title: Present simple for a story

paragraphs: So Mateo is on the last train home, and he's tired. Then he sees a brown wallet under the seat.
Inside, there's a lot of money and a family photo. But there's no name.
For a moment, Mateo thinks about the money. Nobody sees him. But somebody is looking for this wallet.
So he gives it to a train worker. A week later, the owner sends a letter. "Thank you," she writes. "People are still kind."

grammar.body: "He could keep it" says it was possible; "no one would know" imagines the result. Neither thing happened.
grammar.example: He could just keep it, and no one would ever know.
grammar.title: Could and would for a choice not taken

grammar.body: "Couldn't stop thinking" means the thought kept coming back. After stop, the next verb takes -ing.
grammar.example: But he couldn't stop thinking about that photo.
grammar.title: Couldn't stop + -ing

grammar.body: "You didn't just give back my money" = you did that, and something more as well.
grammar.example: "You didn't just give back my money," she wrote.
grammar.title: Didn't just … : not only

paragraphs: Mateo was on the last train home, and he just wanted to sleep. Then he saw something under the seat: a brown wallet.
Inside there was a lot of money and a photo of a smiling family. But there was no name and no phone number.
For a moment, Mateo thought about the money. Nobody saw him. He could just keep it, and no one would ever know.
But he couldn't stop thinking about that photo. Somebody was probably looking for it. So at the next station, he gave it to a train worker.
A week later, a letter came from the owner. "You didn't just give back my money," she wrote. "You reminded me that people are still kind."

grammar.body: "All he wanted was sleep" puts the one thing he wanted at the end, for weight: it means he wanted nothing else.
grammar.example: Mateo was on the last train home after a long day, and all he wanted was sleep.
grammar.title: All he wanted was …

grammar.body: "Nobody had seen him" and "he'd found it" go one step further back in the past than the rest of the story.
grammar.example: Nobody had seen him, so he could just keep it and no one would ever know.
grammar.title: Past perfect: had seen, had found

grammar.body: "He caught himself thinking" = he suddenly noticed what he was thinking, often something he isn't proud of.
grammar.example: For a moment, Mateo caught himself thinking about the money.
grammar.title: Catch yourself + -ing

paragraphs: Mateo was on the last train home after a long day, and all he wanted was sleep. Then he noticed a brown wallet under the seat in front of him.
Inside was quite a bit of cash and a photo of a smiling family, but no name and no phone number.
For a moment, Mateo caught himself thinking about the money. Nobody had seen him, so he could just keep it and no one would ever know.
But he couldn't stop thinking about that photo. Someone was probably looking everywhere for it. So at the next station, he handed it to a train worker and explained where he'd found it.
A week later, a letter came from the owner. "You didn't just give me back my money," she wrote. "You reminded me that people are still kind."

grammar.body: "Wanting nothing more than his bed" adds what he felt while the main action went on; it shares the subject, Mateo.
grammar.example: After a long, hard day, Mateo was riding the last train home, wanting nothing more than his bed.
grammar.title: An -ing clause for a state of mind

grammar.body: "He did think about the money" admits something honestly: yes, it really happened, even if only for a second.
grammar.example: For a second, Mateo did think about the money.
grammar.title: Did + verb for emphasis

grammar.body: "Nobody would be any the wiser" is an idiom: nobody would ever know or find out.
grammar.example: Nobody had seen him; he could just pocket it, and nobody would be any the wiser.
grammar.title: None the wiser / any the wiser

paragraphs: After a long, hard day, Mateo was riding the last train home, wanting nothing more than his bed. Then something under the seat in front of him caught his eye: a worn brown wallet.
Inside was a fair bit of cash, a train ticket and a photo of a happy, smiling family, but no name and no phone number.
For a second, Mateo did think about the money. Nobody had seen him; he could just pocket it, and nobody would be any the wiser.

Still, he couldn't get that photo out of his head. Somewhere, someone was almost certainly turning their bag inside out for this very wallet. So at the next stop he handed it to a train attendant and told them exactly where he'd found it.
A week later, a short letter turned up from the owner. "You didn't just give me back my money," she wrote. "You reminded me that people are still kind."

stories.summary: A tired traveler finds a stranger's wallet full of cash, and he's only got one stop to decide what to do.
stories.title: The Wallet on the Train

grammar.body: The base verb with no subject tells someone what to do: look at the path.
grammar.example: "Look at your side of the path."
grammar.title: The imperative to ask someone to do something

grammar.body: "There are" says that several things exist in a place: there are flowers. With one thing or an uncountable noun, use "there is".
grammar.example: There are flowers there.
grammar.title: There are + plural noun

paragraphs: A woman carries water home every day in two clay pots. One pot has a crack, so it loses water.
After two years, the cracked pot is sad. "I'm sorry," it says. "I only give you half."
The woman smiles. "Look at your side of the path." There are flowers there. The other side is just dry earth.
"I know about your crack," she says. "So I put seeds on your side. You water them. Your crack makes something beautiful."

grammar.body: "I've always known" covers the whole time from the past up to now: she knew from the start and she still knows.
grammar.example: "I've always known about your crack," she said.
grammar.title: Present perfect with always

grammar.body: "Speak up" means to finally say something you kept to yourself. "Finally" shows it took a long time.
grammar.example: The cracked pot felt ashamed, and after two years it finally spoke up.
grammar.title: Phrasal verb: speak up

grammar.body: "Was making" describes an action in progress over a period of time in the past, while something else was happening.
grammar.example: What you called a flaw was quietly making something beautiful.
grammar.title: Past continuous for something going on

paragraphs: A water carrier in an old village had two big clay pots. One was perfect. The other had a thin crack, so it was half empty when she got home.
The cracked pot felt ashamed, and after two years it finally spoke up. "I'm sorry. I leak all the way home."
The water carrier smiled. "On the way home today, look at the path," she said. "But only at your side."
So the pot looked. All along its side, there were flowers. The other side was just dry earth.
"I've always known about your crack," she said. "So I planted seeds on your side, and you watered them every day. What you called a flaw was quietly making something beautiful."

grammar.body: "However carefully she walked" means "no matter how carefully she walked": the result was always the same.
grammar.example: The other had a thin crack, and however carefully she walked, it got home only half full.
grammar.title: However + adjective or adverb

grammar.body: "While" can join two opposite pictures, not only two things at the same time: flowers on one side, dry earth on the other.
grammar.example: All along its side, flowers were blooming, while the other side was nothing but dry earth.
grammar.title: While for a contrast

grammar.body: "Kept calling" means it called it a flaw again and again, over a long time.
grammar.example: What you kept calling a flaw was quietly growing something beautiful.
grammar.title: Kept + -ing for repetition

paragraphs: In an old village, a water carrier had two big clay pots. One was perfect. The other had a thin crack, and however carefully she walked, it got home only half full.
The cracked pot felt more and more ashamed. After two years, it finally said, "I'm sorry. I leak all the way home, and you only get half the water."
She just smiled. "On the way home today, look at the path," she said. "But only at your own side."
So the pot did. All along its side, flowers were blooming, while the other side was nothing but dry earth.

"I've known about your crack all along," she said gently. "That's why I planted seeds on your side. Every day, you watered them without knowing it. What you kept calling a flaw was quietly growing something beautiful."

grammar.body: "Whose" links a person to something that belongs to them: a water carrier whose pots = a water carrier, and her pots.
grammar.example: In an old village there was once a water carrier whose two clay pots hung from either end of a pole.
grammar.title: Whose for possession in a relative clause

grammar.body: "What it saw as failure" means "the thing that it saw as failure": the pot's own view, not necessarily the truth.
grammar.example: After two years of what it saw as failure, it couldn't keep quiet any longer.
grammar.title: What as "the thing that"

grammar.body: "You've been watering" stresses an action that started in the past and has gone on, day after day, up to now.
grammar.example: Every day, you've been watering them without knowing it.
grammar.title: Present perfect continuous for an ongoing action

paragraphs: In an old village there was once a water carrier whose two clay pots hung from either end of a pole. One was flawless. The other had a hairline crack, and however carefully she walked, it never reached her door more than half full.
The cracked pot grew more and more ashamed. After two years of what it saw as failure, it couldn't keep quiet any longer. "I'm sorry," it said. "After all your hard work, you get barely half."
She just smiled. "On the way home today," she said, "watch the path, but only your side of it."
So the pot watched. Its side was full of flowers, red, yellow and blue, while the other side was bare, dry earth.

"I've known about your crack from day one," she said. "That's exactly why I scattered seeds along your side. Every day, you've been watering them without knowing it. What you kept calling a flaw was quietly growing something beautiful."

stories.summary: A water carrier's leaky pot is ashamed of its crack, until it sees what that crack has been quietly growing all along.
stories.title: The Cracked Pot

grammar.body: "Every" takes a singular noun and a singular verb: every week, every day, every single day.
grammar.example: Every week, a businessman buys the last loaf.
grammar.title: Every + singular noun

grammar.body: The base verb with no subject tells someone what to do: bake, open.
grammar.example: Open a second shop.
grammar.title: The imperative for advice

paragraphs: Marta has a little bakery. It opens at seven, and by noon the bread is gone.
Every week, a businessman buys the last loaf. And every week he says: "Bake more bread. Open a second shop. You can be big!"
"Big for what?" Marta asks. He has no answer. In the afternoon, she works in her garden and visits her father. She draws, too.
One day, the businessman understands. Her small bakery already gives her everything. She doesn't need more.

grammar.body: "You should" + base verb gives advice: you should bake = it is a good idea to bake.
grammar.example: "You should bake twice as much.
grammar.title: Should for advice

grammar.body: In everyday talk "get it" means understand: he finally got it = he finally understood.
grammar.example: One week, the businessman finally got it.
grammar.title: Got it: understood

paragraphs: Marta's little bakery opened at seven, and by noon the bread was gone. Every single day.
A businessman came through town every week. Every week he bought the last loaf and said the same thing: "You should bake twice as much. Open a second shop. You could be big."
Marta weighed his words carefully, the way she weighed her flour. "Big for what?" she asked. He never had an answer.
In the afternoons, she worked in her garden, visited her father and drew in a little sketchbook. With a bigger bakery, there'd be no time for that.
One week, the businessman finally got it. Marta's small bakery already gave her exactly what she wanted. More would only take something away.

grammar.body: "She'd ask" (she would ask) describes something she did again and again in the past, like "used to".
grammar.example: "Big for what?" she'd ask, and he never quite had an answer ready.
grammar.title: Would for a past habit

grammar.body: "The way she weighed her flour" means "in the same way as": it compares two actions.
grammar.example: Marta weighed his words the way she weighed her flour, slowly and carefully.
grammar.title: The way + clause for comparison

grammar.body: "Would have taken something away" imagines a past that did not happen: if she had grown, she would have lost something.
grammar.example: Marta's small bakery already gave her exactly what she wanted, and making it bigger would only have taken something away.
grammar.title: Would have + past participle

paragraphs: Marta's little bakery opened at seven every morning and, without fail, it was sold out by noon.
A businessman came through town every week. Every week he bought the last loaf and gave her the same advice: bake twice as much, open a second shop, get big.
Marta weighed his words the way she weighed her flour, slowly and carefully. "Big for what?" she'd ask, and he never quite had an answer ready.
In the afternoons, the ones a bigger bakery would have swallowed whole, she worked in her garden and visited her father. She also filled a little sketchbook with drawings.
It took a few visits, but the businessman got there in the end. Marta's small bakery already gave her exactly what she wanted, and making it bigger would only have taken something away.

grammar.body: "Would have eaten up" imagines a past that never came true: with a bigger business, the afternoons would have gone.
grammar.example: In the afternoons, the very ones a bigger business would have eaten up, she looked after her garden and sat with her father.
grammar.title: Would have for a past that didn't happen

grammar.body: "Quite a few" means more than a few, a fairly large number; it sounds relaxed and spoken.
grammar.example: It took quite a few of these chats, but in the end the businessman finally got it.
grammar.title: Quite a few: a fair number

grammar.body: "Drawings nobody had asked her to make": the asking would have come before the drawing, so it takes had + past participle.
grammar.example: She also filled a small sketchbook with drawings nobody had asked her to make.
grammar.title: Past perfect after nobody

paragraphs: Marta's little bakery opened at seven every morning and, without fail, sold out of bread by noon.
A businessman came through town every week. Every time, he bought the last loaf and gave her the same well-meant advice: double what you bake, open a second shop, make the place bigger.
Marta weighed his words the way she weighed her flour, carefully and never too generously. "Big for what?" she'd ask, gently, and he never quite came up with an answer.

In the afternoons, the very ones a bigger business would have eaten up, she looked after her garden and sat with her father. She also filled a small sketchbook with drawings nobody had asked her to make.
