Max Verstappen partió desde la pole con Red Bull, lideró las 62 vueltas de principio a fin y ganó por siete segundos. En nueve visitas anteriores nunca había ganado en Singapur; lo hizo, por fin, en su Gran Premio número 250.
Charles Leclerc fue segundo con Ferrari y Kimi Antonelli, tercero con Mercedes, a 24 segundos, por delante de los McLaren de Lando Norris y Oscar Piastri.

George Russell, relegado al fondo de la parrilla por una penalización del motor, remontó hasta terminar noveno. Lewis Hamilton, que había empezado tercero, se fue cayendo hasta el sexto lugar en el tramo final.

Verstappen encadena ya dos victorias seguidas, aunque el campeonato se le ha escapado casi del todo. Antonelli tiene 102 puntos de ventaja y podría ser campeón ya en la próxima carrera, en Austin, el 25 de octubre.

stories.summary: El domingo 11 de octubre de 2026, Max Verstappen ganó por fin bajo las luces de Singapur: a la décima, y primero en todas las vueltas.
stories.title: Singapur, por fin

grammar.body: Places in a race use ordinal numbers, which work like adjectives: primo, secondo, terzo, nono. Arriva secondo = he finishes second.
grammar.example: Charles Leclerc arriva secondo con la Ferrari.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers for places

grammar.body: This A1 report tells the race in the present: parte, arriva, vince. It sounds like a friend telling you what happens.
grammar.example: George Russell parte in fondo e arriva nono.
grammar.title: The present for a race report

grammar.body: Fra (or tra) + a length of time means 'in' from now: fra due settimane = in two weeks. C'è = there is.
grammar.example: Fra due settimane c'è la gara ad Austin, negli Stati Uniti.
grammar.title: Fra + time: in two weeks

paragraphs: È domenica 11 ottobre 2026, e la Formula 1 è a Singapore. La gara è di notte, sotto le luci della città. E fa caldo.
Max Verstappen parte primo con la Red Bull. Resta davanti per tutti i giri e vince. È la sua prima vittoria a Singapore!
Charles Leclerc arriva secondo con la Ferrari. Kimi Antonelli è terzo con la Mercedes. E nel campionato Antonelli è primo.
George Russell parte in fondo e arriva nono. Fra due settimane c'è la gara ad Austin, negli Stati Uniti.

grammar.body: Verbs of movement like partire, arrivare and rimanere take essere, and the participle agrees with the subject: è partito, è arrivato. Most other verbs take avere: ha vinto.
grammar.example: Lewis Hamilton è partito terzo, ma è arrivato sesto.
grammar.title: Passato prossimo with essere and avere

grammar.body: Con … di vantaggio gives the winning margin: con sette secondi di vantaggio = seven seconds ahead.
grammar.example: Ha vinto con sette secondi di vantaggio.
grammar.title: Con + amount + di vantaggio

grammar.body: Potere is followed straight by an infinitive: può vincere = he can win. Già here means as early as.
grammar.example: Ma nel campionato Antonelli ha 102 punti di vantaggio, e può vincere il titolo già ad Austin, il 25 ottobre.
grammar.title: Può + infinitive: he can

paragraphs: Domenica 11 ottobre 2026 la Formula 1 ha corso di notte a Singapore. Era una notte calda e umida, e le luci della città erano accese.
Max Verstappen è partito primo con la Red Bull ed è rimasto davanti per tutti i giri. Ha vinto con sette secondi di vantaggio. Era la sua decima gara a Singapore, e la prima vittoria.
Charles Leclerc è arrivato secondo con la Ferrari. Kimi Antonelli è arrivato terzo con la Mercedes, a 24 secondi dal vincitore.
George Russell è partito in fondo alla griglia, per una penalità al motore, ed è arrivato nono. Lewis Hamilton è partito terzo, ma è arrivato sesto.
Adesso Verstappen ha vinto due gare di fila. Ma nel campionato Antonelli ha 102 punti di vantaggio, e può vincere il titolo già ad Austin, il 25 ottobre.

grammar.body: Anche se (even though) takes the ordinary indicative: anche se era la sua decima gara = even though it was his tenth race.
grammar.example: Anche se era la sua decima gara a Singapore, lì non aveva mai vinto: ci è riuscito al suo 250º Gran Premio.
grammar.title: Anche se + indicative

grammar.body: Era partito (had started) puts the start before the rest of the race, which is told in the passato prossimo.
grammar.example: George Russell, che era partito in fondo per una penalità al motore, ha rimontato fino al nono posto.
grammar.title: Trapassato prossimo for the earlier event

grammar.body: The conditional potrebbe (could) says something may happen soon. Chiudere i conti (to settle the accounts) is how Italians say to wrap up a title.
grammar.example: Ma il campionato è nelle mani di Antonelli, che ha 102 punti di vantaggio e potrebbe chiudere i conti già alla prossima gara, ad Austin.
grammar.title: Potrebbe: the conditional for a real possibility

paragraphs: Domenica 11 ottobre 2026 la Formula 1 ha corso sotto i riflettori di Singapore, in una notte calda e umida.

Max Verstappen è partito primo con la Red Bull, è rimasto davanti per tutti i giri e ha vinto con sette secondi di vantaggio. Anche se era la sua decima gara a Singapore, lì non aveva mai vinto: ci è riuscito al suo 250º Gran Premio.
Charles Leclerc è arrivato secondo con la Ferrari, mentre Kimi Antonelli ha chiuso terzo con la Mercedes, a 24 secondi dal vincitore. Quarto e quinto Lando Norris e Oscar Piastri, con la McLaren.
George Russell, che era partito in fondo per una penalità al motore, ha rimontato fino al nono posto. Lewis Hamilton è partito terzo, ma nel finale è scivolato al sesto.
Per Verstappen sono due vittorie di fila. Ma il campionato è nelle mani di Antonelli, che ha 102 punti di vantaggio e potrebbe chiudere i conti già alla prossima gara, ad Austin.

grammar.body: A past participle can stand for a whole clause: finito in fondo alla griglia = having ended up at the back of the grid. It agrees with the subject, Russell.
grammar.example: George Russell, finito in fondo alla griglia per una penalità al motore, è risalito fino al nono posto.
grammar.title: A past participle clause

grammar.body: After a preposition the relative pronoun is cui: il caldo per cui è famosa = the heat it is famous for. The preposition never goes to the end.
grammar.example: Domenica 11 ottobre 2026 la Formula 1 ha corso sotto i riflettori tra le strade di Singapore, con il caldo umido per cui la gara notturna è famosa.
grammar.title: Per cui: preposition + relative pronoun

grammar.body: Farcela means to manage, to pull it off; in the past it becomes ce l'ha fatta = he made it. Very common when someone succeeds at last.
grammar.example: A Singapore, in nove tentativi, non aveva mai vinto: ce l'ha fatta al decimo, nel weekend del suo 250º Gran Premio.
grammar.title: Farcela: to make it

paragraphs: Domenica 11 ottobre 2026 la Formula 1 ha corso sotto i riflettori tra le strade di Singapore, con il caldo umido per cui la gara notturna è famosa.

Max Verstappen è partito dalla pole con la Red Bull, è rimasto in testa per tutti i 62 giri e ha vinto con sette secondi di vantaggio. A Singapore, in nove tentativi, non aveva mai vinto: ce l'ha fatta al decimo, nel weekend del suo 250º Gran Premio.
Charles Leclerc ha chiuso secondo con la Ferrari e Kimi Antonelli terzo con la Mercedes, staccato di 24 secondi, davanti alle McLaren di Lando Norris e Oscar Piastri.
George Russell, finito in fondo alla griglia per una penalità al motore, è risalito fino al nono posto. Lewis Hamilton, che era partito terzo, nel finale è scivolato al sesto.

Per Verstappen sono due vittorie di fila. Il campionato però resta nelle mani di Antonelli, che ha 102 punti di vantaggio e potrebbe diventare campione già alla prossima gara, ad Austin, il 25 ottobre.

stories.summary: Domenica 11 ottobre 2026 Max Verstappen ha vinto per la prima volta sotto le luci di Singapore: al decimo tentativo, e in testa dal primo all'ultimo giro.
stories.title: Singapore, finalmente

grammar.body: With he, she or it, the present tense verb takes -s: he fills, he kicks, he works, he scores.
grammar.example: He kicks it in the street every day.
grammar.title: He + verb with -s

grammar.body: This A1 story is told in the present, although it happens in the 1940s and in 1958. The years show when.
grammar.example: Then it's 1958, and Edson is seventeen.
grammar.title: Present tense for a true story

grammar.body: "At fifteen" means "when he is fifteen years old". English uses "at" before an age.
grammar.example: At fifteen, he's in a big club.
grammar.title: At + age

paragraphs: It's the 1940s in Bauru, Brazil. A boy called Edson loves football. His family is poor. He has no ball.
So he fills a sock with newspaper. That's his ball! He kicks it in the street every day.
He also works in tea shops. At fifteen, he's in a big club. At sixteen, he's in Brazil's team.
Then it's 1958, and Edson is seventeen. In the World Cup final, he scores twice. Now the world knows him: Pelé.

grammar.body: Regular verbs add -ed (stuffed, kicked, worked, scored). Some common verbs change: grow → grew, teach → taught, go → went, win → won.
grammar.example: So Edson stuffed a sock with newspaper and kicked that.
grammar.title: Past simple: regular and irregular

grammar.body: English says "was born" (be + born) for a birth, with "on" before the date and "in" before the place.
grammar.example: Edson Arantes do Nascimento was born in Brazil on 23 October 1940.
grammar.title: Was born

grammar.body: The last sentence stops at "were": it means "the hours in the street were important". English often leaves out the repeated word.
grammar.example: The hours in the street were.
grammar.title: A short answer with "were"

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento was born in Brazil on 23 October 1940. He grew up in Bauru, and his family was poor.
His dad, a footballer, taught him the game. But they had no money for a ball. So Edson stuffed a sock with newspaper and kicked that.
He was out in the street with it every day. He also worked in tea shops.
At fifteen he joined Santos, a big club. At sixteen he was in Brazil's team. In 1958, at seventeen, he went to the World Cup in Sweden.
In the final he scored twice, and Brazil won 5–2. People called him Pelé. The ball was never important. The hours in the street were.

grammar.body: "Who the world knows as Pelé" adds information about a person (careful writing would say "whom"); "which no other player has done" comments on the whole idea before it.
grammar.example: He went on to win the World Cup three times, which no other player has done.
grammar.title: Relative clauses: who, which

grammar.body: "He'd stuffed" (he had stuffed) shows the action that came first: he stuffed the sock, and then he kicked it around.
grammar.example: The family couldn't afford a ball, so the boy usually kicked a sock he'd stuffed with newspaper.
grammar.title: Past perfect: had + past participle

grammar.body: "Has ever scored" looks at all the time up to now: from 1958 until today, nobody younger.
grammar.example: He scored twice, Brazil won 5–2, and nobody younger has ever scored in a final.
grammar.title: Present perfect with ever

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, who the world knows as Pelé, was born on 23 October 1940 and grew up in Bauru, in Brazil.
His father, a footballer called Dondinho, taught him the game. The family couldn't afford a ball, so the boy usually kicked a sock he'd stuffed with newspaper.
He was out in the street with it for hours, and he worked in tea shops for money. At fifteen he signed for Santos, and a year later he was playing for Brazil.
On 29 June 1958, at the World Cup final in Sweden, he was seventeen. He scored twice, Brazil won 5–2, and nobody younger has ever scored in a final.
He went on to win the World Cup three times, which no other player has done. The sock didn't matter. The thousands of hours with it did.

grammar.body: "If the sock had been" imagines a different past; "the story would be" gives the result now. Both halves are unreal.
grammar.example: If the sock had been a leather ball, the story would be the same: what made him wasn't the ball, it was the hours.
grammar.title: Mixed conditional: if + had been, would be

grammar.body: "He was the one who taught" puts the stress on one person: not somebody else, but his father.
grammar.example: His father, Dondinho, was a footballer himself, and he was the one who taught the boy the game.
grammar.title: He was the one who …

grammar.body: "Went on to win" means that later, as the next step in his life, he won. It links an early event to what followed.
grammar.example: Pelé, as everyone called him by then, went on to win the tournament again in 1962 and 1970, and that third title is still unmatched.
grammar.title: Went on to + verb

paragraphs: The ball was a sock. In the 1940s, in Bauru, Brazil, a boy called Edson Arantes do Nascimento stuffed it with newspaper, because his family couldn't afford a real one.
His father, Dondinho, was a footballer himself, and he was the one who taught the boy the game. Edson worked in tea shops and spent every spare hour with the sock.
Santos signed him at fifteen; Brazil picked him at sixteen. On 29 June 1958, aged seventeen, he scored twice in the World Cup final against Sweden, and Brazil won 5–2.
Nobody that young has scored in a final since. Pelé, as everyone called him by then, went on to win the tournament again in 1962 and 1970, and that third title is still unmatched.
He died on 29 December 2022, aged eighty-two. If the sock had been a leather ball, the story would be the same: what made him wasn't the ball, it was the hours.

stories.summary: In the 1940s, a poor boy in Brazil kicked a sock full of newspaper around the street; at seventeen, he scored twice in a World Cup final.
stories.title: A Ball Made from a Sock

grammar.body: After a negation, un, une and des become de: il a un ballon, but il n'a pas de ballon.
grammar.example: Sa famille est pauvre, et il n'a pas de ballon.
grammar.title: Ne … pas de: no ball

grammar.body: French uses avoir to give an age: « Edson a dix-sept ans », word for word "has seventeen years".
grammar.example: En 1958, Edson a dix-sept ans.
grammar.title: Avoir for age

grammar.body: « À quinze ans » = at fifteen (years old). Ans is never left out.
grammar.example: À quinze ans, il est dans un grand club.
grammar.title: À + age: at fifteen

paragraphs: On est dans les années 1940, à Bauru, au Brésil. Edson adore le football. Sa famille est pauvre, et il n'a pas de ballon.
Alors il remplit une chaussette de papier journal. C'est son ballon ! Il joue dans la rue tous les jours.
Il travaille dans des salons de thé. À quinze ans, il est dans un grand club. À seize ans, il joue pour le Brésil.
En 1958, Edson a dix-sept ans. En finale de la Coupe du monde, il marque deux buts. Le monde connaît son nom : Pelé.

grammar.body: Most verbs: avoir + participle: a rempli, a marqué, a gagné. -er verbs end in -é, -ir verbs in -i.
grammar.example: En finale, il a marqué deux buts, et le Brésil a gagné 5-2.
grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir

grammar.body: Naître, entrer, partir take être: il est né, il est entré, il est parti.
grammar.example: En 1958, il est parti à la Coupe du monde en Suède.
grammar.title: Passé composé with être: est né, est parti

grammar.body: The imparfait of être and avoir describes how things were: poor, seventeen years old.
grammar.example: Il avait dix-sept ans.
grammar.title: Était, avait: the background

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento est né au Brésil le 23 octobre 1940. Il a grandi à Bauru, et sa famille était pauvre.
Son père, un footballeur, lui a appris le jeu. Mais ils n'avaient pas d'argent pour un ballon. Alors Edson a rempli une chaussette de papier journal, et il a joué avec.
Il passait ses journées dans la rue avec sa chaussette. Il a aussi travaillé dans des salons de thé pour aider sa famille.
À quinze ans, il est entré à Santos, un grand club. À seize ans, il jouait pour le Brésil. En 1958, il est parti à la Coupe du monde en Suède. Il avait dix-sept ans.
En finale, il a marqué deux buts, et le Brésil a gagné 5-2. On l'appelait Pelé. Le ballon n'a jamais compté. Les heures dans la rue, oui.

grammar.body: « Avait remplie » is the earlier action; the participle takes -e because its object, « qu' » (la chaussette), comes first.
grammar.example: Comme la famille n'avait pas les moyens d'acheter un ballon, le garçon jouait d'habitude avec une chaussette qu'il avait remplie de papier journal.
grammar.title: Plus-que-parfait and agreement: avait remplie

grammar.body: When "which" refers to the whole clause before it, French uses ce que: ce qu'aucun autre joueur n'a fait.
grammar.example: Il a gagné la Coupe du monde trois fois, ce qu'aucun autre joueur n'a fait.
grammar.title: Ce que: which, for a whole idea

grammar.body: « Si » answers or contrasts a negative: the sock didn't matter; the hours, yes, they did.
grammar.example: Les milliers d'heures passées avec elle, si.
grammar.title: Si: yes, after a negative

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, que le monde connaît sous le nom de Pelé, est né le 23 octobre 1940. Il a grandi à Bauru, au Brésil.

Son père, Dondinho, un footballeur, lui a appris le jeu. Comme la famille n'avait pas les moyens d'acheter un ballon, le garçon jouait d'habitude avec une chaussette qu'il avait remplie de papier journal.
Il passait des heures dans la rue avec elle, et travaillait dans des salons de thé pour gagner de l'argent. À quinze ans, il a signé à Santos, et un an après, il jouait pour le Brésil.
Le 29 juin 1958, en finale de la Coupe du monde en Suède, il avait dix-sept ans. Il a marqué deux buts, le Brésil a gagné 5-2, et depuis, personne de plus jeune n'a marqué en finale.
Il a gagné la Coupe du monde trois fois, ce qu'aucun autre joueur n'a fait. La chaussette, ça n'avait pas d'importance. Les milliers d'heures passées avec elle, si.

grammar.body: An unreal past condition: si + plus-que-parfait (avait été), then conditional past (aurait été).
grammar.example: Si la chaussette avait été un vrai ballon de cuir, l'histoire aurait été la même : ce qui a fait Pelé, ce n'est pas le ballon, ce sont les heures.
grammar.title: Si + plus-que-parfait, conditional past

grammar.body: « C'est … qui » stresses one person: it was he, and nobody else, who taught the boy. After c'est, use lui, not il.
grammar.example: Son père, Dondinho, était lui-même footballeur, et c'est lui qui a appris le jeu au garçon.
grammar.title: C'est lui qui: the cleft sentence

grammar.body: « Ce troisième titre, personne ne l'a égalé »: the object comes first and is picked up by l'. Typical of speech.
grammar.example: Pelé, comme on l'appelait déjà, a encore gagné le tournoi en 1962 et en 1970, et ce troisième titre, personne ne l'a égalé.
grammar.title: Putting the object first

paragraphs: Le ballon, c'était une chaussette. Dans les années 1940, à Bauru, au Brésil, un garçon qui s'appelait Edson Arantes do Nascimento la bourrait de papier journal. Sa famille n'avait pas les moyens de lui en offrir un vrai.
Son père, Dondinho, était lui-même footballeur, et c'est lui qui a appris le jeu au garçon. Edson travaillait dans des salons de thé, et il passait avec la chaussette chaque heure qui lui restait.
Santos l'a recruté à quinze ans, et le Brésil l'a sélectionné à seize. Le 29 juin 1958, à dix-sept ans, il a marqué deux fois en finale de la Coupe du monde contre la Suède, et le Brésil a gagné 5-2.
Personne d'aussi jeune n'a marqué en finale depuis. Pelé, comme on l'appelait déjà, a encore gagné le tournoi en 1962 et en 1970, et ce troisième titre, personne ne l'a égalé.

Il est mort le 29 décembre 2022, à quatre-vingt-deux ans. Si la chaussette avait été un vrai ballon de cuir, l'histoire aurait été la même : ce qui a fait Pelé, ce n'est pas le ballon, ce sont les heures.

stories.summary: Dans les années 1940, un garçon pauvre du Brésil jouait dans la rue avec une chaussette pleine de papier journal ; à dix-sept ans, il a marqué deux fois en finale de la Coupe du monde.
stories.title: Un ballon fait d'une chaussette

grammar.body: To say someone has no thing, German uses „kein“ with the noun's ending: der Ball → „keinen Ball“ as the object.
grammar.example: Er hat keinen Ball.
grammar.title: Kein: the negative article

grammar.body: „Mit fünfzehn“ means „at fifteen“. When it opens the sentence, the verb comes next, then the subject.
grammar.example: Mit fünfzehn spielt er in einem großen Verein.
grammar.title: Mit + age, and the verb stays second

grammar.body: German „shoots“ goals: „ein Tor schießen“, plural „zwei Tore schießen“.
grammar.example: Im Finale der WM schießt er zwei Tore.
grammar.title: Tore schießen: to score goals

paragraphs: Es sind die 1940er Jahre in Bauru, Brasilien. Der kleine Edson mag Fußball sehr. Seine Familie ist arm. Er hat keinen Ball.
Also füllt er eine Socke mit Zeitungen. Das ist sein Ball! Jeden Tag spielt er damit auf der Straße.
Er arbeitet auch in Teestuben. Mit fünfzehn spielt er in einem großen Verein. Mit sechzehn spielt er für Brasilien.
Es ist 1958. Edson ist siebzehn. Im Finale der WM schießt er zwei Tore. Jetzt kennt ihn die Welt: Pelé.

grammar.body: Most verbs make the Perfekt with „haben“ and the Partizip II at the end. Two participles can share one „hat“.
grammar.example: Also hat Edson eine Socke mit Zeitungspapier gefüllt und damit gespielt.
grammar.title: Perfekt with haben: hat … gefüllt

grammar.body: Verbs of movement or change, like „kommen“, „fahren“ and „aufwachsen“, take „sein“ in the Perfekt.
grammar.example: Mit fünfzehn ist er zum Verein Santos gekommen.
grammar.title: Perfekt with sein: ist … gekommen

grammar.body: „Um“ + „zu“ + infinitive at the end says why someone does something.
grammar.example: Er hat auch in Teestuben gearbeitet, um seiner Familie zu helfen.
grammar.title: Um … zu: in order to

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento ist am 23. Oktober 1940 in Brasilien geboren. Er ist in Bauru aufgewachsen, seine Familie war arm.
Sein Vater, ein Fußballer, hat ihm das Spiel beigebracht. Aber ein Ball war zu teuer. Also hat Edson eine Socke mit Zeitungspapier gefüllt und damit gespielt.
Jeden Tag war er damit auf der Straße. Er hat auch in Teestuben gearbeitet, um seiner Familie zu helfen.
Mit fünfzehn ist er zum Verein Santos gekommen. Mit sechzehn war er in Brasiliens Mannschaft. 1958 ist er mit siebzehn zur WM nach Schweden gefahren.
Im Finale hat er zwei Tore geschossen, und Brasilien hat 5:2 gewonnen. Man hat ihn Pelé genannt. Der Ball war nie wichtig. Die Stunden auf der Straße waren es.

grammar.body: „Den“ and „die“ refer to a noun; „was“ refers to the whole idea before it (winning three times).
grammar.example: Er hat die Weltmeisterschaft dreimal gewonnen, was kein anderer Spieler geschafft hat.
grammar.title: Relative clauses: den, die, was

grammar.body: „Hatte“ + participle puts an action before another past one: he had stuffed the sock before playing with it.
grammar.example: Weil sich die Familie keinen Ball leisten konnte, hat der Junge mit einer Socke gespielt, die er mit Zeitungspapier ausgestopft hatte.
grammar.title: Plusquamperfekt: ausgestopft hatte

grammar.body: A separable verb puts „ge“ between the particle and the stem in the Partizip II: beibringen → „beigebracht“.
grammar.example: Sein Vater, ein Fußballer namens Dondinho, hat ihm das Fußballspielen beigebracht.
grammar.title: Separable verbs in the Perfekt: beigebracht

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, den die Welt als Pelé kennt, ist am 23. Oktober 1940 geboren und in Bauru, Brasilien, aufgewachsen.

Sein Vater, ein Fußballer namens Dondinho, hat ihm das Fußballspielen beigebracht. Weil sich die Familie keinen Ball leisten konnte, hat der Junge mit einer Socke gespielt, die er mit Zeitungspapier ausgestopft hatte.
Er war stundenlang damit auf der Straße und hat für Geld in Teestuben gearbeitet. Mit fünfzehn hat er bei Santos unterschrieben, mit sechzehn hat er für Brasilien gespielt.

Am 29. Juni 1958, im Finale der Weltmeisterschaft in Schweden, war er siebzehn. Er hat zwei Tore geschossen, Brasilien hat 5:2 gewonnen, und kein jüngerer Spieler hat je in einem Finale ein Tor geschossen.
Er hat die Weltmeisterschaft dreimal gewonnen, was kein anderer Spieler geschafft hat. Die Socke war egal. Was gezählt hat, waren die Tausende von Stunden.

grammar.body: Starting with the verb „Wäre“ replaces „Wenn die Socke … gewesen wäre“: an unreal condition in the past.
grammar.example: Wäre die Socke ein Lederball gewesen, hätte das nichts geändert: Nicht der Ball hat ihn geformt, sondern die Stunden.
grammar.title: Konjunktiv II without wenn: Wäre die Socke …

grammar.body: „Er war es, der …“ = he was the one who …: it puts weight on the person, and the relative clause has its verb at the end.
grammar.example: Sein Vater Dondinho war Fußballer, und er war es, der dem Jungen das Fußballspielen beigebracht hat.
grammar.title: Er war es, der …

grammar.body: The object „Einen echten Ball“ comes first for emphasis; the verb stays second and the subject follows. „Nämlich“ adds the reason.
grammar.example: Einen echten Ball konnte sich seine Familie nämlich nicht leisten.
grammar.title: Something other than the subject in first place

paragraphs: Der Ball war eine Socke. In den 1940er Jahren hat ein Junge namens Edson Arantes do Nascimento sie in Bauru, Brasilien, mit Zeitungspapier ausgestopft. Einen echten Ball konnte sich seine Familie nämlich nicht leisten.
Sein Vater Dondinho war Fußballer, und er war es, der dem Jungen das Fußballspielen beigebracht hat. Edson hat in Teestuben gearbeitet und jede freie Stunde mit der Socke verbracht.
Santos hat ihn mit fünfzehn unter Vertrag genommen, Brasilien mit sechzehn geholt. Am 29. Juni 1958 hat er mit siebzehn im Finale gegen Schweden zwei Tore geschossen, und Brasilien hat 5:2 gewonnen.

So jung hat seitdem keiner in einem Finale ein Tor geschossen. Pelé, wie ihn da schon alle genannt haben, hat das Turnier auch 1962 und 1970 gewonnen, und drei Titel hat bis heute kein anderer geschafft.
Er ist am 29. Dezember 2022 gestorben, mit zweiundachtzig. Wäre die Socke ein Lederball gewesen, hätte das nichts geändert: Nicht der Ball hat ihn geformt, sondern die Stunden.

stories.summary: In den 1940er Jahren hat ein armer Junge in Brasilien auf der Straße mit einer Socke voller Zeitungspapier gespielt, und mit siebzehn hat er im Finale einer Weltmeisterschaft zwei Tore geschossen.
stories.title: Ein Ball aus einer Socke

grammar.body: Spanish "has" years where English "is" years old: tiene diecisiete años = he is seventeen. The verb is tener, never ser or estar.
grammar.example: Edson tiene diecisiete años.
grammar.title: Tener + años: saying an age

grammar.body: A los quince años means "at fifteen". The word años can be left out the second time: a los dieciséis.
grammar.example: A los quince años juega en un gran club.
grammar.title: A los + age

grammar.body: After no tiene Spanish usually drops the article: no tiene pelota = he has no ball.
grammar.example: No tiene pelota.
grammar.title: No article after "no tiene"

paragraphs: Estamos en los años cuarenta, en Bauru, Brasil. Edson es un niño pobre. No tiene pelota.
Así que llena un calcetín con papel de periódico. ¡Esa es su pelota! Juega con ella en la calle cada día.
También trabaja en tiendas de té para ayudar a su familia. A los quince años juega en un gran club. A los dieciséis, ya está en la selección de Brasil.
Y llega 1958. Edson tiene diecisiete años. En la final de la Copa del Mundo, mete dos goles. Ahora el mundo conoce su nombre: Pelé.

grammar.body: For a finished action, he/she forms end in -ó for -ar verbs (llenó, trabajó, viajó) and in -ió for -er and -ir verbs (nació, creció, metió). The accent is always written.
grammar.example: Edson Arantes do Nascimento nació en Brasil el 23 de octubre de 1940 y creció en Bauru.
grammar.title: Pretérito indefinido: -ó and -ió

grammar.body: For how things were or what kept happening, Spanish uses the imperfect: era pobre, no tenían dinero, se pasaba el día. The events around it stay in the indefinido.
grammar.example: Pero no tenían dinero para una pelota.
grammar.title: Era, tenía, jugaba: the background

grammar.body: After a negative sentence, sí alone affirms the opposite: las horas, sí = the hours were (important). Spanish does not repeat the verb.
grammar.example: Las horas en la calle, sí.
grammar.title: Sí in place of a whole phrase

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento nació en Brasil el 23 de octubre de 1940 y creció en Bauru. Su familia era pobre.
Su padre era futbolista y le enseñó a jugar. Pero no tenían dinero para una pelota. Así que Edson llenó un calcetín con papel de periódico, y a jugar.
Se pasaba el día en la calle con el calcetín. También trabajaba en tiendas de té para ayudar a su familia.
A los quince años entró en el Santos. A los dieciséis ya jugaba con la selección de Brasil. En 1958 viajó a Suecia para la Copa del Mundo, con diecisiete años.
En la final metió dos goles, y Brasil ganó 5-2. Ya todos lo llamaban Pelé. La pelota nunca fue lo importante. Las horas en la calle, sí.

grammar.body: When the relative pronoun is a person and the object of the verb, Spanish uses a quien (with the personal a): a quien todo el mundo conoce = whom everybody knows.
grammar.example: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, a quien todo el mundo conoce como Pelé, nació el 23 de octubre de 1940 y creció en Bauru, en Brasil.
grammar.title: A quien: whom, for a person

grammar.body: Había rellenado shows the action that came first: he stuffed the sock, and then he practised with it.
grammar.example: Como en casa no había dinero para una pelota, el niño practicaba con un calcetín que él mismo había rellenado de papel de periódico.
grammar.title: Pluscuamperfecto: había + participle

grammar.body: Ha marcado and ha conseguido look at all the time up to now: no younger player, no other player, ever since.
grammar.example: Ganó la Copa del Mundo tres veces, algo que ningún otro jugador ha conseguido.
grammar.title: Pretérito perfecto up to today

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, a quien todo el mundo conoce como Pelé, nació el 23 de octubre de 1940 y creció en Bauru, en Brasil.
Su padre, un futbolista llamado Dondinho, le enseñó a jugar. Como en casa no había dinero para una pelota, el niño practicaba con un calcetín que él mismo había rellenado de papel de periódico.
Se pasaba horas en la calle con él, y trabajaba en tiendas de té para ganar algo de dinero. A los quince años fichó por el Santos, y al año siguiente ya jugaba con Brasil.
El 29 de junio de 1958, en la final de la Copa del Mundo en Suecia, tenía diecisiete años. Metió dos goles, Brasil ganó 5-2, y desde entonces nadie más joven ha marcado en una final del Mundial.
Ganó la Copa del Mundo tres veces, algo que ningún otro jugador ha conseguido. El calcetín no importaba. Los miles de horas con él, sí.

grammar.body: Si el calcetín hubiera sido… la historia sería…: an unreal condition about the past takes hubiera + participle, and the result goes in the conditional.
grammar.example: Si el calcetín hubiera sido una pelota de cuero, la historia sería la misma: lo que hizo a Pelé no fue la pelota, sino las horas.
grammar.title: Si + pluperfect subjunctive

grammar.body: Ser + stressed element + quien puts the weight on one person: it was he, not somebody else, who taught the boy. Ser takes the tense of the main action (fue… enseñó).
grammar.example: Su padre, Dondinho, también era futbolista, y fue él quien le enseñó el juego al niño.
grammar.title: Fue él quien…: the cleft sentence

grammar.body: Volvió a ganar = he won again: volver a + infinitive is the everyday way to say "again".
grammar.example: Pelé, como ya lo llamaban, volvió a ganar el torneo en 1962 y en 1970: tres veces campeón, algo que nadie ha igualado.
grammar.title: Volver a + infinitive

paragraphs: La pelota era un calcetín. En los años cuarenta, en las calles de Bauru, Brasil, un niño llamado Edson Arantes do Nascimento lo rellenaba de papel de periódico. No había dinero para una de verdad.
Su padre, Dondinho, también era futbolista, y fue él quien le enseñó el juego al niño. Edson trabajaba en tiendas de té y le dedicaba al calcetín todas sus horas libres.

El Santos lo fichó a los quince años; la selección lo llamó a los dieciséis. El 29 de junio de 1958, con diecisiete años, metió dos goles en la final de la Copa del Mundo, y Brasil le ganó 5-2 a Suecia.
Desde entonces, nadie tan joven ha marcado en una final del Mundial. Pelé, como ya lo llamaban, volvió a ganar el torneo en 1962 y en 1970: tres veces campeón, algo que nadie ha igualado.
Murió el 29 de diciembre de 2022, a los ochenta y dos años. Si el calcetín hubiera sido una pelota de cuero, la historia sería la misma: lo que hizo a Pelé no fue la pelota, sino las horas.

stories.summary: En los años cuarenta, un niño pobre de Brasil daba patadas por la calle a un calcetín lleno de papel de periódico; a los diecisiete años, metió dos goles en una final del Mundial.
stories.title: Una pelota hecha con un calcetín

grammar.body: Italian says age with avere (to have): Edson ha diciassette anni = Edson is seventeen. Without the verb, a + number works too: a quindici anni = at fifteen.
grammar.example: Poi arriva il 1958, ed Edson ha diciassette anni.
grammar.title: Age with avere: ha diciassette anni

grammar.body: Italian puts the article before mio, tuo, suo: la sua famiglia = his family. With a single family member (suo padre) the article drops.
grammar.example: Ma la sua famiglia è povera, e non ha un pallone.
grammar.title: The article before the possessive

grammar.body: Ci can stand for 'with it': ci gioca = he plays with it (with the sock).
grammar.example: Ci gioca in strada tutti i giorni.
grammar.title: Ci for 'with it'

paragraphs: Sono gli anni Quaranta, a Bauru, in Brasile. Edson è un bambino e ama il calcio. Ma la sua famiglia è povera, e non ha un pallone.
Così riempie un calzino di carta vecchia. Ecco il suo pallone! Ci gioca in strada tutti i giorni.
Lavora anche nei negozi di tè. A quindici anni gioca in un grande club. A sedici è nella squadra del Brasile.
Poi arriva il 1958, ed Edson ha diciassette anni. Nella finale dei Mondiali fa due gol. Adesso tutto il mondo conosce il suo nome: Pelé.

grammar.body: The passato prossimo tells the one event (ha riempito = he filled); the imperfetto tells what he did again and again (giocava = he played with it, day after day).
grammar.example: Così Edson ha riempito un calzino di giornali, e giocava con quello.
grammar.title: Passato prossimo and imperfetto

grammar.body: The imperfetto (era, aveva) describes the situation, while the passato prossimo tells what happened in it.
grammar.example: Nel 1958 è andato ai Mondiali in Svezia, e aveva solo diciassette anni.
grammar.title: Era, aveva: the background

grammar.body: After a negative sentence, sì alone says 'but this one yes': le ore in strada sì = the hours in the street were.
grammar.example: Le ore in strada sì.
grammar.title: Sì instead of repeating the verb

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento è nato in Brasile il 23 ottobre 1940. È cresciuto a Bauru, e la sua famiglia era povera.
Suo padre era un calciatore e gli ha insegnato il gioco. Ma non avevano soldi per un pallone. Così Edson ha riempito un calzino di giornali, e giocava con quello.
Era in strada con il calzino tutti i giorni. Lavorava anche nei negozi di tè, per aiutare la famiglia.
A quindici anni ha firmato con il Santos, un grande club. A sedici era già nella squadra del Brasile. Nel 1958 è andato ai Mondiali in Svezia, e aveva solo diciassette anni.
Nella finale ha fatto due gol, e il Brasile ha vinto 5–2. La gente lo ha chiamato Pelé. Il pallone non è mai stato importante. Le ore in strada sì.

grammar.body: Che refers back to a noun; cosa che (or il che) refers back to a whole idea: tre volte, cosa che nessun altro ha fatto = three times, which nobody else has done.
grammar.example: In tutto ha vinto la Coppa del Mondo tre volte, cosa che nessun altro giocatore ha fatto.
grammar.title: Che and cosa che: relative clauses

grammar.body: Aveva riempito (had filled) puts one past action before another: imperfetto of avere plus the participle.
grammar.example: La famiglia non poteva permettersi un pallone, così il bambino giocava di solito con un calzino che aveva riempito di giornali.
grammar.title: Trapassato prossimo: aveva riempito

grammar.body: Restava, lavorava: the imperfetto tells habits and long stretches of time, not single events.
grammar.example: Restava in strada per ore con quel calzino e lavorava nei negozi di tè per guadagnare qualcosa.
grammar.title: Imperfetto for what went on and on

paragraphs: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, che il mondo conosce come Pelé, è nato il 23 ottobre 1940 ed è cresciuto a Bauru, in Brasile.

Suo padre, un calciatore che si chiamava Dondinho, gli ha insegnato il gioco. La famiglia non poteva permettersi un pallone, così il bambino giocava di solito con un calzino che aveva riempito di giornali.
Restava in strada per ore con quel calzino e lavorava nei negozi di tè per guadagnare qualcosa. A quindici anni ha firmato per il Santos, e un anno dopo giocava già nel Brasile.
Il 29 giugno 1958, nella finale dei Mondiali in Svezia, aveva diciassette anni. Ha fatto due gol, il Brasile ha vinto 5–2, e nessuno più giovane ha mai fatto gol in una finale.
In tutto ha vinto la Coppa del Mondo tre volte, cosa che nessun altro giocatore ha fatto. Il calzino non contava. Le migliaia di ore con quel calzino sì.

grammar.body: Se il calzino fosse stato (past subjunctive) un pallone, la storia sarebbe (present conditional) la stessa: a past condition with a result that is still true now.
grammar.example: Se il calzino fosse stato un pallone di cuoio, la storia sarebbe la stessa: a fare di lui Pelé non è stato il pallone, ma le ore.
grammar.title: Mixed conditional: se + fosse stato, sarebbe

grammar.body: È stato lui a insegnargli = it was he who taught him: essere + person + a + infinitive puts the weight on who did it.
grammar.example: Suo padre, Dondinho, era calciatore anche lui, ed è stato lui a insegnargli il gioco.
grammar.title: È stato lui a + infinitive

grammar.body: Come + imperfetto describes what had become usual: come ormai lo chiamavano tutti = as everyone called him by then. The events stay in the passato prossimo: ha vinto.
grammar.example: Pelé, come ormai lo chiamavano tutti, ha vinto il torneo anche nel 1962 e nel 1970, e quel terzo titolo è un record che nessuno ha ancora eguagliato.
grammar.title: Come lo chiamavano: as they called him

paragraphs: Il pallone era un calzino. Negli anni Quaranta, per le strade di Bauru, in Brasile, un bambino di nome Edson Arantes do Nascimento lo riempiva di giornali, perché la famiglia non poteva permettersene uno vero.
Suo padre, Dondinho, era calciatore anche lui, ed è stato lui a insegnargli il gioco. Edson lavorava nei negozi di tè e passava col calzino tutte le ore che gli restavano.

Il Santos l'ha preso a quindici anni, il Brasile l'ha convocato a sedici. Il 29 giugno 1958, a diciassette anni, ha fatto due gol nella finale dei Mondiali contro la Svezia, e il Brasile ha vinto 5–2.

Da allora nessuno così giovane ha più fatto gol in una finale. Pelé, come ormai lo chiamavano tutti, ha vinto il torneo anche nel 1962 e nel 1970, e quel terzo titolo è un record che nessuno ha ancora eguagliato.
È morto il 29 dicembre 2022, a ottantadue anni. Se il calzino fosse stato un pallone di cuoio, la storia sarebbe la stessa: a fare di lui Pelé non è stato il pallone, ma le ore.

stories.summary: Negli anni Quaranta un bambino povero in Brasile calciava per strada un calzino pieno di giornali; a diciassette anni ha fatto due gol in una finale dei Mondiali.
stories.title: Un pallone fatto con un calzino

grammar.body: "Can" + the base verb says what is possible: fathers can stay home. Questions put "can" before the subject.
grammar.example: What can a husband or partner do?
grammar.title: Can + verb

grammar.body: To say no in the present with he, she or it, use doesn't + the base verb, with no -s: he doesn't smoke.
grammar.example: He doesn't smoke.
grammar.title: He doesn't + verb

grammar.body: Yes/no questions with "be" put the verb first: Is she sad?
grammar.example: Is she sad for more than two weeks?
grammar.title: A question that starts with the verb

paragraphs: It's 1974, and Sweden has a new law. Fathers can stay home with a new baby too. But almost no fathers do.
In 1995, one month is only for the father. People call it the father's month.
What can a husband or partner do? He goes to the doctor with her. He doesn't smoke. He holds the baby and gets up at night.
Is she sad for more than two weeks? Then they talk to the midwife or the doctor.

grammar.body: The negative past simple is didn't + the base verb: he didn't use it (not "didn't used").
grammar.example: If the father didn't use his month, the family lost it.
grammar.title: Past simple, and "didn't"

grammar.body: "Could stay home" says what was possible in the past.
grammar.example: After a birth, the mother or the father could stay home and still get paid.
grammar.title: Could: the past of can

grammar.body: "Before the birth" and "after the birth" take a noun; they set the time for the whole sentence.
grammar.example: Before the birth, he can go to the appointments and stop smoking.
grammar.title: Before and after + noun

paragraphs: On 1 January 1974, Sweden made a new law. After a birth, the mother or the father could stay home and still get paid.
But that year, fathers took only half a per cent of the days.
In 1995, Sweden set one month aside for each parent. If the father didn't use his month, the family lost it. People called it the father's month. Today fathers take about thirty per cent of the days.
What can a husband or partner do? Before the birth, he can go to the appointments and stop smoking. After the birth, he can hold the baby and share the nights.
Is she sad for more than two weeks? Then ask the midwife or the doctor.

grammar.body: "If the father didn't take his" is a real condition in the past: whenever this happened, the result followed. His = his month.
grammar.example: If the father didn't take his, the family lost it, and people called it the father's month.
grammar.title: Didn't + base verb in an if-clause

grammar.body: "Who could share" adds information about the parents just named.
grammar.example: On 1 January 1974 Sweden became the first country to give parental leave to both parents, who could share 180 paid days.
grammar.title: Relative clause with who

grammar.body: "Should" + the base verb gives advice: they should talk to the midwife.
grammar.example: If it stays, they should talk to the midwife or the doctor.
grammar.title: Should + verb for advice

paragraphs: On 1 January 1974 Sweden became the first country to give parental leave to both parents, who could share 180 paid days.
But that year, mothers took 99.5 per cent of the days. So in 1995, Sweden kept one month for each parent. If the father didn't take his, the family lost it, and people called it the father's month.
Today fathers take about thirty per cent of the days.

That month gave fathers time to learn what a husband or partner can do. Before the birth, he can go to the appointments and stop smoking, because smoke can harm the baby. Afterwards he can hold the baby, do some of the feeds and share the nights.
The sadness of the first days usually goes within two weeks. If it stays, they should talk to the midwife or the doctor.

grammar.body: "What those months made room for" is the subject of "is"; the sentence puts the new information at the end.
grammar.example: What those months made room for is what any husband or partner can do.
grammar.title: A wh-clause as the subject

grammar.body: "A month the father didn't use" leaves out "that": a month that the father didn't use.
grammar.example: From 1995, one month was set aside for each parent, and a month the father didn't use was lost.
grammar.title: Reduced relative clause

grammar.body: After "it's", -ing forms can name activities in a list: holding, doing, sharing.
grammar.example: Afterwards, it's holding the baby, doing some of the feeds, sharing the nights.
grammar.title: -ing forms in a list

paragraphs: On 1 January 1974, Sweden became the first country to swap maternity leave for parental leave: 180 paid days that either parent could take. That year, mothers took 99.5 per cent of them.
From 1995, one month was set aside for each parent, and a month the father didn't use was lost. Before the reform, more than half of fathers took no leave; afterwards, fewer than one in five.
The father's month, as people called it, became two in 2002 and three in 2016. Today fathers take about thirty per cent of the days.

What those months made room for is what any husband or partner can do. Before the birth, that's going to appointments and quitting smoking, since second-hand smoke can harm the baby. Afterwards, it's holding the baby, doing some of the feeds, sharing the nights.
Low mood that lasts more than two weeks, in her or him, is a reason to see the midwife or the doctor.

stories.summary: In 1974 Sweden let fathers stay home with a new baby, and almost none did; in 1995 it set one month aside just for them, and that changed what a father does.
stories.title: The Father's Month

grammar.body: « Peuvent » (from pouvoir, can) is followed by a verb in the infinitive: les pères peuvent rester.
grammar.example: Les pères aussi peuvent rester à la maison avec le bébé.
grammar.title: Pouvoir + infinitive: can

grammar.body: In speech, a question can keep the normal word order and put « quoi » (what) at the end: il fait quoi ? = what does he do?
grammar.example: Et un mari ou un partenaire, il fait quoi ?
grammar.title: Il fait quoi ? A spoken question

grammar.body: Spoken French often asks a yes-or-no question with no change at all, just a rising voice and a question mark. With « depuis », the verb stays in the present.
grammar.example: Elle est triste depuis plus de deux semaines ?
grammar.title: A question with the voice only

paragraphs: En 1974, la Suède a une nouvelle loi. Les pères aussi peuvent rester à la maison avec le bébé. Mais presque aucun ne le fait.
En 1995, un mois est juste pour le père. Les gens l'appellent « le mois du père ».
Et un mari ou un partenaire, il fait quoi ? Il va chez le médecin avec la mère. Il ne fume pas. Il tient le bébé et se lève la nuit.
Elle est triste depuis plus de deux semaines ? Ils en parlent à la sage-femme ou au médecin.

grammar.body: The spoken past is avoir + past participle: a fait, ont pris, a réservé. An object pronoun goes before avoir: les gens l'ont appelé.
grammar.example: Alors, en 1995, la Suède a réservé un mois à chaque parent.
grammar.title: Passé composé for what happened

grammar.body: « Avant la naissance » says when; to stop doing something is « arrêter de » + infinitive: arrêter de fumer.
grammar.example: Avant la naissance, il peut aller aux rendez-vous et arrêter de fumer.
grammar.title: Avant / après + noun, arrêter de + verb

grammar.body: In a positive imperative, the pronoun goes after the verb with a hyphen: parlez-en = talk about it. « En » stands for « de ça ».
grammar.example: Alors, parlez-en à la sage-femme ou au médecin.
grammar.title: Parlez-en: imperative with en

paragraphs: Le 1er janvier 1974, la Suède a fait une nouvelle loi. Après une naissance, la mère ou le père pouvait rester à la maison et garder son salaire.
Mais cette année-là, les pères ont pris seulement un demi pour cent des jours.

Alors, en 1995, la Suède a réservé un mois à chaque parent. Si le père ne prenait pas son mois, la famille le perdait. Les gens l'ont appelé « le mois du père ». Aujourd'hui, les pères prennent environ trente pour cent des jours.
Et un mari ou un partenaire, qu'est-ce qu'il peut faire ? Avant la naissance, il peut aller aux rendez-vous et arrêter de fumer. Après, il peut tenir le bébé et partager les nuits.
La mère est triste depuis plus de deux semaines ? Alors, parlez-en à la sage-femme ou au médecin.

grammar.body: « Qui » is the subject of the clause it opens and adds information about the noun before it: les deux parents, qui pouvaient se partager…
grammar.example: Le 1er janvier 1974, la Suède est devenue le premier pays à donner un congé parental aux deux parents, qui pouvaient se partager 180 jours payés.
grammar.title: Relative clause with qui

grammar.body: « Le sien » replaces « son mois » so the noun isn't repeated; it agrees with the thing owned (le mois → le sien).
grammar.example: Si le père ne prenait pas le sien, le mois était perdu, et les gens ont commencé à l'appeler « le mois du père ».
grammar.title: Le sien: his own

grammar.body: « Il vaut mieux » + infinitive gives friendly advice: il vaut mieux en parler = it's best to talk about it.
grammar.example: Si elle reste, il vaut mieux en parler à la sage-femme ou au médecin.
grammar.title: Il vaut mieux: it's better to

paragraphs: Le 1er janvier 1974, la Suède est devenue le premier pays à donner un congé parental aux deux parents, qui pouvaient se partager 180 jours payés.

Mais cette année-là, les mères ont pris 99,5 pour cent des jours. En 1995, on a réservé un mois à chaque parent. Si le père ne prenait pas le sien, le mois était perdu, et les gens ont commencé à l'appeler « le mois du père ».
Aujourd'hui, les pères prennent environ trente pour cent des jours.

Ce mois a donné aux pères le temps d'apprendre ce qu'un mari ou partenaire peut faire. Avant la naissance, il peut aller aux rendez-vous et arrêter de fumer, parce que la fumée peut faire du mal au bébé. Après, il peut tenir le bébé, donner une partie des repas et partager les nuits.
La tristesse des premiers jours passe en général en deux semaines. Si elle reste, il vaut mieux en parler à la sage-femme ou au médecin.

grammar.body: French puts the weight at the end by naming the topic first (ce que ces mois ont permis) and taking it up again with « c'est ».
grammar.example: Ce que ces mois ont permis, c'est ce qu'un mari ou un partenaire peut faire.
grammar.title: Ce que …, c'est …

grammar.body: « En » replaces « des jours » before a number or amount: les mères en ont pris 99,5 pour cent = mothers took 99.5 per cent of them.
grammar.example: Cette année-là, les mères en ont pris 99,5 pour cent.
grammar.title: En for « of them »

grammar.body: After a colon or a time phrase, French can list actions as bare infinitives: tenir le bébé, donner une partie des repas, partager les nuits.
grammar.example: Après, tenir le bébé, donner une partie des repas, partager les nuits.
grammar.title: Infinitives in a list

paragraphs: Le 1er janvier 1974, la Suède est devenue le premier pays à remplacer le congé maternité par un congé parental : 180 jours payés, que l'un ou l'autre parent pouvait prendre. Cette année-là, les mères en ont pris 99,5 pour cent.

À partir de 1995, un mois a été réservé à chaque parent, et un mois que le père ne prenait pas était perdu. Avant la réforme, plus de la moitié des pères ne prenaient aucun congé ; après, moins d'un sur cinq.
Le mois du père, comme on l'appelait, est passé à deux mois en 2002, puis à trois en 2016. Aujourd'hui, les pères prennent environ trente pour cent des jours.

Ce que ces mois ont permis, c'est ce qu'un mari ou un partenaire peut faire. Avant la naissance, aller aux rendez-vous et arrêter de fumer, puisque le tabagisme passif peut faire du mal au bébé. Après, tenir le bébé, donner une partie des repas, partager les nuits.
Un moral en berne qui dure plus de deux semaines, chez elle comme chez lui, c'est une raison d'aller voir la sage-femme ou le médecin.

stories.summary: En 1974, la Suède a laissé les pères rester à la maison avec un nouveau bébé, et presque aucun ne l'a fait ; en 1995, elle leur a réservé un mois, et ça a changé ce que fait un père.
stories.title: Le mois du père

grammar.body: The modal „können“ sits second and sends the main verb to the very end: „können … zu Hause bleiben“.
grammar.example: Auch Väter können jetzt mit dem Baby zu Hause bleiben.
grammar.title: Können + infinitive at the end

grammar.body: „Aufstehen“ (to get up) splits in the present: „steht“ second, „auf“ at the end of the clause.
grammar.example: Er hält das Baby und steht nachts auf.
grammar.title: Separable verbs: steht … auf

grammar.body: Without a question word, the verb comes first: „Ist sie … traurig?“
grammar.example: Ist sie länger als zwei Wochen traurig?
grammar.title: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb

paragraphs: Es ist 1974, und Schweden hat ein neues Gesetz. Auch Väter können jetzt mit dem Baby zu Hause bleiben. Aber fast kein Vater macht das.
1995 gibt es dann einen Monat nur für den Vater. Die Leute nennen ihn Papamonat.
Was kann ein Ehemann oder Partner tun? Er geht mit ihr zur Ärztin. Er raucht nicht. Er hält das Baby und steht nachts auf.
Ist sie länger als zwei Wochen traurig? Dann fragen die beiden die Hebamme oder die Ärztin.

grammar.body: Most verbs form the Perfekt with „haben“; the participle goes to the end: „haben … genommen“.
grammar.example: Aber 1974 haben Väter nur ein halbes Prozent der Tage genommen.
grammar.title: Perfekt: haben + Partizip II at the end

grammar.body: When the „wenn“ clause comes first, its verb is last, and the main clause starts with its verb: „…, hat die Familie …“.
grammar.example: Wenn der Vater seinen Monat nicht genommen hat, hat die Familie ihn verloren.
grammar.title: A wenn-clause first: verb, comma, verb

grammar.body: „Vor“ (before) and „nach“ (after) take the dative when they mean time: „vor der Geburt“, „nach der Geburt“.
grammar.example: Vor der Geburt kann er zu den Terminen mitgehen und mit dem Rauchen aufhören.
grammar.title: Vor and nach with the dative

paragraphs: Am ersten Januar 1974 hat Schweden ein neues Gesetz gemacht. Nach einer Geburt kann die Mutter oder der Vater zu Hause bleiben. Geld gibt es trotzdem.
Aber 1974 haben Väter nur ein halbes Prozent der Tage genommen.

Deshalb hat Schweden 1995 jedem Elternteil einen Monat reserviert. Wenn der Vater seinen Monat nicht genommen hat, hat die Familie ihn verloren. Die Leute haben ihn Papamonat genannt. Heute nehmen Väter etwa dreißig Prozent der Tage.
Was kann ein Ehemann oder Partner tun? Vor der Geburt kann er zu den Terminen mitgehen und mit dem Rauchen aufhören. Danach kann er das Baby halten und die Nächte teilen.
Ist sie länger als zwei Wochen traurig? Dann fragen die beiden die Hebamme oder die Ärztin.

grammar.body: „Einführen“ (to introduce) puts „ge“ between particle and stem: „hat … eingeführt“.
grammar.example: Am ersten Januar 1974 hat Schweden als erstes Land eine Elternzeit für beide Eltern eingeführt: 180 bezahlte Tage, die sie sich teilen konnten.
grammar.title: Separable verb in the Perfekt: eingeführt

grammar.body: Speech often says „hat man … reserviert“ (they set aside) where writing would use a passive (wurde … reserviert).
grammar.example: Deshalb hat man 1995 für jeden Elternteil einen Monat reserviert.
grammar.title: „man“ instead of a passive

grammar.body: „Sollten“ + infinitive gives advice: „sollten die beiden … sprechen“ = they should talk to …
grammar.example: Bleibt sie, sollten die beiden mit der Hebamme oder der Ärztin sprechen.
grammar.title: Sollten: a piece of advice

paragraphs: Am ersten Januar 1974 hat Schweden als erstes Land eine Elternzeit für beide Eltern eingeführt: 180 bezahlte Tage, die sie sich teilen konnten.

Aber in dem Jahr haben Mütter 99,5 Prozent der Tage genommen. Deshalb hat man 1995 für jeden Elternteil einen Monat reserviert. Wenn der Vater seinen Monat nicht genommen hat, ist er verfallen, und die Leute haben ihn Papamonat genannt.
Heute nehmen Väter etwa dreißig Prozent der Tage.

In diesem Monat haben Väter gelernt, was ein Ehemann oder Partner tun kann. Vor der Geburt kann er zu den Terminen mitgehen und mit dem Rauchen aufhören, weil Rauch dem Baby schaden kann. Danach kann er das Baby halten, einen Teil der Mahlzeiten übernehmen und die Nächte teilen.
Die Traurigkeit der ersten Tage vergeht meistens in zwei Wochen. Bleibt sie, sollten die beiden mit der Hebamme oder der Ärztin sprechen.

grammar.body: „Verfallen“ (to lapse, expire) is a change of state, so its Perfekt takes „sein“: „ist verfallen“. The relative clause „den der Vater nicht genommen hat“ sits inside, with its verb last.
grammar.example: Ab 1995 hatte jeder Elternteil einen eigenen Monat, und ein Monat, den der Vater nicht genommen hat, ist verfallen.
grammar.title: „verfallen“ with sein

grammar.body: „Aus etwas wird etwas“ = something turns into something: „aus dem Papamonat sind zwei geworden“.
grammar.example: Aus dem Papamonat, wie die Leute ihn genannt haben, sind 2002 zwei geworden und 2016 drei.
grammar.title: Aus … werden: to turn into

grammar.body: Advice and to-do lists often use bare infinitives instead of full sentences: „das Baby halten, … die Nächte teilen“.
grammar.example: Danach: das Baby halten, einen Teil der Mahlzeiten übernehmen, die Nächte teilen.
grammar.title: Infinitives in a list

paragraphs: Am ersten Januar 1974 hat Schweden als erstes Land den Mutterschaftsurlaub durch eine Elternzeit ersetzt: 180 bezahlte Tage, die jeder Elternteil nehmen konnte. In dem Jahr haben Mütter 99,5 Prozent davon genommen.

Ab 1995 hatte jeder Elternteil einen eigenen Monat, und ein Monat, den der Vater nicht genommen hat, ist verfallen. Vorher hat mehr als die Hälfte der Väter keine Elternzeit genommen, danach weniger als jeder fünfte.
Aus dem Papamonat, wie die Leute ihn genannt haben, sind 2002 zwei geworden und 2016 drei. Heute nehmen Väter etwa dreißig Prozent der Tage.

Diese Monate haben Platz geschaffen für das, was jeder Ehemann oder Partner tun kann. Vor der Geburt: zu den Terminen mitgehen und mit dem Rauchen aufhören, weil Passivrauch dem Baby schaden kann. Danach: das Baby halten, einen Teil der Mahlzeiten übernehmen, die Nächte teilen.
Wenn die Stimmung länger als zwei Wochen schlecht bleibt, bei ihr oder ihm, ist das ein Grund, die Hebamme oder die Ärztin zu fragen.

stories.summary: 1974 hat Schweden den Vätern erlaubt, bei einem neuen Baby zu Hause zu bleiben, und fast keiner hat es gemacht; seit 1995 gibt es einen Monat nur für sie, und der hat verändert, was ein Vater tut.
stories.title: Der Papamonat

grammar.body: Spanish can name a whole group with el + singular noun: el padre = fathers in general. The plural "los padres" usually means the parents, mother and father together.
grammar.example: El padre también puede quedarse en casa con su bebé.
grammar.title: El padre: the singular for a whole group

grammar.body: The negative is just "no" before the verb, with no helping verb: fuma → no fuma. The ending -a already says "he" or "she", so él is left out.
grammar.example: No fuma.
grammar.title: No + verb, and no subject pronoun

grammar.body: When the direct object is a person, Spanish puts "a" before it, and a + el becomes al: tiene al bebé = he holds the baby.
grammar.example: Tiene al bebé en brazos y se levanta por la noche.
grammar.title: A before a person: al bebé

paragraphs: Es 1974, y Suecia tiene una ley nueva. El padre también puede quedarse en casa con su bebé. Pero casi ningún padre lo hace.
En 1995, un mes es solo para el padre. La gente lo llama el mes del padre.
¿Qué puede hacer un marido o una pareja? Va al médico con la madre. No fuma. Tiene al bebé en brazos y se levanta por la noche.
¿La madre está triste más de dos semanas? Entonces hablan con la matrona o el médico.

grammar.body: A finished action in the past takes the indefinido: -ar verbs end in -ó for he/she (reservó, tomó, llamó), and hacer is irregular (hizo).
grammar.example: Por eso, en 1995 Suecia reservó un mes para la madre y otro para el padre.
grammar.title: Pretérito indefinido: hizo, reservó, tomó

grammar.body: For what was true every time, not one single event, Spanish uses the imperfect: -ar verbs take -aba (usaba), -er and -ir verbs take -ía (perdía, podían).
grammar.example: Si el padre no usaba su mes, la familia lo perdía.
grammar.title: Usaba, perdía: how the rule worked

grammar.body: An instruction to one person uses the tú imperative, which for regular verbs looks like the él/ella present form: pregunta = ask.
grammar.example: Entonces pregunta a la matrona o al médico.
grammar.title: The tú imperative: pregunta

paragraphs: El 1 de enero de 1974, Suecia hizo una ley nueva. Después de un nacimiento, la madre o el padre podían quedarse en casa y seguir cobrando.
Pero ese año, el padre tomó solo el 0,5 por ciento de los días.

Por eso, en 1995 Suecia reservó un mes para la madre y otro para el padre. Si el padre no usaba su mes, la familia lo perdía. La gente lo llamó el mes del padre. Hoy el padre toma alrededor del treinta por ciento de los días.
¿Qué puede hacer un marido o una pareja? Antes del nacimiento, puede ir a las consultas y no fumar. Después, puede tener al bebé en brazos y compartir las noches.
¿La madre está triste durante más de dos semanas? Entonces pregunta a la matrona o al médico.

grammar.body: Spanish avoids "fue reservado" and prefers se + a third-person verb when it does not matter who acted: se reservó un mes = a month was reserved; se perdía = it was lost.
grammar.example: Así que en 1995 se reservó un mes para cada uno.
grammar.title: Se + verb instead of the passive

grammar.body: Soler says what normally happens, not what always happens: se suele pasar = it usually goes away. The se of pasarse can go before soler.
grammar.example: La tristeza de los primeros días se suele pasar en unas dos semanas.
grammar.title: Soler + infinitive: usually

grammar.body: Conviene hablar = it's a good idea to talk. Convenir gives friendly advice without saying "you must".
grammar.example: Si no se va, conviene hablar con la matrona o el médico.
grammar.title: Conviene + infinitive: it's a good idea

paragraphs: El 1 de enero de 1974, Suecia fue el primer país con un permiso parental para los dos. La madre y el padre podían repartirse 180 días pagados.
Pero ese año las madres se quedaron con el 99,5 por ciento. Así que en 1995 se reservó un mes para cada uno. Si el padre no tomaba el suyo, se perdía, y la gente lo llamó el mes del padre.
Hoy el padre toma alrededor del treinta por ciento de los días.

Ese mes le dio al padre tiempo para aprender lo que puede hacer un marido o una pareja. Antes del nacimiento, puede ir a las consultas y no fumar, porque el humo puede hacerle daño al bebé. Después, puede tener al bebé en brazos, darle de comer algunas veces y compartir las noches.
La tristeza de los primeros días se suele pasar en unas dos semanas. Si no se va, conviene hablar con la matrona o el médico.

grammar.body: When the relative clause describes something not identified (whichever month went unused), Spanish uses the subjunctive: el mes que el padre no usara.
grammar.example: Desde 1995 hubo un mes para cada uno, y el mes que el padre no usara se perdía.
grammar.title: Subjunctive in a relative clause: no usara

grammar.body: Where English lists actions with -ing forms, Spanish uses the infinitive: tener, darle, compartir = holding, feeding, sharing. Pronouns are attached to it (darle).
grammar.example: Después, tener al bebé en brazos, darle de comer algunas veces, compartir las noches.
grammar.title: The infinitive as a noun in a list

grammar.body: Pasó a ser dos = it went on to be two. Pasar a ser describes a change into a new state or number.
grammar.example: El mes del padre, como lo llamaba la gente, pasó a ser dos en 2002 y tres en 2016.
grammar.title: Pasar a ser: to become

paragraphs: El 1 de enero de 1974, Suecia fue el primer país en cambiar el permiso de maternidad por un permiso parental: 180 días pagados que podía tomar cualquiera de los dos. Ese año, las madres se quedaron con el 99,5 por ciento.
Desde 1995 hubo un mes para cada uno, y el mes que el padre no usara se perdía. Antes de la reforma, más de la mitad de los padres no tomaba ni un día; después, menos de uno de cada cinco.
El mes del padre, como lo llamaba la gente, pasó a ser dos en 2002 y tres en 2016. Hoy el padre toma alrededor del treinta por ciento de los días.

Esos meses dejaron sitio para lo que puede hacer cualquier marido o pareja. Antes del nacimiento, ir a las consultas y no fumar, porque el humo de otros puede hacerle daño al bebé. Después, tener al bebé en brazos, darle de comer algunas veces, compartir las noches.
Si el ánimo bajo dura más de dos semanas, en ella o en él, conviene ir a la matrona o al médico.

stories.summary: En 1974 Suecia dejó que el padre se quedara en casa con su bebé, y casi ninguno lo hizo; en 1995 le guardó un mes solo para él, y eso cambió lo que hace un padre.
stories.title: El mes del padre

grammar.body: Potere (can) is followed directly by an infinitive: può fare = he can do; possono stare = they can stay.
grammar.example: E un marito o un partner, che cosa può fare?
grammar.title: Potere + infinitive

grammar.body: To say 'not', put non before the verb: non fuma = he does not smoke.
grammar.example: Non fuma.
grammar.title: Non before the verb

grammar.body: The present + da says how long something has been going on: è triste da più di due settimane = she has been sad for more than two weeks.
grammar.example: La mamma è triste da più di due settimane?
grammar.title: Da + time with the present

paragraphs: È il 1974, in Svezia. C'è una legge nuova. I padri possono stare a casa con il neonato. Ma quasi nessun padre lo fa.
Allora, nel 1995, c'è un mese solo per il padre. La gente lo chiama il mese del papà.
E un marito o un partner, che cosa può fare? Va con la mamma alle visite dal medico. Non fuma. Tiene in braccio il bambino e di notte si alza.
La mamma è triste da più di due settimane? Allora ne parlano con l'ostetrica o con il medico.

grammar.body: Most verbs form the passato prossimo with avere: ha riservato = it set aside; hanno preso = they took.
grammar.example: Così, nel 1995, la Svezia ha riservato un mese a ogni genitore.
grammar.title: Passato prossimo: avere + past participle

grammar.body: Potevano says what was possible over a period: they could stay at home, from then on.
grammar.example: Dopo una nascita, la madre o il padre potevano restare a casa ed essere pagati lo stesso.
grammar.title: Potevano: the imperfetto of potere

grammar.body: Prima di + article + noun = before: prima della nascita. Dopo can stand alone: dopo = afterwards.
grammar.example: Prima della nascita può andare alle visite e smettere di fumare.
grammar.title: Prima di and dopo + noun

paragraphs: Il primo gennaio 1974 la Svezia ha fatto una legge nuova. Dopo una nascita, la madre o il padre potevano restare a casa ed essere pagati lo stesso.
Ma quell'anno i papà hanno preso appena lo 0,5 per cento dei giorni.

Così, nel 1995, la Svezia ha riservato un mese a ogni genitore. Se il padre non usava il suo mese, la famiglia lo perdeva. La gente l'ha chiamato il mese del papà. Oggi i padri prendono circa il trenta per cento dei giorni.
E un marito o un partner, che cosa può fare? Prima della nascita può andare alle visite e smettere di fumare. Dopo, può tenere in braccio il bambino e fare a turno di notte.
La mamma è triste da più di due settimane? Allora parlatene con l'ostetrica o con il medico.

grammar.body: After il primo, l'ultimo or l'unico, Italian uses a + infinitive: il primo paese a dare = the first country to give.
grammar.example: Il primo gennaio 1974 la Svezia è diventata il primo paese a dare il congedo parentale a tutti e due i genitori.
grammar.title: Il primo a + infinitive

grammar.body: Andare + past participle can replace essere in the passive; andare perso is the everyday way to say 'to be lost, wasted'.
grammar.example: Se il padre non lo prendeva, andava perso, e la gente l'ha chiamato il mese del papà.
grammar.title: Andare perso: to be lost

grammar.body: È meglio + infinitive gives friendly advice: è meglio parlarne = it's best to talk about it.
grammar.example: Se resta, è meglio parlarne con l'ostetrica o con il medico.
grammar.title: È meglio + infinitive

paragraphs: Il primo gennaio 1974 la Svezia è diventata il primo paese a dare il congedo parentale a tutti e due i genitori. Potevano dividersi 180 giorni pagati.

Quell'anno le madri hanno preso il 99,5 per cento dei giorni. Così, nel 1995, la Svezia ha riservato un mese a ogni genitore. Se il padre non lo prendeva, andava perso, e la gente l'ha chiamato il mese del papà.
Oggi i padri prendono circa il trenta per cento dei giorni.

Quel mese ha dato ai padri il tempo di capire che cosa può fare un marito o un partner. Prima della nascita può andare alle visite e smettere di fumare, perché il fumo può far male al bambino. Dopo, può tenere in braccio il bambino, occuparsi di qualche poppata e dividere le notti.
La tristezza dei primi giorni di solito passa entro due settimane. Se resta, è meglio parlarne con l'ostetrica o con il medico.

grammar.body: Ne stands for 'of the days' before a quantity: le madri ne hanno preso il 99,5 per cento = mothers took 99.5 per cent of them.
grammar.example: Quell'anno le madri ne hanno preso il 99,5 per cento.
grammar.title: Ne for 'of them'

grammar.body: Italian says 'what' in the middle of a sentence with quello che: quello che qualunque marito può fare = what any husband can do.
grammar.example: E quei mesi hanno fatto spazio a quello che qualunque marito o partner può fare.
grammar.title: Quello che: the relative 'what'

grammar.body: A list of infinitives names actions without a subject, the way a checklist does: tenerlo in braccio, dividere le notti.
grammar.example: Dopo: tenerlo in braccio, occuparsi di qualche poppata, dividere le notti.
grammar.title: Infinitives that name actions in a list

paragraphs: Il primo gennaio 1974 la Svezia è diventata il primo paese a sostituire il congedo di maternità con un congedo parentale: 180 giorni pagati che poteva prendere l'uno o l'altro genitore. Quell'anno le madri ne hanno preso il 99,5 per cento.

Dal 1995 c'era un mese riservato a ciascun genitore, e il mese che il padre non usava andava perso. Prima della riforma più della metà dei padri non prendeva neanche un giorno di congedo; dopo, meno di uno su cinque.
Il mese del papà, come lo chiamavano tutti, nel 2002 è raddoppiato e nel 2016 è arrivato a tre mesi. Oggi i padri prendono circa il trenta per cento dei giorni.

E quei mesi hanno fatto spazio a quello che qualunque marito o partner può fare. Prima della nascita: andare alle visite e smettere di fumare, visto che il fumo passivo può far male al bambino. Dopo: tenerlo in braccio, occuparsi di qualche poppata, dividere le notti.
Se l'umore resta giù per più di due settimane, a lei o a lui, è il momento di parlarne con l'ostetrica o con il medico.

stories.summary: Nel 1974 la Svezia ha permesso ai padri di restare a casa con il neonato, e quasi nessuno lo ha fatto; nel 1995 ha messo da parte un mese per loro, e questo ha cambiato quello che fa un padre.
stories.title: Il mese del papà

grammar.body: A1 tells a past story in the present simple. It makes the story near and easy: she goes, she talks, the women study.
grammar.example: She talks to women students there.
grammar.title: Present simple for a true story

grammar.body: "Can't" (cannot) says that something is not possible or not allowed. The verb after it has no -s and no to.
grammar.example: The women study, but they can't get a full degree.
grammar.title: Can't + verb

paragraphs: So it's October 1928, and the writer Virginia Woolf goes to Cambridge. She talks to women students there.
The women study, but they can't get a full degree. That only changes in 1948.
In 1929 her talks become a book. A woman needs money and "a room of her own", it says. Then she can write stories.
Money means time. A lock on the door means quiet. Even one free hour at the kitchen table counts.

grammar.body: "Couldn't" (could not) says that something was not possible in the past. The verb after it stays plain.
grammar.example: These women studied at Cambridge, but they couldn't get a full degree.
grammar.title: Couldn't: the past of can't

grammar.body: Many common verbs have their own past form: give → gave, speak → spoke, become → became, write → wrote.
grammar.example: A year later, her talks became a book, A Room of One's Own.
grammar.title: Irregular past: gave, spoke, became

paragraphs: On 20 and 26 October 1928, the writer Virginia Woolf gave two talks in Cambridge. She spoke to the women students of Newnham and Girton colleges.
These women studied at Cambridge, but they couldn't get a full degree. That only changed in 1948.
A year later, her talks became a book, A Room of One's Own. She wrote that a woman needs money and "a room of her own" to write fiction.
Later in the book, she even gave a price: five hundred pounds a year. And she wanted a lock on the door.
The money meant time to think. The lock meant quiet. One hour that nobody interrupts, even at the kitchen table, counts too.

grammar.body: "Wouldn't" can say that someone refused to do something in the past: the university did not agree to give the degree.
grammar.example: They could go to lectures and take exams, but the university wouldn't give them a full degree until 1948.
grammar.title: Would not for a past refusal

grammar.body: "If she is to write" means "if she wants to be able to write". It names the goal; the main clause says what is needed for it.
grammar.example: Its main idea fits in one line: "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."
grammar.title: If … is to: a condition for a goal

grammar.body: "Even" adds the least expected case: the hour counts, and it counts in a very ordinary place too.
grammar.example: Any work that needs thought needs a bit of money and an hour nobody interrupts, even at the kitchen table.
grammar.title: Even for something surprising

paragraphs: On 20 and 26 October 1928, Virginia Woolf gave two talks to women students at Newnham and Girton, two colleges in Cambridge.
They could go to lectures and take exams, but the university wouldn't give them a full degree until 1948.
A year later the talks became a short book, A Room of One's Own. Its main idea fits in one line: "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."
Later she gets exact: five hundred pounds a year and a lock on the door. The money buys time to think, and the lock buys the freedom to think for yourself.
And it isn't only for the rich or for novelists. Any work that needs thought needs a bit of money and an hour nobody interrupts, even at the kitchen table.

grammar.body: "Turn A into B" means change A so that it becomes B: the talks became a book.
grammar.example: In 1929 she turned the talks into a book, A Room of One's Own.
grammar.title: Turn something into something

grammar.body: "And yet" joins two facts that do not seem to fit together; it is stronger than but.
grammar.example: They could go to lectures and take the same exams as the men, and yet Cambridge wouldn't give them a full degree until 1948.
grammar.title: And yet for a strong contrast

grammar.body: "Neither A nor B" says that both A and B are not true. The verb stays positive: "is neither", not "is not neither".
grammar.example: Today the line is neither a luxury for the rich nor advice just for novelists.
grammar.title: Neither … nor

paragraphs: On 20 and 26 October 1928, Virginia Woolf gave two talks to the women students of Newnham and Girton, the university's colleges for women.
They could go to lectures and take the same exams as the men, and yet Cambridge wouldn't give them a full degree until 1948.
In 1929 she turned the talks into a book, A Room of One's Own. The whole argument comes down to one sentence: "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."
Later on she's very precise: five hundred pounds a year and a lock on the door. The money buys time to think; the lock, the freedom to think for yourself.

Today the line is neither a luxury for the rich nor advice just for novelists. Any work that needs thought needs enough money not to be afraid and an hour nobody can interrupt, even at six in the morning at the kitchen table.

stories.summary: In October 1928 Virginia Woolf told the women students of Cambridge what a writer needs, and her answer still fits in one line.
stories.title: A Room of One's Own

grammar.body: « Elle parle » tells a 1928 event in the present, the way people tell a story out loud.
grammar.example: Elle parle à des étudiantes.
grammar.title: The present tense for a true story

grammar.body: After a negative, un or une becomes de: avoir un diplôme → ne pas avoir de diplôme.
grammar.example: Ces femmes étudient, mais elles ne peuvent pas avoir de diplôme complet.
grammar.title: Ne … pas de after a negative

grammar.body: Speech names the topic first and then says what it is with c'est: une serrure, c'est le calme.
grammar.example: Une serrure à la porte, c'est le calme.
grammar.title: Topic first, then c'est

paragraphs: On est en octobre 1928, et l'écrivaine Virginia Woolf va à Cambridge. Elle parle à des étudiantes.
Ces femmes étudient, mais elles ne peuvent pas avoir de diplôme complet. Ça change seulement en 1948.
En 1929, ses conférences deviennent un livre. Pour écrire des histoires, une femme a besoin d'argent. Et il lui faut « une chambre à soi ».
L'argent, ça donne du temps. Une serrure à la porte, c'est le calme. Même une heure libre à la table de la cuisine, ça compte.

grammar.body: « A donné » = gave: avoir + participle for a finished event on a given date.
grammar.example: Les 20 et 26 octobre 1928, l'écrivaine Virginia Woolf a donné deux conférences à Cambridge.
grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir

grammar.body: With être, the participle agrees with the subject: les conférences sont devenues (feminine plural, -es).
grammar.example: Un an plus tard, ses conférences sont devenues un livre, Une chambre à soi.
grammar.title: Devenir takes être, and the participle agrees

grammar.body: « C'était le calme » describes what the lock meant, not an event: the imparfait of être.
grammar.example: La serrure, c'était le calme.
grammar.title: C'était: the background of the past

paragraphs: Les 20 et 26 octobre 1928, l'écrivaine Virginia Woolf a donné deux conférences à Cambridge. Elle a parlé aux étudiantes de Newnham et de Girton, deux collèges pour femmes.
Ces femmes étudiaient à Cambridge, mais elles ne pouvaient pas avoir de diplôme complet. Ça a changé seulement en 1948.
Un an plus tard, ses conférences sont devenues un livre, Une chambre à soi. Pour elle, une femme a besoin d'argent pour écrire de la fiction. Et il lui faut aussi « une chambre à soi ».
Plus loin, elle a donné un chiffre : cinq cents livres sterling par an. Et elle voulait une serrure à la porte.
L'argent, ça voulait dire du temps pour penser. La serrure, c'était le calme. Une heure où personne ne vous dérange, ça compte aussi, même à la table de la cuisine.

grammar.body: « Ne … qu'en 1948 » = not until 1948, only in 1948: ne before the verb, que before the part that is limited.
grammar.example: Elles pouvaient suivre les cours et passer les examens, mais l'université ne leur a donné un diplôme complet qu'en 1948.
grammar.title: Ne … que: only

grammar.body: « Pour pouvoir écrire » = in order to be able to write: pour + infinitive gives the purpose.
grammar.example: L'idée principale tient en une ligne : « une femme doit avoir de l'argent et une chambre à soi pour pouvoir écrire de la fiction ».
grammar.title: Pour + infinitive: the goal

grammar.body: After a noun of time, « où » means when: une heure où personne ne vous dérange = an hour when nobody disturbs you.
