Participaron más de sesenta fabricantes. Los modelos que más público atrajeron no fueron ni los más grandes ni los más rápidos: eran coches eléctricos pequeños y más asequibles, pensados para ciudades con mucho tráfico.
Varios fabricantes desempolvaron nombres célebres, entre ellos una versión eléctrica de un diminuto coche francés de 1948, pensado para llevar a dos agricultores a través de un campo arado.

El salón en sí se remonta al 15 de junio de 1898, en el jardín de las Tullerías. Y había una condición. Ningún coche podía exponerse a menos que hubiera ido antes a Versalles y regresado por sus propios medios.
Aquel verano llegaron unas 140.000 personas, y entre las máquinas nuevas ya había taxis eléctricos: coches pequeños y silenciosos, hechos para las calles de la ciudad.

stories.summary: En 1898, cada coche del primer salón del automóvil del mundo tuvo que demostrar que podía ir a Versalles y volver; en octubre de 2026, el mismo salón de París se llenó de pequeños coches eléctricos.
stories.title: El salón que empezó en un jardín

grammar.body: C'è goes with one thing, ci sono with more: a Parigi c'è il salone; nel 1898 ci sono già auto elettriche.
grammar.example: Nel 1898 ci sono già auto elettriche.
grammar.title: C'è, ci sono: there is, there are

grammar.body: Dovere is followed directly by the infinitive: deve andare = it must go.
grammar.example: Ogni auto deve prima andare a Versailles e tornare.
grammar.title: Dovere + infinitive: must

grammar.body: Auto is short for automobile and is feminine; it is the same in the singular and the plural, only the article changes.
grammar.example: Tante auto nuove sono piccole ed elettriche, per la città.
grammar.title: L'auto, le auto: a word that never changes

paragraphs: È ottobre 2026, e a Parigi c'è il grande salone dell'auto. Dura sei giorni, e arrivano più di mezzo milione di persone.
Tante auto nuove sono piccole ed elettriche, per la città. Alcune auto nuove hanno perfino nomi vecchi.
Il primo salone è nel 1898, in un giardino di Parigi. Ogni auto deve prima andare a Versailles e tornare.
E sai una cosa? Nel 1898 ci sono già auto elettriche. Le auto piccole e silenziose per la città non sono un'idea nuova.

grammar.body: The imperfetto of dovere describes a rule that held every time: ogni auto doveva andare = every car had to go.
grammar.example: Prima del salone, ogni auto doveva andare a Versailles e tornare.
grammar.title: Doveva: a rule in the past

grammar.body: Ordinals are written with a small raised letter that matches the noun: la 91ª (novantunesima) volta, il 33º paese.
grammar.example: Dal 13 al 18 ottobre 2026 Parigi ha avuto il suo grande salone dell'auto, per la 91ª volta.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers: la 91ª volta

grammar.body: After milione Italian needs di before the noun: un milione di persone, mezzo milione di persone. The verb agrees with persone.
grammar.example: In sei giorni sono arrivate più di mezzo milione di persone.
grammar.title: Mezzo milione di persone

paragraphs: Dal 13 al 18 ottobre 2026 Parigi ha avuto il suo grande salone dell'auto, per la 91ª volta. In sei giorni sono arrivate più di mezzo milione di persone.
C'erano più di sessanta produttori di auto. E le auto più amate non erano grandi né veloci. Erano piccole auto elettriche, più economiche, per la città.
Alcuni produttori hanno riportato vecchi nomi famosi. Uno ha mostrato la versione elettrica di una piccolissima auto francese del 1948.
Il primo salone è stato nel 1898, in un giardino in pieno centro di Parigi. Prima del salone, ogni auto doveva andare a Versailles e tornare.
Nel 1898 sono venute circa 140.000 persone a vedere le nuove macchine. E alcune erano già taxi elettrici, piccoli e silenziosi, fatti per la città.

grammar.body: The pluperfect passive puts one past fact before another: the car had been designed for farmers long before 2026.
grammar.example: Uno ha presentato la versione elettrica di una piccolissima auto francese del 1948, che era stata progettata per i contadini.
grammar.title: Trapassato prossimo: era stata progettata

grammar.body: When the subject stays the same, 'before' is prima di + infinitive: prima di essere esposta = before being shown.
grammar.example: Prima di essere esposta, ogni auto doveva andare a Versailles e tornare.
grammar.title: Prima di + infinitive

paragraphs: Dal 13 al 18 ottobre 2026 il Salone dell'Auto di Parigi ha aperto le porte per la 91ª volta, a Porte de Versailles. In sei giorni l'hanno visitato 518.372 persone.

Hanno partecipato più di sessanta produttori. E le auto che attiravano la folla non erano le più grandi né le più veloci. Erano piccole auto elettriche, più economiche, fatte per le strade della città.
Diversi produttori hanno anche riportato in vita nomi famosi del passato. Uno ha presentato la versione elettrica di una piccolissima auto francese del 1948, che era stata progettata per i contadini.
Tutto è cominciato nel 1898, sulla terrazza del giardino delle Tuileries, in pieno centro di Parigi. Prima di essere esposta, ogni auto doveva andare a Versailles e tornare.
Quell'estate sono venute circa 140.000 persone. E tra le nuove macchine c'erano taxi elettrici, piccoli e silenziosi, costruiti per le strade della città.

grammar.body: Né… né… means neither… nor…, and the verb keeps its non: non erano né i più grandi né i più veloci.
grammar.example: I modelli che hanno attirato più gente non erano né i più grandi né i più veloci: erano piccole auto elettriche, più accessibili, per le strade affollate delle città.
grammar.title: Né … né …: neither … nor …

grammar.body: Solo se = only if. Era andata and era tornata (imperfetto of essere + participle) put one past event before another: the car had already been there and back before it went on show.
grammar.example: All'epoca un'auto poteva essere esposta solo se prima era andata da sola fino a Versailles ed era tornata.
grammar.title: Solo se + trapassato prossimo

grammar.body: Tra cui (among which, including) adds examples after a plural: nomi celebri, tra cui… = famous names, among them…
grammar.example: Diversi costruttori hanno riportato in vita nomi celebri, tra cui la versione elettrica di una minuscola auto francese del 1948, fatta per portare due contadini attraverso un campo arato.
grammar.title: Tra cui: among them

paragraphs: Dal 13 al 18 ottobre 2026 il Salone dell'Auto di Parigi, il più antico del mondo, ha aperto per la 91ª volta, e in sei giorni l'hanno visitato 518.372 persone.

Hanno partecipato più di sessanta costruttori. I modelli che hanno attirato più gente non erano né i più grandi né i più veloci: erano piccole auto elettriche, più accessibili, per le strade affollate delle città.
Diversi costruttori hanno riportato in vita nomi celebri, tra cui la versione elettrica di una minuscola auto francese del 1948, fatta per portare due contadini attraverso un campo arato.
Il salone in sé è nato il 15 giugno 1898, nel giardino delle Tuileries. All'epoca un'auto poteva essere esposta solo se prima era andata da sola fino a Versailles ed era tornata.
Quell'estate sono arrivate circa 140.000 persone, e tra le nuove macchine c'erano già allora dei taxi elettrici: veicoli piccoli e silenziosi, costruiti per le strade della città.

stories.summary: Nel 1898, al primo salone dell'auto del mondo, ogni macchina doveva prima arrivare fino a Versailles e tornare; nell'ottobre 2026 lo stesso salone di Parigi era pieno di piccole auto elettriche.
stories.title: Il salone nato in un giardino

grammar.body: Sports talk often uses the present simple to make a match feel live: they play, he scores, they win.
grammar.example: Luis Díaz scores three goals, and Bayern win 6–1.
grammar.title: Present simple for a match report

grammar.body: In British English a team is a group of people, so the verb is often plural: Bayern are, Bayern win.
grammar.example: So Bayern are first in Germany.
grammar.title: A team takes a plural verb

paragraphs: It's Saturday, 17 October 2026, and Bayern Munich play RB Leipzig at home. Luis Díaz scores three goals, and Bayern win 6–1.
So Bayern are first in Germany. In England, Manchester City win again. That's seven wins in seven games.
In Spain, Barcelona win 5–2 at Real Betis. That's nine wins in nine games! Inter and Paris Saint-Germain win too.
And next weekend, Formula 1 is back. The race is in Austin, in the United States.

grammar.body: Many sports verbs are irregular in the past simple: beat stays beat, win becomes won; score is regular: scored.
grammar.example: On Saturday, 17 October 2026, Bayern Munich beat RB Leipzig 6–1 at home.
grammar.title: Irregular past: beat, won, scored

grammar.body: Ordinal numbers give a position in a list: first, second, third, then -th: the ninth win, the seventh game.
grammar.example: It was their ninth win in nine games.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers: their ninth win

paragraphs: On Saturday, 17 October 2026, Bayern Munich beat RB Leipzig 6–1 at home. Luis Díaz scored three of the goals.
So Bayern are now top of the Bundesliga with 14 points. Dortmund have 14 points too, but Bayern have the better goal difference.
In England, Manchester City won 3–2 against Ipswich, so they're still perfect: seven games, seven wins. Arsenal are second after a 1–0 win in Nottingham.
In Spain, Barcelona won 5–2 at Real Betis. It was their ninth win in nine games. In Italy, Inter won 3–1 in Bologna.
In France, Paris Saint-Germain were 1–0 down in Strasbourg. But they scored three late goals and won 3–1. Next weekend, it's Formula 1 in Austin.

grammar.body: "As" can join two events that happen together; here, the goals and the win.
grammar.example: On Saturday, 17 October 2026, Luis Díaz scored three goals as Bayern Munich beat RB Leipzig 6–1 at the Allianz Arena.
grammar.title: As for two things at the same time

grammar.body: The present perfect links the past to now: the seven wins are a result that is true today.
grammar.example: In England, Manchester City beat Ipswich Town 3–2, so they've now won all seven league games.
grammar.title: Present perfect: they've now won

grammar.body: A clause between commas adds extra information about a noun; for a team you can use who.
grammar.example: Arsenal, who won 1–0 at Nottingham Forest on Sunday, are second, three points behind.
grammar.title: Non-defining relative clause: who won

paragraphs: On Saturday, 17 October 2026, Luis Díaz scored three goals as Bayern Munich beat RB Leipzig 6–1 at the Allianz Arena. Bayern were already 3–0 up at half-time.
Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise and Harry Kane got the others. That puts Bayern top of the Bundesliga on 14 points, level with Dortmund but ahead on goal difference.
In England, Manchester City beat Ipswich Town 3–2, so they've now won all seven league games. Arsenal, who won 1–0 at Nottingham Forest on Sunday, are second, three points behind.
Barcelona's perfect start carried on with a 5–2 win at Real Betis: nine games, nine wins. In Italy, Inter came from behind to win 3–1 in Bologna.
In France, Paris Saint-Germain were losing 1–0 in Strasbourg until the 77th minute, then scored three times to win 3–1. Next weekend, it's Formula 1 in Austin.

grammar.body: Sports talk loves phrasal verbs that carry a picture: sweep aside (beat easily), edge past (beat narrowly), shake off (recover from).
grammar.example: In England, Manchester City edged past Ipswich Town 3–2 to make it seven out of seven, while Arsenal, 1–0 winners at Nottingham Forest, stay three points behind.
grammar.title: Phrasal verbs in sports talk

grammar.body: "Until" marks how long a situation lasted; "before" + -ing introduces what changed it.
grammar.example: In France, Paris Saint-Germain were 1–0 down in Strasbourg until the 77th minute, before scoring three times to win 3–1.
grammar.title: Until … before: a turning point

grammar.body: "Make it seven out of seven" means a result extends a run to that number: this win is the seventh in seven games.
grammar.example: Barcelona's flawless start just keeps going: a 5–2 win at Real Betis makes it nine out of nine.
grammar.title: Make it + number for a run

paragraphs: On Saturday, 17 October 2026, Luis Díaz scored a hat-trick at the Allianz Arena as Bayern Munich swept RB Leipzig aside 6–1, and they were already 3–0 up by half-time.
Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise and Harry Kane added the rest, and the win took Bayern top of the Bundesliga on 14 points, level with Dortmund but ahead on goal difference.
In England, Manchester City edged past Ipswich Town 3–2 to make it seven out of seven, while Arsenal, 1–0 winners at Nottingham Forest, stay three points behind.
Barcelona's flawless start just keeps going: a 5–2 win at Real Betis makes it nine out of nine. And in Italy, Inter shook off an early goal to win 3–1 in Bologna.
In France, Paris Saint-Germain were 1–0 down in Strasbourg until the 77th minute, before scoring three times to win 3–1. Next weekend, all eyes turn to Formula 1 in Austin.

stories.summary: On Saturday 17 October 2026 Luis Díaz scored three goals as Bayern beat Leipzig 6–1, and Manchester City and Barcelona kept their perfect starts going.
stories.title: Three Goals for Díaz

grammar.body: This A1 report is told in the present, as if the match were happening now: joue, marque, gagne. The date in the first sentence says when it happens.
grammar.example: Luis Díaz marque trois buts.
grammar.title: Present tense for a match report

grammar.body: French often puts an article before a club's name: le Bayern, le Real Betis, le Paris Saint-Germain (masculine), but l'Inter (feminine). Some clubs, like Manchester City or Barcelona, usually go without one.
grammar.example: Avec ça, le Bayern est premier en Allemagne.
grammar.title: Le before a club name

grammar.body: Feminine countries take en: en Espagne, en Angleterre, en Allemagne. A plural country takes aux (à + les): aux États-Unis. A city takes à: à Austin.
grammar.example: En Espagne, Barcelona gagne 5-2 chez le Real Betis.
grammar.title: En + country, aux + plural country

paragraphs: On est le samedi 17 octobre 2026. Le Bayern Munich joue à la maison contre le RB Leipzig. Luis Díaz marque trois buts. Le Bayern gagne 6-1.
Avec ça, le Bayern est premier en Allemagne. En Angleterre, Manchester City gagne encore : sept matchs, sept victoires.
En Espagne, Barcelona gagne 5-2 chez le Real Betis. Pour Barcelona, c'est neuf matchs, neuf victoires. L'Inter et le Paris Saint-Germain gagnent aussi.
Et le week-end prochain, c'est le retour de la Formule 1. La course est à Austin, aux États-Unis.

grammar.body: The spoken past is avoir in the present + a past participle: battre → a battu, marquer → a marqué, gagner → a gagné. It tells what happened in the match.
grammar.example: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, le Bayern Munich a battu le RB Leipzig 6-1 à domicile.
grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir: a battu, a marqué

grammar.body: Short adverbs like longtemps, déjà, bien or encore usually sit between avoir and the past participle: « Strasbourg a longtemps mené » = Strasbourg led for a long time.
grammar.example: En France, Strasbourg a longtemps mené 1-0 contre le Paris Saint-Germain.
grammar.title: Longtemps between avoir and the participle

grammar.body: Bon (good) has an irregular comparative: meilleur, never plus bon. It agrees with its noun: une meilleure différence (feminine).
grammar.example: Dortmund a aussi 14 points, mais le Bayern a une meilleure différence de buts.
grammar.title: Meilleur, meilleure: better

paragraphs: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, le Bayern Munich a battu le RB Leipzig 6-1 à domicile. Luis Díaz a marqué trois buts à lui tout seul.
Avec cette victoire, le Bayern est premier de la Bundesliga avec 14 points. Dortmund a aussi 14 points, mais le Bayern a une meilleure différence de buts.
En Angleterre, Manchester City a gagné 3-2 contre Ipswich. C'est un sans-faute : sept matchs, sept victoires. Arsenal est deuxième, après une victoire 1-0 à Nottingham.
En Espagne, Barcelona a gagné 5-2 chez le Real Betis, et ça fait neuf sur neuf. En Italie, l'Inter a gagné 3-1 à Bologne.
En France, Strasbourg a longtemps mené 1-0 contre le Paris Saint-Germain. Mais à la fin, Paris a marqué trois buts et a gagné 3-1. Le week-end prochain, place à la Formule 1, à Austin.

grammar.body: The imparfait (perdait) describes a situation that lasted; the passé composé (a marqué) tells the event that ended it. Puis (then) marks the turn.
grammar.example: En France, le Paris Saint-Germain perdait 1-0 à Strasbourg jusqu'à la 77e minute, puis il a marqué trois fois pour gagner 3-1.
grammar.title: Imparfait and passé composé: perdait, puis a marqué

grammar.body: Qui introduces extra information about the noun before it and is the subject of its clause. Between commas, the clause can be left out without changing the main sentence.
grammar.example: Arsenal, qui s'est imposé 1-0 chez Nottingham Forest dimanche, est deuxième, à trois points.
grammar.title: Relative clause with qui: Arsenal, qui s'est imposé

grammar.body: En + present participle (-ant) says how something happens, at the same time as the main verb: Barcelona continued its run by winning.
grammar.example: En Espagne, Barcelona a continué son sans-faute en gagnant 5-2 chez le Real Betis : neuf matchs, neuf victoires.
grammar.title: Gérondif: en gagnant

paragraphs: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, à l'Allianz Arena, le Bayern Munich a battu le RB Leipzig 6-1, avec trois buts de Luis Díaz. À la mi-temps, c'était déjà 3-0.

Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise et Harry Kane ont marqué les trois autres. Le Bayern est en tête de la Bundesliga avec 14 points, à égalité avec Dortmund, mais avec une meilleure différence de buts.
En Angleterre, Manchester City a battu Ipswich Town 3-2, et ça fait sept matchs, sept victoires. Arsenal, qui s'est imposé 1-0 chez Nottingham Forest dimanche, est deuxième, à trois points.
En Espagne, Barcelona a continué son sans-faute en gagnant 5-2 chez le Real Betis : neuf matchs, neuf victoires. En Italie, l'Inter a renversé la situation pour gagner 3-1 à Bologne.

En France, le Paris Saint-Germain perdait 1-0 à Strasbourg jusqu'à la 77e minute, puis il a marqué trois fois pour gagner 3-1. Le week-end prochain, la Formule 1 revient à Austin, pour le Grand Prix des États-Unis.

grammar.body: « S'offrir un triplé » (to treat yourself to a hat-trick) is a typical spoken sports phrase; s'offrir is reflexive, so the passé composé takes être.
grammar.example: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, à l'Allianz Arena, Luis Díaz s'est offert un triplé.
grammar.title: S'offrir: to treat oneself to

grammar.body: A past participle between commas replaces a whole clause (qui avait été menée) and agrees with its noun: l'Inter is feminine, so menée.
grammar.example: En Italie, l'Inter, menée très tôt, a renversé la situation et l'a emporté 3-1 à Bologne.
grammar.title: Past participle as a compact clause: menée

grammar.body: Jusqu'à says how long a situation lasted; avant de + infinitive introduces what changed it, with the same subject as the main verb.
grammar.example: En France, le Paris Saint-Germain était mené 1-0 à Strasbourg jusqu'à la 77e minute, avant de marquer trois fois pour s'imposer 3-1.
grammar.title: Jusqu'à … avant de: a turning point

paragraphs: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, à l'Allianz Arena, Luis Díaz s'est offert un triplé. Le Bayern Munich menait déjà 3-0 à la pause, et il a fini par écraser le RB Leipzig 6-1.

Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise et Harry Kane ont complété la marque. Avec cette victoire, le Bayern a pris la tête de la Bundesliga : 14 points, autant que Dortmund, mais une meilleure différence de buts.
En Angleterre, Manchester City a gagné de justesse, 3-2, contre Ipswich Town : sept matchs, sept victoires. Arsenal, vainqueur 1-0 à Nottingham Forest, reste à trois points.

En Espagne, Barcelona a continué sur sa lancée avec un 5-2 chez le Real Betis, sa neuvième victoire en neuf matchs. En Italie, l'Inter, menée très tôt, a renversé la situation et l'a emporté 3-1 à Bologne.
En France, le Paris Saint-Germain était mené 1-0 à Strasbourg jusqu'à la 77e minute, avant de marquer trois fois pour s'imposer 3-1. Le week-end prochain, place à la Formule 1, à Austin.

stories.summary: Le samedi 17 octobre 2026, Luis Díaz a mis trois buts dans le 6-1 du Bayern contre Leipzig, et Manchester City comme Barcelona ont encore tout gagné.
stories.title: Trois buts pour Díaz

grammar.body: German tells a match in the present to make it feel live: Bayern spielt, Díaz schießt, Bayern gewinnt. A club takes a singular verb: Bayern gewinnt.
grammar.example: Luis Díaz schießt drei Tore, und Bayern gewinnt 6:1.
grammar.title: Present tense for a match report

grammar.body: Spoken German often picks up a place or time with „da“ (there, then) at the start; the verb comes next and the subject follows it.
grammar.example: Da gewinnt wieder Manchester City.
grammar.title: „Da“ in first place: verb second

paragraphs: Es ist Samstag, der 17. Oktober 2026. Bayern München spielt zu Hause gegen RB Leipzig. Luis Díaz schießt drei Tore, und Bayern gewinnt 6:1.
Jetzt ist Bayern Erster in Deutschland. Und in England? Da gewinnt wieder Manchester City. Das sind sieben Siege in sieben Spielen.
In Spanien gewinnt Barcelona 5:2 bei Real Betis. Neun Spiele, neun Siege! Auch Inter und Paris Saint-Germain gewinnen.
Und nächstes Wochenende? Da fährt die Formel 1 in Austin, in den USA.

grammar.body: The spoken past is haben + Partizip II, and the participle goes to the end of the sentence: hat … geschossen, hat … gewonnen.
grammar.example: Luis Díaz hat gleich drei Tore geschossen.
grammar.title: Perfekt: haben + Partizip II at the end

grammar.body: Ordinal numbers add -te (up to 19) and take adjective endings: der neunte Sieg, im neunten Spiel.
grammar.example: Das war schon der neunte Sieg im neunten Spiel.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers: der neunte Sieg

grammar.body: German writes a score with a colon and reads it with zu: 3:1 = drei zu eins. It stands without a preposition after gewinnen.
grammar.example: In Italien hat Inter 3:1 in Bologna gewonnen.
grammar.title: Scores: 3:1 is „drei zu eins“

paragraphs: Am Samstag, dem 17. Oktober 2026, hat Bayern München zu Hause 6:1 gegen RB Leipzig gewonnen. Luis Díaz hat gleich drei Tore geschossen.
Bayern ist jetzt mit 14 Punkten Erster in der Bundesliga. Dortmund hat auch 14 Punkte, aber Bayern hat die bessere Tordifferenz.
In England hat Manchester City 3:2 gegen Ipswich gewonnen, sieben Spiele, sieben Siege. Arsenal ist nach einem 1:0 in Nottingham Zweiter.
In Spanien hat Barcelona 5:2 bei Real Betis gewonnen. Das war schon der neunte Sieg im neunten Spiel. In Italien hat Inter 3:1 in Bologna gewonnen.
In Frankreich war Paris Saint-Germain in Straßburg lange 0:1 hinten. Dann hat die Mannschaft spät drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen. Nächstes Wochenende fährt die Formel 1 in Austin.

grammar.body: Anführen (to lead) splits in a main clause: „führt … an“. In the Perfekt the particle joins the participle again: zurückliegen → hat zurückgelegen.
grammar.example: Bayern führt mit 14 Punkten die Bundesliga an, gleichauf mit Dortmund, aber mit besserer Tordifferenz.
grammar.title: Separable verbs: führt … an, zurückgelegen

grammar.body: As an adverb „damit“ means „with that, as a result“ and keeps the main-clause word order; it is not the conjunction „damit“ (so that).
grammar.example: In England hat Manchester City Ipswich 3:2 geschlagen und damit alle sieben Ligaspiele gewonnen.
grammar.title: „damit“: and so, with that

grammar.body: When one „hat“ serves several participles, German says it once: „hat … zurückgelegen, dann drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen“.
grammar.example: In Frankreich hat Paris Saint-Germain in Straßburg bis zur 77. Minute 0:1 zurückgelegen, dann drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen.
grammar.title: One subject, two Perfekt verbs

paragraphs: Am Samstag, dem 17. Oktober 2026, hat Bayern RB Leipzig in der Allianz Arena 6:1 geschlagen. Luis Díaz hat drei Tore geschossen, und zur Pause war es schon 3:0.
Die anderen Tore haben Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise und Harry Kane gemacht. Bayern führt mit 14 Punkten die Bundesliga an, gleichauf mit Dortmund, aber mit besserer Tordifferenz.
In England hat Manchester City Ipswich 3:2 geschlagen und damit alle sieben Ligaspiele gewonnen. Arsenal hat am Sonntag 1:0 bei Nottingham Forest gewonnen und ist Zweiter, drei Punkte dahinter.
Barcelona bleibt perfekt: 5:2 bei Real Betis, neun Spiele, neun Siege. In Italien hat Inter nach frühem Rückstand 3:1 in Bologna gewonnen.

In Frankreich hat Paris Saint-Germain in Straßburg bis zur 77. Minute 0:1 zurückgelegen, dann drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen. Nächstes Wochenende ist wieder Formel 1, beim Großen Preis der USA in Austin.

grammar.body: Hatte/war + Partizip II places an action before another past one: the 3:0 lead came before the final 6:1.
grammar.example: Schon zur Pause hatten die Münchner 3:0 geführt.
grammar.title: Plusquamperfekt: hatten … geführt

grammar.body: In the Perfekt, „sich durchsetzen“ (to prevail, win through) keeps „sich“ after „hat“ and joins the particle to the participle: „hat sich … durchgesetzt“.
grammar.example: In England hat sich Manchester City knapp mit 3:2 gegen Ipswich Town durchgesetzt: sieben Spiele, sieben Siege.
grammar.title: Sich durchsetzen: a reflexive separable verb

grammar.body: „Bevor“ opens a subordinate clause, so the finite verb goes last; with two participles the shared „haben“ closes the clause: „geschossen und … gewonnen haben“.
grammar.example: In Frankreich hat Paris Saint-Germain in Straßburg bis zur 77. Minute 0:1 hinten gelegen, bevor die Pariser noch drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen haben.
grammar.title: „bevor“ with the auxiliary last

paragraphs: Am Samstag, dem 17. Oktober 2026, hat Luis Díaz in der Allianz Arena einen Dreierpack geschnürt, als Bayern München RB Leipzig 6:1 geschlagen hat. Schon zur Pause hatten die Münchner 3:0 geführt.

Die übrigen Tore haben Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise und Harry Kane beigesteuert. Damit stehen die Münchner an der Spitze der Bundesliga, mit 14 Punkten gleichauf mit Dortmund, aber mit der besseren Tordifferenz.
In England hat sich Manchester City knapp mit 3:2 gegen Ipswich Town durchgesetzt: sieben Spiele, sieben Siege. Arsenal hat 1:0 bei Nottingham Forest gewonnen und bleibt drei Punkte dahinter.
Auch Barcelona bleibt makellos: Das 5:2 bei Real Betis war der neunte Sieg im neunten Spiel. In Italien hat Inter in Bologna einen frühen Rückstand gedreht und 3:1 gewonnen.

In Frankreich hat Paris Saint-Germain in Straßburg bis zur 77. Minute 0:1 hinten gelegen, bevor die Pariser noch drei Tore geschossen und 3:1 gewonnen haben. Und nächstes Wochenende ist dann die Formel 1 in Austin dran.

stories.summary: Am Samstag, dem 17. Oktober 2026, hat Luis Díaz beim 6:1 der Bayern gegen Leipzig drei Tore geschossen, und Manchester City und Barcelona haben wieder alles gewonnen.
stories.title: Drei Tore für Díaz

grammar.body: This A1 report tells the match as it happens, in the present. Regular -ar verbs end in -a for él/ella: marcar → marca, ganar → gana.
grammar.example: El Bayern gana 6-1.
grammar.title: Present tense for a match report: marca, gana

grammar.body: Spanish puts the masculine article before football clubs, because it thinks of "el equipo" (the team): el Bayern, el Inter, el Barcelona. The verb is singular: el Bayern gana.
grammar.example: Ahora el Bayern es primero en Alemania.
grammar.title: El before a club name: el Bayern, el Barcelona

grammar.body: Spanish often puts the verb first when the subject is new information: "vuelve la Fórmula 1" = Formula 1 is back.
grammar.example: El próximo fin de semana vuelve la Fórmula 1.
grammar.title: Word order: the verb can come before the subject

paragraphs: Es sábado, 17 de octubre de 2026. El Bayern de Múnich juega en casa contra el RB Leipzig. Y Luis Díaz marca tres goles, ¡tres! El Bayern gana 6-1.
Ahora el Bayern es primero en Alemania. En Inglaterra, el Manchester City gana otra vez: siete partidos, siete victorias.
En España, el Barcelona gana 5-2 en el campo del Real Betis. Ya son nueve victorias en nueve partidos. El Inter y el Paris Saint-Germain también ganan.
El próximo fin de semana vuelve la Fórmula 1. La carrera es en Austin, en Estados Unidos.

grammar.body: Finished actions in the past take the pretérito indefinido. For él/ella, -ar verbs end in a stressed -ó: ganar → ganó, marcar → marcó; ser is irregular: fue.
grammar.example: Luis Díaz marcó tres goles.
grammar.title: Pretérito indefinido: ganó, marcó

grammar.body: When you beat a team, the team takes "a", like a person (a + el = al), and speakers usually add le as well: le ganó 3-2 al Ipswich.
grammar.example: En Inglaterra, el Manchester City le ganó 3-2 al Ipswich.
grammar.title: Ganarle a: the personal a before a team

grammar.body: Ordinal numbers work like adjectives and agree with the noun: noveno partido, but novena victoria (feminine).
grammar.example: Fue su novena victoria en nueve partidos.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers agree: su novena victoria

paragraphs: El sábado 17 de octubre de 2026, el Bayern de Múnich le ganó 6-1 al RB Leipzig en casa. Luis Díaz marcó tres goles.
Así que ahora el Bayern es primero en la Bundesliga, con 14 puntos. El Dortmund también tiene 14, pero el Bayern tiene mejor diferencia de goles.
En Inglaterra, el Manchester City le ganó 3-2 al Ipswich. Su temporada es perfecta: siete partidos, siete victorias. El Arsenal es segundo, después de ganar 1-0 en Nottingham.
En España, el Barcelona ganó 5-2 en el campo del Real Betis. Fue su novena victoria en nueve partidos. Y en Italia, el Inter ganó 3-1 en Bolonia.
En Francia, el Paris Saint-Germain empezó perdiendo 1-0 en Estrasburgo. Pero al final marcó tres goles y ganó 3-1. Y el próximo fin de semana, la Fórmula 1 corre en Austin.

grammar.body: A clause with "que" between commas adds extra information about a noun; for a team, "que" is enough (not "quien"): el Arsenal, que ganó… = Arsenal, who won….
grammar.example: El Arsenal, que ganó 1-0 el domingo en casa del Nottingham Forest, va segundo, a tres puntos.
grammar.title: Relative clause between commas: que ganó

grammar.body: "Ha ganado" (haber + participle) presents the seven wins as a result that is still true today; "ya" (already) often goes with it.
grammar.example: En Inglaterra, el Manchester City le ganó 3-2 al Ipswich Town y ya ha ganado los siete.
grammar.title: Pretérito perfecto: ya ha ganado

grammar.body: The imperfect (perdía) describes the situation that lasted; the indefinido (marcó, ganó) gives the events that changed it.
grammar.example: En Francia, el Paris Saint-Germain perdía 1-0 en Estrasburgo hasta el minuto 77, pero marcó tres goles y ganó 3-1.
grammar.title: Imperfect and indefinido: perdía… marcó

paragraphs: El sábado 17 de octubre de 2026, Luis Díaz marcó tres goles en el Allianz Arena. El Bayern de Múnich le ganó 6-1 al RB Leipzig, y al descanso ya iba 3-0.
Los otros goles los marcaron Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise y Harry Kane. El Bayern es líder de la Bundesliga con 14 puntos, igual que el Dortmund, pero con mejor diferencia de goles.
En Inglaterra, el Manchester City le ganó 3-2 al Ipswich Town y ya ha ganado los siete. El Arsenal, que ganó 1-0 el domingo en casa del Nottingham Forest, va segundo, a tres puntos.
En España, el Barcelona ganó 5-2 en casa del Real Betis: nueve partidos, nueve victorias. En Italia, el Inter remontó y ganó 3-1 en Bolonia.

En Francia, el Paris Saint-Germain perdía 1-0 en Estrasburgo hasta el minuto 77, pero marcó tres goles y ganó 3-1. El próximo fin de semana vuelve la Fórmula 1, con el Gran Premio de Estados Unidos en Austin.

grammar.body: Iba ganando 3-0 = they were winning 3-0 (at that point). Ir + gerund in the imperfect gives a running score at a moment in the match.
grammar.example: El Bayern de Múnich le pasó por encima al RB Leipzig, 6-1, y al descanso ya iba ganando 3-0.
grammar.title: Ir + gerund for the score so far

grammar.body: Darle la vuelta (al partido) means to come from behind and win. The le stands for the match being turned around.
grammar.example: En Italia, el Bologna se adelantó pronto, pero el Inter le dio la vuelta y ganó 3-1 en Bolonia.
grammar.title: Dar la vuelta: to turn a match around

grammar.body: After a situation in the imperfect (perdía… hasta el minuto 77), y ahí + indefinido points to the moment everything turned: ahí cambió todo = that's when it all changed.
grammar.example: En Francia, el Paris Saint-Germain perdía 1-0 en Estrasburgo hasta el minuto 77, y ahí cambió todo: marcó tres goles y acabó ganando 3-1.
grammar.title: Y ahí: the moment it all changed

paragraphs: El sábado 17 de octubre de 2026, Luis Díaz hizo un triplete en el Allianz Arena. El Bayern de Múnich le pasó por encima al RB Leipzig, 6-1, y al descanso ya iba ganando 3-0.
Los otros tres goles fueron de Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise y Harry Kane. El Bayern se pone líder de la Bundesliga con 14 puntos, empatado con el Dortmund, aunque con mejor diferencia de goles.
En Inglaterra, el Manchester City le ganó por la mínima al Ipswich Town, 3-2, y ya son siete de siete. El Arsenal, que ganó 1-0 en el campo del Nottingham Forest, sigue a tres puntos.

El Barcelona sigue con su arranque perfecto: un 5-2 en el campo del Real Betis, y van nueve victorias en nueve partidos. En Italia, el Bologna se adelantó pronto, pero el Inter le dio la vuelta y ganó 3-1 en Bolonia.
En Francia, el Paris Saint-Germain perdía 1-0 en Estrasburgo hasta el minuto 77, y ahí cambió todo: marcó tres goles y acabó ganando 3-1. Y el próximo fin de semana, turno de la Fórmula 1, en Austin.

stories.summary: El sábado 17 de octubre de 2026, Luis Díaz marcó tres goles en el 6-1 del Bayern al Leipzig, y el Manchester City y el Barcelona lo siguen ganando todo.
stories.title: Tres goles de Díaz

grammar.body: This A1 report tells the match in the present: gioca, fa, vince. "Fare un gol" (to make a goal) is the everyday way to say "to score".
grammar.example: Luis Díaz fa tre gol.
grammar.title: Present tense for a match report

grammar.body: Italian puts the article before a club's name and uses a singular verb: il Bayern vince, il Barcelona vince. Most clubs are masculine; Inter is feminine: l'Inter.
grammar.example: Il Bayern vince 6–1.
grammar.title: A club takes the article and a singular verb

grammar.body: Italian can put the subject after the verb to give it weight: "vincono anche l'Inter e il Paris Saint-Germain" = Inter and Paris Saint-Germain win too.
grammar.example: Vincono anche l'Inter e il Paris Saint-Germain.
grammar.title: The subject after the verb

paragraphs: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 il Bayern Monaco gioca in casa contro l'RB Leipzig. Luis Díaz fa tre gol. Il Bayern vince 6–1.
Così il Bayern è primo in Germania. In Inghilterra il Manchester City vince ancora: sette partite, sette vittorie.
In Spagna il Barcelona vince 5–2 in casa del Real Betis. E sono nove partite, nove vittorie! Vincono anche l'Inter e il Paris Saint-Germain.
Il prossimo fine settimana torna la Formula 1, ad Austin, negli Stati Uniti.

grammar.body: The spoken past is a present form of avere plus a past participle: "ha battuto" (beat), "ha vinto" (won), "ha fatto" (made). Vincere and fare have irregular participles: vinto, fatto.
grammar.example: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 il Bayern Monaco ha battuto l'RB Leipzig 6–1 in casa.
grammar.title: Passato prossimo with avere: ha battuto, ha vinto

grammar.body: "Era sotto 1–0" (was 1–0 down) describes the situation at that moment; the passato prossimo in the next sentence ("ha fatto", "ha vinto") tells what changed it.
grammar.example: In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain era sotto 1–0 a Strasburgo.
grammar.title: Era for the situation, then what happened

grammar.body: Ordinal numbers work like adjectives and agree with their noun: "la nona vittoria" (feminine), "l'Arsenal è secondo" (masculine). "È stata" also agrees, because essere's participle follows the subject.
grammar.example: È stata la sua nona vittoria in nove partite.
grammar.title: Ordinal numbers agree: la nona vittoria

paragraphs: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 il Bayern Monaco ha battuto l'RB Leipzig 6–1 in casa. Luis Díaz, da solo, ha fatto tre gol.
Adesso il Bayern è primo in Bundesliga con 14 punti. Anche il Dortmund ha 14 punti, ma il Bayern ha una differenza reti migliore.
In Inghilterra il Manchester City ha vinto 3–2 contro l'Ipswich. Per il City è un inizio perfetto: sette partite, sette vittorie. L'Arsenal è secondo, dopo l'1–0 a Nottingham.
In Spagna il Barcelona ha vinto 5–2 in casa del Real Betis. È stata la sua nona vittoria in nove partite. In Italia l'Inter ha vinto 3–1 a Bologna.
In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain era sotto 1–0 a Strasburgo. Poi, negli ultimi minuti, ha fatto tre gol e ha vinto 3–1. E il prossimo fine settimana la Formula 1 corre ad Austin.

grammar.body: The imperfect "perdeva" (was losing) describes a situation that went on until a point in time; the passato prossimo of the next sentence ("ha vinto") marks the turn.
grammar.example: In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain perdeva 1–0 a Strasburgo fino al 77º minuto.
grammar.title: Imperfect for a situation that lasts

grammar.body: With a number, Italian says "tutti e" / "tutte e" + number + article + noun: "tutte e sette le partite" = all seven games. Tutte agrees with the feminine partite.
grammar.example: In Inghilterra il Manchester City ha battuto l'Ipswich Town 3–2 e ha vinto tutte e sette le partite di campionato.
grammar.title: Tutte e sette: all seven

grammar.body: Speech often puts the object first and repeats it with a pronoun: gli altri gol li hanno fatti… = the other goals, they were scored by… The pronoun li agrees with gol, and so does fatti.
grammar.example: Gli altri gol li hanno fatti Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise e Harry Kane.
grammar.title: Object first, repeated as a pronoun

paragraphs: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026, all'Allianz Arena, il Bayern Monaco ha battuto l'RB Leipzig 6–1, con tre gol di Luis Díaz. All'intervallo era già 3–0.
Gli altri gol li hanno fatti Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise e Harry Kane. Il Bayern è in testa alla Bundesliga con 14 punti, come il Dortmund, ma davanti per differenza reti.

In Inghilterra il Manchester City ha battuto l'Ipswich Town 3–2 e ha vinto tutte e sette le partite di campionato. L'Arsenal, che domenica ha vinto 1–0 sul campo del Nottingham Forest, è secondo a tre punti.
In Spagna il Barcelona non sbaglia un colpo. Ha vinto 5–2 sul campo del Real Betis: nove partite, nove vittorie. In Italia l'Inter ha rimontato e ha vinto 3–1 a Bologna.

In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain perdeva 1–0 a Strasburgo fino al 77º minuto. Poi ha fatto tre gol e ha vinto 3–1. Il prossimo fine settimana torna la Formula 1, con il Gran Premio degli Stati Uniti ad Austin.

grammar.body: "Dopo aver chiuso" (after having closed) puts one action before the main one, with the same subject; in speech you would also hear "dopo che aveva chiuso".
grammar.example: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 Luis Díaz ha fatto tripletta all'Allianz Arena, dove il Bayern Monaco ha travolto l'RB Leipzig 6–1 dopo aver chiuso il primo tempo già sul 3–0.
grammar.title: Dopo aver + past participle: having done

grammar.body: Some spoken verbs carry a fixed la: spuntarla = to win in the end, by a whisker. In the passato prossimo the la stays: l'ha spuntata.
grammar.example: In Inghilterra il Manchester City l'ha spuntata 3–2 sull'Ipswich Town, e così fanno sette vittorie su sette partite.
grammar.title: Spuntarla: to just about win

grammar.body: "Fino al 77º minuto" says how long the situation lasted; "prima di" + infinitive (ribaltare, vincere) says what ended it, with the same subject and no conjugated verb.
grammar.example: In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain è rimasto sotto 1–0 a Strasburgo fino al 77º minuto, prima di ribaltare la partita con tre gol e vincere 3–1.
grammar.title: Prima di + infinitive: the turning point

paragraphs: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 Luis Díaz ha fatto tripletta all'Allianz Arena, dove il Bayern Monaco ha travolto l'RB Leipzig 6–1 dopo aver chiuso il primo tempo già sul 3–0.

A chiudere il conto ci hanno pensato Aleksandar Pavlović, Michael Olise e Harry Kane. Con questa vittoria il Bayern è salito in testa alla Bundesliga con 14 punti, a pari merito con il Dortmund ma davanti per differenza reti.

In Inghilterra il Manchester City l'ha spuntata 3–2 sull'Ipswich Town, e così fanno sette vittorie su sette partite. L'Arsenal, che ha vinto 1–0 sul campo del Nottingham Forest, resta secondo a tre punti.

Il Barcelona, intanto, non si ferma più: ha vinto 5–2 sul campo del Real Betis e ha messo in fila nove vittorie in nove partite. In Italia l'Inter è finita subito sotto, ma ha rimontato e ha vinto 3–1 a Bologna.

In Francia il Paris Saint-Germain è rimasto sotto 1–0 a Strasburgo fino al 77º minuto, prima di ribaltare la partita con tre gol e vincere 3–1. Il prossimo fine settimana tocca alla Formula 1, ad Austin.

stories.summary: Sabato 17 ottobre 2026 Luis Díaz ha fatto tre gol nel 6–1 del Bayern sull'RB Leipzig, e intanto Manchester City e Barcelona hanno vinto ancora: sempre a punteggio pieno.
stories.title: Tre gol per Díaz

grammar.body: "Can" says what someone is able to do; the verb after it has no "to" and no -s.
grammar.example: A child of three can even carry a chair!
grammar.title: Can + verb for what someone is able to do

grammar.body: In speech, "just" often means "only" or makes an action sound simple: she just watches.
grammar.example: Maria just watches and writes it all down.
grammar.title: "Just" in everyday talk

paragraphs: So it's 6 January 1907, in Rome. Maria Montessori is a doctor. She opens a room for small children: their parents work all day.
The chairs and tables are small and light. A child of three can even carry a chair! The children choose their work.
They pour water, sweep the floor and wash their hands. Maria just watches and writes it all down.
Today schools all over the world use her ideas. At home, start with a small jug.

grammar.body: "Could" is the past of "can": it says what someone was able to do.
grammar.example: So a child of three could pick up a chair and sit where she liked.
grammar.title: Could: the past of can

grammar.body: "Not … at all" makes a negative stronger: it is the opposite of what you might expect.
grammar.example: Actually, she wasn't a teacher at all.
grammar.title: Not … at all

paragraphs: On 6 January 1907, Maria Montessori opened a room for children in San Lorenzo, a poor part of Rome.
Actually, she wasn't a teacher at all. She was a doctor, one of the first women in Italy to get a medical degree, in 1896.
About fifty small children came, because their parents worked all day. Maria got small, light chairs and tables for them.
So a child of three could pick up a chair and sit where she liked. The children poured water, swept the floor and chose their own work. Maria just watched and wrote down what they did.
Her way of teaching went around the world. At home, start with a small jug and a small broom.

grammar.body: "Adjective + enough + to + verb" says that something has the quality needed for an action.
grammar.example: Maria got rid of the heavy furniture and brought in small tables and chairs light enough for the children to move.
grammar.title: Light enough to + verb

grammar.body: "Keep + -ing" says that an action went on and on, without stopping.
grammar.example: Her method spread all over the world, and she kept working on it until she died in 1952.
grammar.title: Keep + -ing: going on doing something

grammar.body: "While" joins two actions happening at the same time.
grammar.example: The children poured water, swept and chose their own work, while Maria just watched and took notes.
grammar.title: While for two actions at the same time

paragraphs: On 6 January 1907, Maria Montessori opened a room for small children in San Lorenzo, Rome, in a new building for poor families.
She wasn't even a teacher: she was a doctor, one of the first women in Italy to qualify in medicine, in 1896.
About fifty children aged three to six came, because their parents worked all day. Maria got rid of the heavy furniture and brought in small tables and chairs light enough for the children to move.
Now a three-year-old could pick up a chair and decide where to sit. The children poured water, swept and chose their own work, while Maria just watched and took notes.
Her method spread all over the world, and she kept working on it until she died in 1952. At home, a small jug and broom are a good start.

grammar.body: "Have + object + past participle" means someone else does the action for you: she arranged it, others did it.
grammar.example: Montessori had the heavy furniture taken out and brought in tables and chairs light enough for them to carry.
grammar.title: Have something done

grammar.body: In speech the past perfect is usually contracted (she'd become, they'd gone); it puts one past event before another.
grammar.example: She was a doctor, and in 1896 she'd become one of the first women in Italy to qualify in medicine.
grammar.title: She'd become: the past perfect in speech

grammar.body: "Without" + -ing says that an action does not happen alongside the main one.
grammar.example: Montessori just watched, without stepping in, and wrote down everything she saw.
grammar.title: Without + -ing

paragraphs: On 6 January 1907, Maria Montessori opened a room for about fifty small children in San Lorenzo, a poor part of Rome, in a brand-new block for low-income families.
And here's the thing: she wasn't a teacher at all. She was a doctor, and in 1896 she'd become one of the first women in Italy to qualify in medicine.

The children's parents worked all day, so these three- to six-year-olds were basically on their own. Montessori had the heavy furniture taken out and brought in tables and chairs light enough for them to carry.
Suddenly a three-year-old could choose where to sit and what to do: pour water, sweep the floor, wash her hands. Montessori just watched, without stepping in, and wrote down everything she saw.
Her method spread across the world, and she was still working on it when she died in 1952. At home, it starts with a jug and a broom that fit a child's hands.

stories.summary: In 1907 a doctor in Rome gave about fifty small children chairs they could carry themselves, and found out what kids do when they get to choose.
stories.title: The Small Chair

grammar.body: "Peut" (from pouvoir) says what someone is able to do; the next verb stays in the infinitive: peut porter. "Même" (even) sits between the two.
grammar.example: Un enfant de trois ans peut même porter une chaise !
grammar.title: Pouvoir + infinitive: can

grammar.body: With a reflexive verb the action comes back to the subject: ils se lavent. For your own body French says "les mains" (the hands), not "leurs mains".
grammar.example: Ils versent de l'eau, balaient et se lavent les mains.
grammar.title: Reflexive verbs: se laver les mains

grammar.body: Advice to a friend uses the tu imperative: the present form without "tu", and -er verbs drop their -s: tu commences → commence.
grammar.example: À la maison, commence par un petit pichet.
grammar.title: The tu imperative: commence

paragraphs: Alors, on est le 6 janvier 1907, à Rome. Maria Montessori est médecin. Elle ouvre une salle pour les petits enfants. Pourquoi ? Parce que leurs parents travaillent toute la journée.
Les chaises et les tables sont petites et légères. Un enfant de trois ans peut même porter une chaise ! Et les enfants choisissent leur activité.
Ils versent de l'eau, balaient et se lavent les mains. Maria, elle, regarde juste et elle note tout.
Aujourd'hui, beaucoup d'écoles dans le monde utilisent ses idées. À la maison, commence par un petit pichet.

grammar.body: The spoken past is avoir + past participle for most verbs; some participles are irregular: ouvrir → ouvert, avoir → eu, faire → fait.
grammar.example: Le 6 janvier 1907, Maria Montessori a ouvert une salle pour les enfants.
grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir: a ouvert

grammar.body: Venir forms its past with être, and the participle agrees with the subject: les enfants sont venus, les filles sont venues.
grammar.example: Environ cinquante petits enfants sont venus, parce que leurs parents travaillaient toute la journée.
grammar.title: Passé composé with être: sont venus

grammar.body: "Du tout" after "pas" makes the negative stronger: the opposite of what you would expect.
grammar.example: En fait, elle n'était pas du tout institutrice.
grammar.title: Ne … pas du tout: not at all

paragraphs: Le 6 janvier 1907, Maria Montessori a ouvert une salle pour les enfants. C'était à San Lorenzo, un quartier pauvre de Rome.
En fait, elle n'était pas du tout institutrice. Elle était médecin. En 1896, elle a été une des premières femmes en Italie à avoir son diplôme.
Environ cinquante petits enfants sont venus, parce que leurs parents travaillaient toute la journée. Alors, Maria leur a trouvé des petites tables et des petites chaises, toutes légères.

Un enfant de trois ans pouvait prendre une chaise et s'asseoir où il voulait. Les enfants ont versé de l'eau, balayé le sol et choisi eux-mêmes leur activité. Et Maria ? Elle a juste regardé, et elle a tout noté.
Sa façon d'enseigner a fait le tour du monde. À la maison, commence par un petit pichet et un petit balai.

grammar.body: "Facile à" + infinitive says that something is easy to do: facile à bouger = easy to move. The infinitive has a passive sense here.
grammar.example: Maria a remplacé les meubles lourds par des petites tables et des chaises légères, faciles à bouger.
grammar.title: Facile à + infinitive

grammar.body: "Pendant que" joins two actions going on at the same time; the imparfait (versaient, regardait) shows what kept happening, day after day.
grammar.example: Les enfants versaient de l'eau, balayaient et choisissaient leur activité, pendant que Maria regardait et prenait des notes.
grammar.title: Pendant que + imparfait: at the same time

grammar.body: "Continuer à" + infinitive says an action went on without stopping; in speech "travailler dessus" means to work on it.
grammar.example: Et Maria a continué à travailler dessus jusqu'à sa mort, en 1952.
grammar.title: Continuer à + infinitive: keep doing

paragraphs: Le 6 janvier 1907, Maria Montessori a ouvert une salle pour les petits enfants à San Lorenzo, à Rome. C'était dans un nouvel immeuble pour des familles pauvres.
En fait, elle n'était même pas institutrice. Elle était médecin, et en 1896, elle a été une des premières femmes en Italie à avoir son diplôme de médecine.

Une cinquantaine d'enfants de trois à six ans sont venus, parce que leurs parents travaillaient toute la journée. Maria a remplacé les meubles lourds par des petites tables et des chaises légères, faciles à bouger.

Du coup, un enfant de trois ans pouvait prendre une chaise et décider où s'asseoir. Les enfants versaient de l'eau, balayaient et choisissaient leur activité, pendant que Maria regardait et prenait des notes.
Sa méthode s'est répandue dans le monde entier. Et Maria a continué à travailler dessus jusqu'à sa mort, en 1952. À la maison, un petit pichet et un petit balai, c'est déjà un bon début.

grammar.body: "Faire" + infinitive means someone else does the action for you: a fait sortir = had (the furniture) taken out; one "faire" can carry two infinitives.
grammar.example: Montessori a fait sortir les meubles lourds et installer des tables et des chaises assez légères pour qu'ils puissent les porter.
grammar.title: Faire + infinitive: having something done

grammar.body: Avoir in the imparfait + participle puts one past event before another, and people say it all the time; "décrocher un diplôme" is the spoken way to say get a degree.
grammar.example: En 1896, elle avait décroché son diplôme de médecine, une des premières femmes d'Italie à y arriver.
grammar.title: Plus-que-parfait: avait décroché

grammar.body: After "sans" French uses the infinitive where English uses -ing; "s'en mêler" = to get involved, to interfere.
grammar.example: Montessori se contentait de regarder, sans jamais s'en mêler, et notait tout ce qu'elle voyait.
grammar.title: Sans + infinitive: without doing

paragraphs: Le 6 janvier 1907, Maria Montessori a ouvert une salle pour une cinquantaine de petits enfants à San Lorenzo, un quartier pauvre de Rome. C'était dans un immeuble tout récent, pour des familles modestes.
Et le plus étonnant, c'est qu'elle n'était pas du tout institutrice, mais médecin. En 1896, elle avait décroché son diplôme de médecine, une des premières femmes d'Italie à y arriver.

Les parents travaillaient toute la journée, alors ces petits de trois à six ans étaient pratiquement livrés à eux-mêmes. Montessori a fait sortir les meubles lourds et installer des tables et des chaises assez légères pour qu'ils puissent les porter.

D'un coup, un petit de trois ans pouvait choisir où s'asseoir et quoi faire. Verser de l'eau, balayer le sol, se laver les mains : c'était lui qui décidait. Montessori se contentait de regarder, sans jamais s'en mêler, et notait tout ce qu'elle voyait.
Sa méthode a fait le tour du monde, et elle travaillait encore dessus quand elle est morte, en 1952. À la maison, tout commence par un pichet et un balai faits pour des mains d'enfant.

stories.summary: En 1907, à Rome, une médecin a donné à une cinquantaine de petits enfants des chaises qu'ils pouvaient porter tout seuls, et elle a vu ce que font les enfants quand on les laisse choisir.
stories.title: La petite chaise

grammar.body: In verbs like „zusehen“ (to watch) and „aufschreiben“ (to write down), the small first part splits off in the present and stands at the end of the clause: „sieht … zu“, „schreibt … auf“.
grammar.example: Maria sieht nur zu und schreibt alles auf.
grammar.title: Separable verbs: the particle goes to the end

grammar.body: The modal verb „kann“ stands in second place; the main verb goes to the very end in its infinitive form: „kann … tragen“.
grammar.example: Sogar ein dreijähriges Kind kann einen Stuhl tragen!
grammar.title: Können + infinitive at the end

grammar.body: Advice to a friend uses the du imperative: the du form without „du“ and without -st, and without the umlaut of „du fängst“: fang! The particle still goes to the end, and „einfach“ (just) makes it a friendly tip, not an order.
grammar.example: Fang zu Hause einfach mit einer kleinen Kanne an.
grammar.title: The du imperative: Fang … an!

paragraphs: Also: Rom, 6. Januar 1907. Maria Montessori ist Ärztin. Sie macht einen Raum für kleine Kinder auf. Die Eltern arbeiten nämlich den ganzen Tag.
Die Stühle und Tische sind klein und leicht. Sogar ein dreijähriges Kind kann einen Stuhl tragen! Die Kinder suchen ihre Aufgaben selbst aus.
Sie gießen Wasser ein, fegen und waschen sich die Hände. Maria sieht nur zu und schreibt alles auf.
Heute nutzen Schulen überall ihre Ideen. Fang zu Hause einfach mit einer kleinen Kanne an.

grammar.body: Spoken German tells the past with „haben“ (or „sein“) in second place and the participle at the end. Separable verbs put „ge“ inside: eingießen → eingegossen, aussuchen → ausgesucht.
grammar.example: Die Kinder haben Wasser eingegossen, den Boden gefegt und sich ihre Aufgaben ausgesucht.
grammar.title: Perfekt: haben + participle at the end

grammar.body: Verbs of movement like „kommen“ take „sein“: „sind gekommen“. After „weil“ the whole verb goes to the end, the helper last: „gearbeitet haben“.
grammar.example: Ungefähr fünfzig kleine Kinder sind gekommen, weil ihre Eltern den ganzen Tag gearbeitet haben.
grammar.title: Perfekt with sein, and weil sends the verb to the end

grammar.body: „Gar“ makes „kein“ stronger (not a teacher at all), and after a negation „sondern“, not „aber“, brings in the right answer.
grammar.example: Eigentlich war sie gar keine Lehrerin, sondern Ärztin.
grammar.title: Gar kein …, sondern: not … at all, but

paragraphs: Am 6. Januar 1907 hat Maria Montessori einen Raum für Kinder aufgemacht. Das war in San Lorenzo, einem armen Viertel von Rom.
Eigentlich war sie gar keine Lehrerin, sondern Ärztin. 1896 hat sie als eine der ersten Frauen in Italien ihr Medizinstudium abgeschlossen.
Ungefähr fünfzig kleine Kinder sind gekommen, weil ihre Eltern den ganzen Tag gearbeitet haben. Maria hat kleine, leichte Stühle und Tische geholt.

So konnte ein dreijähriges Kind einen Stuhl nehmen und sich hinsetzen, wo es wollte. Die Kinder haben Wasser eingegossen, den Boden gefegt und sich ihre Aufgaben ausgesucht. Maria hat nur zugeschaut und alles aufgeschrieben.
Ihre Art zu unterrichten ist um die Welt gegangen. Fang zu Hause mit einer kleinen Kanne und einem kleinen Besen an.

grammar.body: A relative clause sends its verb to the end. In „die die Kinder bewegen konnten“ the first „die“ is the relative pronoun (which, for the chairs and tables) and the second is the article of „Kinder“.
grammar.example: Maria hat die schweren Möbel rausgeräumt und kleine, leichte Tische und Stühle reingestellt, die die Kinder bewegen konnten.
grammar.title: Relative clauses: die die Kinder …

grammar.body: „Während“ joins two things happening at once and sends the verb of its clause to the end; in the Perfekt the helper „hat“ comes last.
grammar.example: Die Kinder haben Wasser eingegossen, gefegt und ihre Aufgaben ausgesucht, während Maria nur zugeschaut und mitgeschrieben hat.
grammar.title: Während for two actions at the same time

grammar.body: „Nicht mal“ (spoken for „nicht einmal“) means not even, and „sondern“ then gives the surprising truth. „Dabei“ at the start means and yet: it sets up the surprise.
grammar.example: Dabei war sie nicht mal Lehrerin, sondern Ärztin.
grammar.title: Nicht mal …, sondern: not even … but

paragraphs: Am 6. Januar 1907 hat Maria Montessori einen Raum für kleine Kinder eröffnet. Das war in San Lorenzo in Rom, in einem Neubau für arme Familien.
Dabei war sie nicht mal Lehrerin, sondern Ärztin. 1896 hat sie als eine der ersten Frauen in Italien ihr Medizinstudium abgeschlossen.

Ungefähr fünfzig Kinder zwischen drei und sechs sind gekommen, weil ihre Eltern den ganzen Tag gearbeitet haben. Maria hat die schweren Möbel rausgeräumt und kleine, leichte Tische und Stühle reingestellt, die die Kinder bewegen konnten.

Jetzt konnte ein dreijähriges Kind einen Stuhl hochheben und selbst entscheiden, wo es sitzt. Die Kinder haben Wasser eingegossen, gefegt und ihre Aufgaben ausgesucht, während Maria nur zugeschaut und mitgeschrieben hat.
Ihre Methode ist um die Welt gegangen, und bis zu ihrem Tod 1952 hat sie weitergemacht. Zu Hause? Fang mit einer kleinen Kanne und einem Besen an.

grammar.body: „Etwas machen lassen“ means having someone else do it. With a second infinitive, the Perfekt keeps „lassen“ instead of „gelassen“: „hat die Möbel rausbringen lassen“ = had the furniture taken out.
grammar.example: Montessori hat die schweren Möbel rausbringen lassen und Tische und Stühle reingestellt, die so leicht waren, dass die Kinder sie tragen konnten.
grammar.title: Perfekt of lassen + infinitive: hat … rausbringen lassen

grammar.body: „Hatte“ + participle puts one past event before another, in speech as in writing: she had finished her degree in 1896, eleven years before the room opened.
grammar.example: 1896 hatte sie als eine der ersten Frauen in Italien ihr Medizinstudium abgeschlossen.
grammar.title: Plusquamperfekt: hatte … abgeschlossen

grammar.body: „Ohne … zu“ + infinitive says that something does not happen alongside the main action. With „sich einmischen“ (to interfere) the reflexive „sich“ comes first and „zu“ sits inside: einzumischen.
grammar.example: Die hat nur zugeschaut, ohne sich einzumischen, und alles aufgeschrieben.
grammar.title: Ohne … zu with a reflexive, separable verb

paragraphs: Am 6. Januar 1907 hat Maria Montessori einen Raum für ungefähr fünfzig kleine Kinder eröffnet, in San Lorenzo, einem armen Viertel von Rom. Und das in einem nagelneuen Mietshaus für Familien mit wenig Geld.
Und jetzt kommt's: Sie war gar keine Lehrerin, sondern Ärztin. 1896 hatte sie als eine der ersten Frauen in Italien ihr Medizinstudium abgeschlossen.

Die Eltern haben den ganzen Tag gearbeitet, also waren die Drei- bis Sechsjährigen praktisch auf sich gestellt. Montessori hat die schweren Möbel rausbringen lassen und Tische und Stühle reingestellt, die so leicht waren, dass die Kinder sie tragen konnten.

Plötzlich konnte ein dreijähriges Kind bestimmen, wo es sitzt und was es macht: Wasser eingießen, fegen, sich die Hände waschen. Und Montessori? Die hat nur zugeschaut, ohne sich einzumischen, und alles aufgeschrieben.
Ihre Methode hat sich weltweit verbreitet, und sie hat noch bis zu ihrem Tod 1952 daran gearbeitet. Zu Hause kannst du mit einer Kanne und einem Besen anfangen, die in Kinderhände passen.

stories.summary: 1907 hat eine Ärztin in Rom ungefähr fünfzig kleinen Kindern Stühle gegeben, die sie selbst tragen konnten, und dabei herausgefunden, was Kinder machen, wenn sie es sich aussuchen dürfen.
stories.title: Der kleine Stuhl

grammar.body: Spanish says what someone is without "un" or "una": es médica, not es una médica. The noun also agrees with the person: médico for a man, médica for a woman.
grammar.example: Maria Montessori es médica.
grammar.title: No article before a profession

grammar.body: In speech, "hasta" before a noun means "even": hasta un niño = even a child. After poder the next verb stays in the infinitive: puede llevar = can carry.
grammar.example: ¡Hasta un niño de tres años puede llevar una silla!
grammar.title: Hasta for "even"

grammar.body: With a reflexive verb, Spanish uses the article for parts of the body, not "sus": se lavan las manos = they wash their hands.
grammar.example: Sirven agua, barren el suelo y se lavan las manos.
grammar.title: Se lavan las manos: reflexive verb, no possessive

paragraphs: Pues mira, es el 6 de enero de 1907, en Roma. Maria Montessori es médica. Abre una sala para niños pequeños: sus padres trabajan todo el día.
Las sillas y las mesas son pequeñas y ligeras. ¡Hasta un niño de tres años puede llevar una silla! Los niños eligen qué hacer.
Sirven agua, barren el suelo y se lavan las manos. Maria solo mira y lo apunta todo.
Hoy muchas escuelas de todo el mundo usan sus ideas. ¿Y en casa? Empieza con una jarra pequeña.

grammar.body: For actions repeated day after day, Spanish uses the imperfect: -ía/-ían for -er and -ir verbs (servían, barrían, elegían), -aba/-aban for -ar verbs (miraba, apuntaba). One-off events take the pretérito: llegaron, consiguió.
grammar.example: Los niños servían agua, barrían el suelo y elegían qué hacer.
grammar.title: Imperfect for what happened again and again

grammar.body: For an ability that lasted in the past, Spanish uses the imperfect podía, where English says "could"; the next verb stays in the infinitive.
grammar.example: Un niño de tres años ya podía llevar una silla y elegir dónde sentarse.
grammar.title: Podía: what someone was able to do

grammar.body: "La verdad es que" (literally "the truth is that") is how Spanish speakers say "actually" or "to be honest" before a surprising fact.
grammar.example: La verdad es que no era maestra: era médica.
grammar.title: La verdad es que: "actually" in talk

paragraphs: El 6 de enero de 1907, en Roma, Maria Montessori abrió una sala para niños. Fue en San Lorenzo, un barrio pobre de la ciudad.
La verdad es que no era maestra: era médica. En 1896 fue una de las primeras mujeres de Italia en graduarse en medicina.
Llegaron unos cincuenta niños pequeños: sus padres tenían que trabajar todo el día. Maria les consiguió sillas y mesas pequeñas y ligeras.
Un niño de tres años ya podía llevar una silla y elegir dónde sentarse. Los niños servían agua, barrían el suelo y elegían qué hacer. Maria solo los miraba y lo apuntaba todo.
Su forma de enseñar dio la vuelta al mundo. ¿Y en casa? Pues empieza con una jarra y una escoba pequeñas.

grammar.body: "Pasarse el día" + gerund (-ando, -iendo) is the everyday way to say someone spends the whole day doing something: se pasaban el día trabajando = they worked all day long.
grammar.example: Llegaron unos cincuenta niños de tres a seis años, porque sus padres se pasaban el día trabajando.
grammar.title: Pasarse el día + gerund

grammar.body: "Tan + adjective + que" links a quality to what it makes possible: tan ligeras que podían moverlas = so light that they could move them.
grammar.example: Maria quitó los muebles pesados y trajo mesas y sillas pequeñas, tan ligeras que los niños podían moverlas.
grammar.title: Tan + adjective + que for a result

grammar.body: "Seguir" + gerund says that an action went on without stopping: siguió trabajando = she kept working. Seguir changes e to i in the pretérito: siguió.
grammar.example: Su método se extendió por todo el mundo, y ella siguió trabajando en él hasta que murió en 1952.
grammar.title: Seguir + gerund: going on doing something

paragraphs: El 6 de enero de 1907, Maria Montessori abrió una sala para niños pequeños en San Lorenzo, en Roma. Estaba en un edificio nuevo para familias pobres.
Ni siquiera era maestra: era médica. En 1896 fue una de las primeras mujeres de Italia en graduarse en medicina.

Llegaron unos cincuenta niños de tres a seis años, porque sus padres se pasaban el día trabajando. Maria quitó los muebles pesados y trajo mesas y sillas pequeñas, tan ligeras que los niños podían moverlas.
Y claro, ahora un niño de tres años podía llevar una silla y decidir dónde sentarse. Los niños servían agua, barrían y elegían qué hacer, mientras Maria solo miraba y tomaba notas.
Su método se extendió por todo el mundo, y ella siguió trabajando en él hasta que murió en 1952. En casa, para empezar, basta con una jarra y una escoba pequeñas.

grammar.body: After a negative, Spanish corrects with "sino", not "pero": no era maestra, sino médica answers what the listener might expect of someone opening a school.
grammar.example: Y aquí viene lo bueno: no era maestra, sino médica.
grammar.title: No … sino …: correcting an expectation

grammar.body: "Mandar + infinitive" means you have someone else do it: mandó sacar los muebles = she had the furniture taken out. After "para que" in a past sentence the verb goes in the imperfect subjunctive: pudieran.
grammar.example: Montessori mandó sacar los muebles pesados y trajo mesas y sillas ligeras, para que pudieran llevarlas ellos mismos.
grammar.title: Mandar + infinitive, para que + subjunctive

grammar.body: Había + participle puts one past event before another: by 1907 she had already qualified as a doctor, back in 1896. "Ya" (already) often comes with it in speech.
grammar.example: Ya en 1896 se había graduado en medicina: fue una de las primeras mujeres de Italia en hacerlo.
grammar.title: Se había graduado: the pluperfect

paragraphs: El 6 de enero de 1907, Maria Montessori abrió una sala para unos cincuenta niños pequeños en San Lorenzo, un barrio pobre de Roma. Estaba en un edificio recién estrenado para familias humildes.
Y aquí viene lo bueno: no era maestra, sino médica. Ya en 1896 se había graduado en medicina: fue una de las primeras mujeres de Italia en hacerlo.

Los padres de los niños trabajaban todo el día, así que esos pequeños de tres a seis años estaban prácticamente solos. Montessori mandó sacar los muebles pesados y trajo mesas y sillas ligeras, para que pudieran llevarlas ellos mismos.
De repente, un niño de tres años podía elegir dónde sentarse y qué hacer: servir agua, barrer el suelo, lavarse las manos. Montessori se limitaba a mirar, sin meterse, y apuntaba todo lo que veía.
Su método dio la vuelta al mundo, y ella seguía trabajando en él cuando murió en 1952. En casa, todo empieza con una jarra y una escoba a la medida de un niño.

stories.summary: En 1907, una médica de Roma les dio a unos cincuenta niños pequeños sillas que podían llevar ellos solos, y descubrió qué hacen los niños cuando pueden elegir.
stories.title: La silla pequeña

grammar.body: In everyday Italian you say what someone does for a living with fare + the article + the job: fa il medico = she is a doctor.
grammar.example: Maria Montessori fa il medico.
grammar.title: Fare il + profession

grammar.body: "Può" (from potere) says what someone is able to do, and the next verb stays in the infinitive: può portare = can carry. "Anche" in front means "even".
grammar.example: Anche un bambino di tre anni può portare una sedia!
grammar.title: Potere + infinitive: can

grammar.body: At the end of a sentence, "e basta" says that this is all someone does: guarda e scrive tutto, e basta = she just watches and writes it all down. It is one of the commonest little phrases of spoken Italian.
grammar.example: Maria guarda e scrive tutto, e basta.
grammar.title: E basta: just, and nothing else

paragraphs: Allora, siamo a Roma, il 6 gennaio 1907. Maria Montessori fa il medico. Apre una stanza per bambini piccoli: i genitori lavorano tutto il giorno.
Le sedie e i tavoli sono piccoli e leggeri. Anche un bambino di tre anni può portare una sedia! E i bambini scelgono da soli cosa fare.
Versano l'acqua, spazzano il pavimento e si lavano le mani. Maria guarda e scrive tutto, e basta.
Oggi tante scuole in tutto il mondo usano le sue idee. A casa, comincia con una brocca piccola.

grammar.body: Essere forms its passato prossimo with itself, and the participle agrees with the subject: lei è stata, lui è stato, loro sono stati.
grammar.example: Nel 1896 è stata una delle prime donne in Italia a laurearsi in medicina.
grammar.title: È stata: essere in the passato prossimo

grammar.body: When a direct object pronoun comes before avere, the participle agrees with it: li ha guardati (i bambini), l'ha presa (la sedia).
grammar.example: Maria li ha solo guardati e ha scritto tutto quello che facevano.
grammar.title: Li ha guardati: agreement after lo, la, li, le

grammar.body: The passato prossimo tells what happened (ha aperto, sono arrivati); the imperfect describes how things were and what was possible at the time: poteva = could, voleva = wanted.
grammar.example: Così un bambino di tre anni poteva prendere una sedia e sedersi dove voleva.
grammar.title: Poteva, voleva: the imperfect for the background

paragraphs: Allora, il 6 gennaio 1907 Maria Montessori ha aperto una stanza per bambini a San Lorenzo, a Roma. Era un quartiere povero.
In realtà non era per niente una maestra: era un medico. Nel 1896 è stata una delle prime donne in Italia a laurearsi in medicina.
Sono arrivati una cinquantina di bambini piccoli, perché i genitori lavoravano tutto il giorno. Per loro Maria ha preso apposta sedie e tavoli piccoli e leggeri.

Così un bambino di tre anni poteva prendere una sedia e sedersi dove voleva. I bambini hanno versato l'acqua, spazzato il pavimento e scelto da soli cosa fare. Maria li ha solo guardati e ha scritto tutto quello che facevano.
E il suo modo di insegnare ha fatto il giro del mondo. A casa, comincia con una brocca piccola e una scopa piccola.

grammar.body: The trapassato prossimo (imperfect of essere or avere + past participle) puts one past event before another: by 1907 she had already graduated, in 1896. Laurearsi is reflexive, so it takes essere.
grammar.example: Era un medico: si era laureata in medicina nel 1896, tra le prime donne in Italia.
grammar.title: Si era laureata: the trapassato prossimo

grammar.body: "Così + adjective + che" gives a quality and its result in one go: così leggeri che i bambini potevano spostarli = so light that the children could move them.
grammar.example: Via i mobili pesanti: Maria ha messo tavoli e sedie piccoli, così leggeri che i bambini potevano spostarli.
grammar.title: Così … che: so … that

grammar.body: "Mentre" (while) joins two things going on at the same time; both sides take the imperfect because they describe ongoing, repeated actions: versavano, stava a guardare.
grammar.example: I bambini versavano l'acqua, spazzavano e sceglievano da soli cosa fare, mentre Maria stava a guardare e prendeva appunti.
grammar.title: Mentre + imperfect: at the same time

paragraphs: Il 6 gennaio 1907 Maria Montessori ha aperto una stanza per bambini piccoli a San Lorenzo, a Roma. Era in un palazzo nuovo, costruito apposta per le famiglie povere.
Pensa, non era nemmeno una maestra. Era un medico: si era laureata in medicina nel 1896, tra le prime donne in Italia.

Sono arrivati una cinquantina di bambini dai tre ai sei anni, perché i genitori lavoravano tutto il giorno. Via i mobili pesanti: Maria ha messo tavoli e sedie piccoli, così leggeri che i bambini potevano spostarli.

A quel punto un bambino di tre anni poteva prendere una sedia e decidere dove sedersi. I bambini versavano l'acqua, spazzavano e sceglievano da soli cosa fare, mentre Maria stava a guardare e prendeva appunti.
Il suo metodo ha fatto il giro del mondo, e lei ci ha lavorato fino alla morte, nel 1952. A casa, per cominciare, bastano una brocca piccola e una scopa piccola.

grammar.body: "Fare + infinitive" means someone arranges an action that others carry out: ha fatto portare via i mobili = she had the furniture taken out. "Perché" + subjunctive (potessero) means "so that".
grammar.example: La Montessori ha fatto portare via i mobili pesanti e ha messo tavoli e sedie abbastanza leggeri perché i bambini potessero portarli.
grammar.title: Fare + infinitive: having something done

grammar.body: The trapassato prossimo (era stata = she had been) sets an earlier past event behind the main story; in speech it is the everyday way to say "she'd been".
grammar.example: Era un medico, e già nel 1896 era stata una delle prime donne in Italia a laurearsi in medicina.
grammar.title: Era stata: one past before another

grammar.body: Where English says "without" + -ing, Italian uses senza + the infinitive: senza intervenire. "Se ne stava lì a guardare" is the spoken way to say she just stood there watching and did nothing else.
grammar.example: La Montessori se ne stava lì a guardare, senza mai intervenire, e si segnava tutto quello che vedeva.
grammar.title: Senza + infinitive, starsene lì a + infinitive

paragraphs: Il 6 gennaio 1907 Maria Montessori ha aperto una stanza per una cinquantina di bambini piccoli a San Lorenzo, un quartiere povero di Roma. Era in un palazzo di case popolari nuovo di zecca.
Ed ecco il bello: non era affatto una maestra. Era un medico, e già nel 1896 era stata una delle prime donne in Italia a laurearsi in medicina.

Erano bambini tra i tre e i sei anni, con i genitori al lavoro tutto il giorno: in pratica, restavano da soli. La Montessori ha fatto portare via i mobili pesanti e ha messo tavoli e sedie abbastanza leggeri perché i bambini potessero portarli.

Di colpo un bambino di tre anni poteva scegliere dove sedersi e cosa fare: versare l'acqua, spazzare il pavimento, lavarsi le mani. La Montessori se ne stava lì a guardare, senza mai intervenire, e si segnava tutto quello che vedeva.
Il suo metodo si è diffuso in tutto il mondo, e lei ci stava ancora lavorando quando è morta, nel 1952. A casa puoi cominciare da una brocca e una scopa a misura di bambino.

stories.summary: Nel 1907 una dottoressa di Roma ha dato a una cinquantina di bambini piccoli delle sedie che riuscivano a portare da soli, e ha scoperto cosa fanno i bimbi quando possono scegliere.
stories.title: La piccola sedia

grammar.body: "More men … than anywhere else" compares one place with all the others.
grammar.example: More men die of heart disease here than anywhere else.
grammar.title: More … than: comparing

grammar.body: "No" before a noun means "not any"; "just" here means "only".
grammar.example: He has no new pill, just a plan.
grammar.title: No + noun, just + noun

paragraphs: So it's 1972, in North Karelia, in Finland. More men die of heart disease here than anywhere else. Families are scared.
They ask for help, and a young doctor comes: Pekka Puska. He has no new pill, just a plan.
Almost everyone puts butter on their bread. Slowly, people change to a plant spread and low-fat milk. They eat less salt and more vegetables and berries.
Years later, far fewer men die of heart disease. Ask your doctor about salt.

grammar.body: Regular verbs add -ed (asked, changed); many common verbs are irregular (had, came, went, put, ate).
grammar.example: The next year a young doctor, Pekka Puska, came with a team.
grammar.title: The past simple: regular and irregular

grammar.body: The past negative is didn't + the base verb: he didn't bring, not "he didn't brought".
grammar.example: Actually, he didn't bring any new medicine.
grammar.title: Didn't + verb

paragraphs: In the 1960s, North Karelia in Finland had a sad record. More men died of heart disease there than anywhere else in the world.
People were scared, so in 1971 they asked the government for help. The next year a young doctor, Pekka Puska, came with a team.
Actually, he didn't bring any new medicine. He went to the shops, the dairies and the bakers instead.
Back then, almost everyone put butter on their bread. Slowly, people changed to plant spreads and low-fat milk. They ate less salt and more vegetables.
By 2014, deaths from heart disease in middle age were down by more than 80 percent. Talk to your doctor about salt and fat.

grammar.body: "So that" + a clause gives the reason for an action: what they wanted to happen.
grammar.example: They worked with shops, dairies, bakers, schools and farmers, so that the healthy choice became the easy one.
grammar.title: So that: saying the purpose

grammar.body: "Had" + past participle looks back from a point in the past (2014) to what happened before it.
grammar.example: By 2014, deaths from heart disease in middle age had fallen by 84 percent, and the whole country had copied the idea.
grammar.title: The past perfect: had fallen, had copied

paragraphs: In the 1960s, North Karelia in eastern Finland had a terrible record: more men died of heart disease there than anywhere else. Families were frightened.
In 1971 the region's leaders asked the government for help, and in 1972 a young doctor, Pekka Puska, started the North Karelia Project.
But they didn't hand out pills. They worked with shops, dairies, bakers, schools and farmers, so that the healthy choice became the easy one.
In 1972, nearly nine in ten people put butter on their bread; forty years later it was fewer than one in ten. People switched to plant spreads, used less salt and ate more vegetables and berries.
By 2014, deaths from heart disease in middle age had fallen by 84 percent, and the whole country had copied the idea. Want to change your habits? Talk to your doctor first.

grammar.body: "A lovely place to live": the to-infinitive after a noun says what the place is like for doing something.
grammar.example: Back in the 1960s, North Karelia, in Finland, was a lovely place to live and a dangerous place to be a man.
grammar.title: A … place to + verb

grammar.body: A spoken way to announce the surprising point that comes next.
grammar.example: And here's the thing: the push came from the people themselves.
grammar.title: "Here's the thing" in speech

grammar.body: "On" after a length of time means "later": forty years on = forty years later.
grammar.example: In 1972 nearly nine in ten people spread butter on their bread; forty years on, it was fewer than one in ten.
grammar.title: Forty years on

paragraphs: Back in the 1960s, North Karelia, in Finland, was a lovely place to live and a dangerous place to be a man. More men died of heart disease there than anywhere else on earth.
And here's the thing: the push came from the people themselves. In January 1971 local leaders signed a petition asking the government to act.
